stories.Headline: Anthropic files to go public at a valuation of up to $2 trillion
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed to go public on October 26, 2026, and reports put its valuation between $1.5 and $2 trillion, according to the Darden Report. Three days later, Alphabet lost nearly 13% of its value in a single day, about $500 billion, on worries about whether its AI spending will pay off. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spoke at a JPMorgan Chase investor event on Friday, November 13, 2026, outlining a future in which AI could help make diseases such as cancer and Alzheimer's relics of the past. Amodei told JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon that AI could devise entirely new markets in scientific research, robotics, and cybersecurity. The offering is expected to begin trading on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and Anthropic seeks a valuation of approximately $1.3 trillion to $1.4 trillion.

UVA Darden professors Mike Lenox and Alex Cowan propose that any firm training AI models on unlicensed material, or building on a model that used unlicensed data, must release the weights of those models to the public once a year. Firms keep a lead of six to 18 months, or about a year on average, and the IPOs still happen. The proposal aims to advance competition, safety and fairness, and the professors say the time to adopt it is before AI companies go public. The articles cite patchy rules like the EU AI Act and California's SB 53, and note that under Nasdaq's new fast-entry rules a newly public company of significant size can join the Nasdaq 100 after 15 trading days. The professors say the rule should be given two or three release cycles, 24 to 36 months, since releases happen once a year, then market concentration and prices should be checked.

Amodei said he hopes the company will "underpromise and overdeliver," and that Anthropic is not super fussed on when exactly, what month or what day or what market conditions it goes public into. Lenox and Cowan say the big IPOs are net positive because they broaden ownership and require greater transparency from the firms. The professors say to the public that people should try their proposal first and, if it isn't enough, ask for more, and to insiders that it is their best bet for avoiding something heavier. They say they don't think the timing concern is a reason to stop the IPOs, but it is a reason to settle the rules first. They also say that if market concentration and prices haven't moved after the trial period, the public should ask for more, and they would be the first to say so.

Thomas Raymond, a founding partner of Callan Family Office, said his firm is seeking an allocation in Anthropic's IPO through Charles Schwab, arguing the offering is more attractive than SpaceX's blockbuster listing "simply because of the valuation." Raymond acknowledged that investor enthusiasm has changed since June and said he wouldn't attempt to purchase shares on the open market. He said there is no escaping the fact that the halo isn't as formidable for all things AI now as compared to three or four months ago. The articles say bankers marketing the IPO faced a turbulent backdrop as Treasury yields surged and a widespread Microsoft Outlook outage hampered communications, during the sudden ousting of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company is among Anthropic's biggest investors and chip suppliers. The articles say the people with a direct financial stake in how AI is governed are a fairly small group of founders, employees and investors, and that once the stock lands in index funds, pensions and retirement accounts of the 62% of Americans who own stock, every rule that touches AI's value has tens of millions of people on the other side of it.

The Darden Report says there are two approaches to govern AI now: the status quo of patchy rules with safety left to a few firms policing themselves and creators paid one lawsuit at a time, and heavy government involvement through licensing, a new regulatory agency, steep taxes or a government stake. In a survey of 2,778 AI researchers, the median respondent put the chance that AI leads to human extinction, or something similarly permanent, at 5%, and between 38% and 51% put the chance of a generally bad outcome at 10% or more. In March, a record 59% of voters told NBC News that the economic and political systems are stacked against people like them, and economists Daron Acemoglu and Pascual Restrepo estimate that automation accounts for 50, 70% of the change in the U.S. wage structure over the last four decades. In 2024, a federal judge ruled that Google holds an illegal monopoly in general search, while nobody owns the protocols that move data across the internet, or Linux, which runs most of the world's websites. Since 1980, average price markups in the U.S. have risen from 18% above marginal cost to 67% now, and in five national polls this year between 55% and 77% of Americans said AI is moving too fast or should slow down, while in the AP-NORC poll just 8% said it is moving too slowly.

In the early 2000s, software vendors sat on reported vulnerabilities for a year or more, sometimes never disclosing them, and today the standard is coordinated disclosure, with Google's Project Zero settling on a 90-day deadline. By 2019, Project Zero reported that 97.7% of the issues it found were fixed inside that window, and a patent gives an inventor about 20 years of exclusivity in exchange for publishing how the invention works. The lobbies of JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and Goldman Sachs have been decorated to welcome Anthropic, though the displays are more restrained than the digital images of rockets that greeted visitors during SpaceX's June IPO, or the meteorite exhibit at JPMorgan's new midtown Manhattan headquarters. At Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two banks leading the offering, Anthropic executives met with institutional investors earlier this week, and Goldman is planning an event next week for wealth management clients where bank president John Waldron is expected to interview Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and CFO Krishna Rao. Evercore ISI analysts estimate Anthropic's IPO will generate approximately $395 million in underwriting fees, compared with the roughly $500 million fee pool from SpaceX's June listing, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley each collecting approximately $79 million and JPMorgan, Citigroup and Bank of America earning roughly $44 million each.

stories.Headline: Telus ends its role in two planned Vancouver AI data centres
stories.Summary:
Telus Corp. announced on Sunday that it is ending its participation in two planned artificial intelligence data centres in Vancouver. The company decided to pull out of these projects after facing heavy local opposition and shifting its investment strategy. Telus had previously agreed in May to co-develop these facilities with the real estate developer Westbank Corp. The decision follows a period of protests during the summer where hundreds of people called for cancellations. These projects were intended to meet growing demand for computing power among Canadian businesses and the government.

The plan included a new ten storey building at 150 West Georgia Street and converting the M3 office building at 111 East 5th Avenue. The Mount Pleasant facility was expected to open by late 2026, while the downtown build was slated for 2029. Telus planned to use 63,000 Nvidia Corp. chips and draw up to 163 megawatts of electricity for the two sites. The M3 building is a 26 megawatt facility, and the total network capacity was expected to exceed 150 megawatts by 2032. These projects fall under Prime Minister Mark Carney's Enabling Large-Scale Sovereign AI Data Centres initiative.

Spokesperson Richard Gilhooley stated that the company decided not to proceed with the two Vancouver projects. He noted that Telus will continue expanding its existing facility in Kamloops, British Columbia, to 20 megawatts by 2028. Gilhooley said new sites will scale capacity to meet demand using clean, renewable energy and industry leading power efficiency. A source familiar with the matter added that the level of local opposition made it challenging to proceed. Telus remains open to future opportunities at these sites while evaluating new partnerships and locations for sovereign compute.

Hundreds of protesters raised concerns about the environmental, community, and housing impacts of the proposed data centres. A city councillor proposed a November motion that could require independent environmental assessments and possible fees for data centre owners. Westbank Corp. confirmed the departure of Telus but stated it will continue developing the centres with a new partner. The federal government, through Minister Evan Solomon, touted Telus as a key part of reducing reliance on U.S. providers. The government remains focused on building domestic computing infrastructure for the public sector, researchers, and Canadian companies.

The projects were among the last initiatives of former CEO Darren Entwistle, who retired in June after 26 years. Entwistle and Minister Solomon signed a memorandum of understanding to develop the projects to ensure national security. New CEO Victor Dodig has since altered the company course by selling assets and cutting the dividend. Dodig is shifting the strategy toward leveraging existing fibre networks and assessing data centre shells with secured power. The federal government is targeting 500 megawatts of new domestic processing capacity using backstop and offtake agreements.

Westbank will proceed with the Vancouver projects using a new partner that has not yet been publicly announced. The M3 building application faces a formal public consultation period running from December 2 to 15, 2026. Telus will release more details about its updated AI infrastructure strategy in the coming months. The articles leave open whether the new partner will face the same local opposition as Telus. It remains unclear if the federal government will provide the same support to the new partnership.

stories.Headline: Shenzhen launches AI action plan to increase technological cooperation across the Asia-Pacific region
stories.Summary:
Shenzhen released an AI action plan in September to boost technological cooperation with partners across the Asia-Pacific region. The city is preparing to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19. This event focuses on building an Asia-Pacific community to prosper together through shared innovation and growth. Local firms like EngineAI Robotics Technology Co., Ltd. are testing robot movement for future agricultural use. These efforts aim to expand overseas by developing new applications with local partners in various countries.

The 2026-2028 plan requires stronger cooperation with ASEAN and Belt and Road Initiative countries on software and hardware. Shenzhen's core AI industry earned 220 billion yuan in 2025 with over 2,600 enterprises above designated size. Trade with APEC economies reached 1.98 trillion yuan in early 2026, which is 33 percent higher annually. The city exported 8.27 billion yuan of 3D-printing equipment in early 2026, an increase of 127.5 percent. A new center in Qianhai, Shenzhen, will promote APEC cooperation regarding the flow of cross-border data.

Hu Zhenyu said the AI industry is now bringing entire industrial chains to overseas markets instead of products. Yao Qiyuan noted that robot fighting tests capabilities that could later help harvest oil palm fruit in Malaysia. Bai Xue stated that integrated supply chains and AI innovation have boosted the competitiveness of Chinese 3D printers. Shi Xiaoliang hopes APEC will allow SmartMore Corporation to deepen talent exchanges and share China's practical AI experience. Yang Qian said open-source technologies are lowering barriers for the digital transformation of small and medium enterprises.

Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for over 97 percent of businesses and half of the private output. These smaller firms are affected by the shift toward affordable and easy-to-deploy digital products and AI solutions. SmartMore Corporation has served over 730 enterprises worldwide, including partners in Japan, the Republic of Korea, and Southeast Asia. APEC's 21 member economies house 3 billion people and represent 61.6 percent of the global real GDP. Eduardo Pedrosa said Shenzhen's research and innovation can benefit the entire region and the rest of the world.

The APEC Artificial Intelligence Initiative for 2026-2030 was adopted in 2025 to foster resilient and secure economic growth. On July 23, ministers in Chengdu adopted the Chengdu Statement to promote AI transformation in agriculture and services. China announced in July that it would provide 5,000 AI training opportunities for developing countries over five years. The Huaqiangbei electronics market now attracts visitors interested in AI glasses, 3D printers, and various humanoid robots. Ni Yueju suggested that Northeast Asian cooperation should start with smart manufacturing and in-vehicle AI applications.

China will establish the Qianhai center as an open platform for regulatory alignment, policy research, and business services. The city will continue to implement its AI action plan through the end of the year 2028. Future cooperation may include green computing, public data sharing, and improving the resilience of regional technology supply chains. The articles leave open how specific regulatory alignments will be reached between the different APEC member economies. It remains unclear how the 5,000 AI training opportunities will be distributed among the various developing countries.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid scandal before Shenzhen Apec summit
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive of Nvidia on November 12. He left the company after reports revealed affairs with a female executive and a suspected Chinese spy. This scandal occurred just before a major CEO summit in Shenzhen, China. The event is hosted by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum on November 17 and 18. These events have complicated the economic relationship between the United States and China.

The summit involves meetings between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and possibly Vladimir Putin on November 19. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will participate in a bilateral dialogue regarding artificial intelligence. The US has banned advanced AI chips, like the Blackwell, from reaching China. In January, the Trump administration allowed sales of the less powerful H200 chip to China. Oracle cancelled a US$7 billion contract giving Tencent access to AI chips in South-east Asia.

Chinese ambassador Xie Feng expressed high hopes for major-power cooperation at the Shenzhen summit. He promoted a China-led AI alliance called Waico to foster regional prosperity. President Xi Jinping has consistently described openness and cooperation as the way to achieve prosperity. He urged regional economies to keep global supply chains stable and avoid protectionism. The Communist Party publication Qiushi highlighted these themes through a series of previous Apec speeches.

China hawks in Congress are using the scandal to push three Bills restricting technology exports. US tech executives will likely press for more leniency for their companies in China. Some observers, including Ryan Hass of the Brookings Institution, have low expectations for big changes. Paul Triolo noted that US cloud giants like Microsoft and Amazon could face scrutiny in 2027. Chris Miller stated that chip rules are more likely to tighten after the midterms.

China has required senior AI researchers at firms like Alibaba and DeepSeek to get travel approval. Regulators blocked SoftBank's US$5.4 billion acquisition of a robotics firm and ordered Meta to unwind a deal. The US provided over US$2.5 billion in loans to companies like MP Materials and USA Rare Earth. A trade truce from Busan, South Korea, saw tariffs fall to 30 per cent in May 2025. The countries also announced a 30-for-30 deal to lower barriers on US$30 billion of mutual exports.

The Busan agreement is set to expire on January 10, 2027, potentially resuming the trade war. The US may take new offensive measures, such as financial sanctions, against various Chinese companies. China could retaliate by restricting access to rare earths and powerful magnets used in fighter jets. Xi Jinping previously ordered military forces to be ready for a Taiwan invasion by 2027. Articles leave open whether a great power war or an AI-enabled cyberattack will occur.

stories.Summary:
US officials launched a fresh regulatory probe into Alibaba Group Holding on November 15, 2026. This investigation focuses on allegations involving the CEO of Nvidia and various Alibaba cloud partners. Regulators are reviewing claims that Alibaba linked data centers provided remote access to advanced AI chips. These specific Nvidia processors are currently subject to strict US export controls. The probe examines if cloud access allowed Chinese clients to use restricted hardware.

The investigation looks at whether cloud access bypassed the need for direct chip shipments to China. This scrutiny affects Alibaba Cloud, which provides infrastructure for merchants and enterprises in China and abroad. The company has a three year AI and cloud capex plan totaling RMB 380b. T Head has shipped 470,000 AI chips as part of this broader technology strategy. Alibaba also targets an ARR of RMB 16b plus for model and application services during 2026.

US regulators are responsible for the probe and are examining the company's cloud relationships. They are reviewing whether remote access to restricted Nvidia processors violated existing export rules. Officials are investigating if these arrangements allowed restricted AI hardware to reach Chinese users. The probe focuses on the link between technology capabilities and the broader retail platform. Regulators want to know if cloud-based access served as a loophole for restricted chips.

Business customers using Alibaba's core cloud services are affected by this potential threat to hardware access. If regulators close remote access, Alibaba may need to rework how AI workloads are provisioned. The company might have to adjust which customers it serves from specific data centers. This could lead to higher operational costs or lower performance for some cloud services. AI lab losses and negative free cash flow could remain in focus for longer.

Alibaba runs a large commerce ecosystem and provides cloud infrastructure for many global enterprises. The company utilizes T Head for chip shipments to support its AI and cloud goals. Its financial narrative relies on turning massive capex spending into profitable model and cloud services. The business is currently valued at a fair value of 186 dollars by some analysts. This operational risk sits primarily within the Alibaba Cloud division of the company.

Investors should watch upcoming quarterly reports for explicit commentary on US export rules. T Head Hong Kong listing documents may also provide signals regarding chip sourcing and capex. The articles leave open whether regulators will actually block remote access to Nvidia processors. It is unclear if Alibaba will successfully meet its 2026 revenue targets for AI services. The final outcome of the probe into the Nvidia CEO remains an open question.

stories.Headline: 42Gears earns ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system
stories.Summary:
42Gears announced on November 13, 2026, that it had achieved certification to ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the international standard for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems. The company made the announcement from Bengaluru, Karnataka, according to a GlobeNewswire release dated November 13, 2026. The certification followed a rigorous independent audit conducted by the British Standards Institution, known as BSI. 42Gears is described in the announcement as a global leader in Unified Endpoint Management. The certification recognizes 42Gears for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving structured governance across its AI-enabled enterprise capabilities.

The certification covers 42Gears' role as a producer, provider, and user of AI systems integrated within its flagship SureMDM platform. This includes the use of third-party large language models to deliver AI-powered unified endpoint management services across Banking and Financial Services, Healthcare and Life Sciences, Industrial and Supply Chain Operations, and Consumer and Commercial Services. The certification demonstrates that 42Gears embeds accountability, transparency, and human oversight across the AI lifecycle. It also establishes governance frameworks for the responsible development, deployment, and use of AI technologies, including the adoption and use of large language models. The certification complements 42Gears' existing portfolio, including ISO/IEC 27001, SOC 2 Type II, PCI DSS, and HIPAA compliance programs.

Onkar Singh, Co-founder and CEO of 42Gears, said enterprise IT teams want the efficiency and intelligence of AI but not at the expense of security, transparency, or regulatory compliance. Singh said achieving the ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification validates the company's commitment to responsible AI innovation. He said customers in banking, healthcare, and mission-critical operations can deploy SureMDM's AI capabilities knowing they are backed by internationally audited governance and strict human oversight. The announcement states that the certification provides verified assurance that SureMDM's AI management framework meets rigorous international compliance benchmarks. It also states that the certification enforces clear accountability mechanisms and human oversight controls over AI-assisted decision-making and workflows.

The announcement states that the certification establishes a structured methodology for identifying, evaluating, and mitigating AI-related risks across the entire deployment lifecycle. It states that the certification ensures strict security, privacy, and vendor oversight protocols when leveraging external large language models. The announcement says the certification offers heightened confidence for organizations operating in heavily regulated industries. 42Gears products are used by more than 23,000 customers across more than 170 countries. The products are available through more than 1,000 global partners, in cloud and on-premises deployments across all major mobile, desktop, and specialized operating systems.

42Gears is described as a trusted authority in Unified Endpoint Management and Security, delivering one strategy to manage, secure, and empower diverse, complex technology environments. The company says it goes beyond traditional MDM and RMM, enabling IT teams and managed service providers to start where they are and grow without switching. It says this helps scale from endpoint management and Zero Trust security to identity and access management, automation, and self-healing technology. The announcement lists key benefits including independently audited AI governance and governed third-party LLM integration. It also lists end-to-end risk and impact assessment, transparency and human oversight, and a comprehensive compliance posture.

The announcement does not state when the audit began or how long it took. It does not give the cost of the certification or say whether it must be renewed. It does not name the auditors who conducted the BSI review or describe any findings. It does not say which specific third-party large language models 42Gears uses within SureMDM. It does not give a date for when the certified AI capabilities became available to customers.

stories.Headline: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent demands answers from Nvidia over AI chip sales to China
stories.Summary:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia on Sunday, November 15, 2026, to explain its chip sales to China. He wants to know if the company knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach the Chinese market. This demand follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang three days before the Treasury chief spoke on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures. Bessent is investigating if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips. The US government forbids these sales to stay ahead of China in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

President Donald Trump authorized sales of H200 chips to the Chinese in late 2025, but not the most advanced models. Bessent stated that nothing above the H200s can be sold to China, including the banned Blackwell and Rubin GPUs. The investigation focuses on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company where Alice Huang, the alleged lover of Jensen Huang, worked. The US suspects Megaspeed bought Nvidia chips for Southeast Asian data centers and then routed those chips into China. Bessent wants answers and an internal investigation into Jensen Huang's behavior within the next 10 days.

Scott Bessent said it is more important to examine Nvidia's culture of compliance than Jensen Huang's affair with a spy. He questioned who knew about the obvious shell companies and if Nvidia used them as a workaround for export controls. Bessent believes that anyone at the company responsible for these actions must be held accountable for the suspected illegal sales. He also suggested that the Commerce Department, run by Howard Lutnick, failed by not blacklisting the company known as Megaspeed. Bessent noted that many other government departments had pushed for the blacklisting of the Singaporean firm before the Commerce Department.

The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe into whether chips were unlawfully rerouted or smuggled into China. Nvidia refuted allegations last year, stating it had already investigated the claims, but the FBI is now looking into the affair. Data center operators in Southeast Asia may face stricter checks on purchases of advanced US chips due to these recent developments. Senators have summoned Jensen Huang to testify before the Banking Committee next month, and Howard Lutnick has also agreed to testify. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify behind closed doors in the House of Representatives before the Thanksgiving holiday.

Nvidia dominates the global market for high-end data center chips with an estimated share of around 80 percent of the industry. The company is known for GPUs that power AI chatbots, autonomous vehicles, delivery robots, and the proprietary CUDA software toolkit. In Singapore, the Aspire 2B national research supercomputer uses more than 1,500 H200 GPUs to help over 9,000 public researchers. Competitors include Intel, AMD, and Chinese firms like Cambricon and Huawei, which is accelerating its next-generation chips for a 2027 debut. Hyperscalers like Google, Microsoft, and Amazon have also developed their own in-house chipsets to perform specific AI training tasks.

Nvidia is due to publish its quarterly results on Tuesday, while Bessent urges the company to pick an outsider as CEO. The US administration will ultimately decide on the future availability of advanced AI models such as the H200 for export. DeepSeek plans to deploy 160,000 Huawei 950DT chips at a new data center in Inner Mongolia to operate its models. The articles leave open whether the Justice Department's criminal probe will lead to charges against Nvidia or its former executives. It remains unclear if the Commerce Department will eventually blacklist Megaspeed following the pressure from other federal agencies.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave reports strong revenue growth and raises 2026 guidance
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares jumped over 20 percent on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, after strong revenue growth eased concerns about its debt expansion. This surge ignited a rally in battered AI cloud stocks, though shares later fell 10.19 percent to 50.83 dollars on Friday. The company reported third quarter revenue rose 168 percent to 3.7 billion dollars, which was above the top of guidance. CoreWeave raised its 2026 revenue guidance to between 13.0 billion and 13.3 billion dollars, while its backlog stood at 133 billion dollars. The company also reported that its corporate debt is about 41.6 billion dollars, with 2026 capex guidance between 37 billion and 39 billion dollars.

The company will not tap unsecured debt markets after borrowing costs spiked, and cash flow from existing contracts will cover all debt repayments. Nvidia invested 2 billion dollars in CoreWeave in January 2026, and the chipmaker's shares rose 2 percent following the initial CoreWeave earnings. Other neo cloud stocks including Nebius, Iren, Oracle, and Applied Digital climbed between 6 and 14 percent during the Wednesday rally. Most of these stocks, except for Nebius, had lost between 32 and 48 percent of their value this year as of Tuesday. Nebius had surged 60 percent, but it was due to report its own results before the opening bell on Thursday.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told Reuters that greater scrutiny could slow industry data center construction, but it would not alter his company's plans. He stated there would be no impact to the planned capacity additions for CoreWeave over the next year, nor would costs increase. Dan Sheehan of Telos Wealth Advisors said the earnings addressed the fear that had driven the recent selloff of AI infrastructure stocks. Bernstein analysts led by Madison Rezaei called the quarter the best they could have asked for, noting that strategic moves made sense. However, these analysts warned that CoreWeave would be among the first and hardest hit when the AI computing capacity crunch eases.

Investors in AI infrastructure stocks cheered the results, but the industry was reeling from the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang faced allegations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who was allegedly a spy for Beijing, potentially aiding chip shipments to China. Republican Senator Kevin Cramer of the Senate Banking Committee called for Huang to step down as CEO during this escalating leadership crisis. ARK Invest bought 283,022 shares of CoreWeave worth about 16 million dollars on Thursday, despite the deepening turmoil surrounding Nvidia. The market value of Nvidia stood to add nearly 100 billion dollars, while other cloud companies could gain some 36 billion dollars.

The industry faced a blow from a Democratic midterm sweep last week, with winners campaigning for tighter regulation and data center construction moratoriums. This political shift specifically targeted the crucial market of Texas, where new data center construction could be limited by these proposed new regulations. SoftBank took a 3.7 billion dollar writedown on non-refundable equipment payments for US data centers, leading to a second quarter net loss. This loss of 7 billion dollars was the first for SoftBank in nearly two years, highlighting the risks of mistiming large AI investments. Additionally, U.S. producer prices rose 6.5 percent annually in October, marking the largest yearly increase in four years for the country.

CoreWeave shares continued to slide on Friday, extending a 6.86 percent drop from Thursday as the Nvidia leadership shock hit linked names. The stock price on Friday approached the 52 week closing low of 43.66 dollars, which had been set on November 5. Reports also emerged regarding potential loan talks for CoreWeave involving 4 billion dollars, though the company's financial cushion remains thin. The next major test for the sector is the Nvidia report on November 17, which may show changes in partner support. The articles leave open whether the Federal Reserve will raise rates following a 0.4 percent rise in October consumer prices.

stories.Headline: Apple launches HomeView with Siri AI and confirms a December update for voice door unlocks
stories.Summary:
Apple began selling its HomeView product on Friday, November 13, 2026, to serve as a center for the home. The company describes this new device as an artificial intelligence powered product designed for household connectivity and control. It features a seven inch Liquid Retina display and a twelve megapixel Center Stage camera for user recognition. Users can place the device on a tabletop or mount it on a wall for their convenience. The system is powered by Apple Intelligence with Siri AI to help customers manage their smart home.

The device costs 299 dollars, though wall mounted setups start from 358.95 dollars, and it is not sold in the EU. It recognizes six people by face and voice to show personal content from Messages, Calendar, and other relevant information. HomeView ships with software version 26.5 and prompts users to update to version 27.2, which was released November 12. It uses an A18 chip to lock camera and microphone data so that it is never shared with Apple. The device works with the Home app to manage settings, automations, and various smart home accessories.

Greg Joswiak, senior vice president of worldwide marketing, said the device keeps households better connected and informed via Siri AI. Executive Chair Tim Cook posted on X that the product provides intelligence, entertainment, and connection personal to every user. Kaiann Drance, vice president of product marketing for home, stated that Siri AI allows for a previously impossible experience. Lilian Rincon, vice president of product marketing for AI, described the new version of the digital assistant as much more capable. An Apple spokesperson told Joanna Stern that recognized users can already unlock doors using the on screen interface.

Reviewer Joanna Stern found that Siri AI refused to unlock her front door or garage door and claimed it had no camera. Some X users called it the worst piece of tech they ever purchased, citing a schizophrenic Siri with multiple voices. Other affected buyers reported that the device is glitchy, unable to open apps, or unable to play music via Apple Music. One user shared a video of a song glitching and argued that the 299 dollar device should just work. These users experienced technical issues with pictures and music, and some found that Apple support had no answers.

Reports from July indicated that Apple was preparing a major push into the smart home product and software market. This move puts Apple in closer competition with the Google Nest Hub and the Amazon Echo as AI advances. A March PYMNTS Intelligence report found that 54 percent of U.S. adults were using AI for personal tasks. Researchers in Tokyo and Michigan previously showed that light aimed at microphones could inject voice commands into older Siri devices. Those researchers noted that attackers could potentially brute force a smart lock PIN or open garage doors using such methods.

Apple confirmed a December 2026 update will extend voice control to security accessories once the HomeView recognizes the person asking. The company has not yet provided a specific release day or a version number for this upcoming December software update. Users must currently use the touchscreen or the Home app for locks and garage doors until the voice fix arrives. It remains open whether the update will require a recognized voice, a recognized face, or both to open doors. The articles leave open if a paired device must also vouch for the person to ensure secure voice unlocking.

stories.Headline: Shufti launches patented on-device AI age verification that keeps facial images on the user's device
stories.Summary:
Shufti launched its Privacy-Preserving Age Verification Solution, incorporating patented on-device AI technology, on Nov. 13, 2026, in London, according to a GlobeNewswire release. The company described itself as a Glocal identity verification, Anti-Money Laundering and fraud prevention platform. The solution lets businesses confirm users' age eligibility without the facial image or any other higher-assurance proof of age leaving the user's device. The technology is protected by US Patent No. 12,749,342 B1, titled AGE VERIFICATION, issued by the United States Patent and Trademark Office. The patent covers an AI-based system combining on-device facial analysis, split inference and encrypted One-Time Age Tokens.

The solution uses patented split-inference technology to divide AI processing between the user's device and a secure verification server. AI models analyse facial characteristics to estimate age and assess liveness locally, helping identify spoofing attempts involving photographs, masks, screen replays and manipulated images. The device generates an encrypted One-Time Age Token containing intermediate AI outputs rather than transmitting the original facial image. The verification server validates the token, completes the remaining AI processing and determines whether the user meets the required threshold, such as 18 or 21. Tokens are time-limited, can be marked as used after verification and may be restricted to a specific merchant to prevent unauthorised reuse or sharing across platforms.

Shufti's wider Age Verification Solution lets businesses select the level of assurance appropriate to their risk exposure, users and regulatory requirements while minimising collection and exposure of personally identifiable information. It offers docless age checks through facial age estimation or eIDV, configurable age thresholds and confidence-based escalation, risk-based verification, document verification or authoritative database checks, and biometric liveness detection supported by iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance. Shahid Hanif, CEO of Shufti, said a business should not have to collect someone's full identity simply to confirm whether they are old enough to access a service. He said the company developed the solution to help businesses prevent underage access without requiring every legitimate user to provide higher-assurance proof of age. He said the patented on-device approach keeps facial information on the user's device while securely confirming age eligibility, and called the US patent an important milestone.

The articles said a self-declared "I am over 18" click offers little assurance, while an ID upload and selfie can provide stronger evidence but many users are reluctant to share such personal information, particularly for sensitive services. Businesses collecting these records must also manage their security, retention and deletion. In the UK, Ofcom does not recognise self-declaration as a highly effective age assurance method under the UK Online Safety Act. The European Commission is advancing privacy-preserving proof-of-age tools that allow users to establish age eligibility without revealing their identity. The solution supports adult entertainment platforms checking age before content access, social media services applying minimum-age policies, gaming and gambling operators verifying eligibility at registration, and e-commerce businesses checking age before restricted purchases.

Shufti said dividing the final AI model between the device and server reduces exposure of the complete model, making it harder to reverse-engineer the verification process or manipulate locally generated results. The articles said an adult entertainment platform may need to confirm a visitor is over 18, while a regulated gambling operator may also require documentary proof of identity. Shufti's Glocal Trust OS unifies KYC, KYB, eIDV, age assurance, AML screening, agentic transaction monitoring, Know Your Agent and fraud prevention. Shufti's biometric liveness technology holds iBeta Level 3 PAD conformance under ISO/IEC 30107-3. Shufti is recognised as a Leading vendor in Liminal's 2026 Age Verification and Age Estimation Indexes, receiving the highest-tier Exceptional rating for Market Presence in both categories.

Shufti invited businesses to book a personalised demo of the patented Age Verification Solution. The articles listed Aroosa Virk, Brand and Communications Manager at Shufti, as media contact at partnership@shuftipro.com. A photo accompanying the announcement was available at a GlobeNewswire attachment link. The articles did not say when the solution would become generally available or how it would be priced. The articles did not name any business that has adopted the solution.

stories.Headline: California teachers union asks Newsom to pause student-facing generative AI in K-8 classrooms
stories.Summary:
The California Federation of Teachers sent a letter on Wednesday urging Gov. Gavin Newsom to issue an executive order pausing artificial intelligence in K-8 public school classrooms, EdSource reported on November 13, 2026. The union represents 120,000 teachers from preschool to college, according to EdSource. The Sacramento Bee first reported the letter, EdSource said. The union cited an MIT study linking ChatGPT use to weaker brain connectivity while writing essays, EdSource reported. It also cited Wharton Healthcare Analytics Lab research finding students who used GPT-4 scored 17% lower on a math test than students who had not used it, EdSource said.

Parriva reported that CFT President Jeff Freitas asked Newsom in a November 10 letter for an executive order imposing a three-year moratorium on student-facing technologies containing generative AI features. The union announced its request publicly on November 11, Parriva said. Parriva reported the formal request does not explicitly limit the moratorium to kindergarten through eighth grade. The letter separately endorses national American Federation of Teachers recommendations, including no student-facing AI in elementary schools and a prohibition on social companion chatbots for children younger than 16, Parriva reported. Parriva said the CFT letter does not establish that every AI-powered administrative, accessibility or instructional system would be prohibited.

Freitas said in a statement that students' brain development shouldn't be monetized for billionaire profit, EdSource reported. He said this is a public health and safety emergency and that leaders need to treat it as one and act now, according to EdSource. The union said educators need more time to be prepared to supervise AI use, EdSource reported. Parriva reported the union wants time for lawmakers, educators and the next governor to develop longer-term safeguards. Parriva reported CFT is asking California to pause student-facing generative AI while policymakers develop safeguards.

Parriva reported that Los Angeles Unified has restricted student access to generative AI on district-issued devices while continuing to teach students how the technology works. LAUSD restricts student access to generative AI platforms on district-owned devices and school accounts during the 2026, 27 school year, Parriva reported. At its November 13 Generative AI Ad Hoc Committee meeting, LAUSD published presentations on digital citizenship, parent concerns and research, according to Parriva. Parriva reported that district educators described lessons on evaluating AI-generated information, protecting privacy and developing responsible technology habits. Parriva reported that Schools Beyond Screens L.A., a parent advocacy organization, urged stronger restrictions and independent oversight.

Parriva reported that one study involving high-school mathematics students found access to an unrestricted AI tool could improve performance during practice while undermining performance on subsequent unassisted work. A RAND presentation prepared for LAUSD's November 13 committee distinguished general-purpose chatbots from educational systems designed to guide students through problems, Parriva reported. Parriva reported that legislation enacted in 2026, including AB 1159, addresses the use of covered student data in AI development and training, subject to legal exceptions and applicable effective dates. The California Department of Education has issued model AI policy guidance addressing acceptable use, privacy and district oversight, according to Parriva. Parriva reported that the district provides presentation materials in Spanish.

Parriva reported that parents can ask their child's school which generative AI products students can access, whether any are required for assignments and what personal information those products collect. Parents can also request the district's written AI policy, ask how teachers supervise student use and find out whether non-AI alternatives are available, Parriva reported. Parriva reported that the research leaves questions about younger children, long-term outcomes and which safeguards are effective. Parriva reported that the November 13 presentations document competing recommendations, not a new policy adopted by the committee. Parriva reported that LAUSD is already limiting access while reviewing its longer-term approach.

stories.Headline: OECD reports AI adoption accelerates across member countries but gaps persist among businesses and generations
stories.Summary:
The OECD reported on 5 November 2026 that AI adoption is accelerating across its member countries, but that major gaps persist among businesses and between generations. The organisation said the world of work is changing rapidly because of new technologies such as artificial intelligence, along with new forms of work, greening, demographic change and globalisation. It also said critical minerals have become central to economic security, as they are essential to energy and digital transitions, defence and advanced manufacturing. The OECD published the findings on its website as part of its work on effective governance to harness the benefits of AI and mitigate its risks. The OECD said its work on investment supports governments in attracting more and better-quality investment, with priority given to security and sustainability.

It also described how the trend towards the international dispersion of certain value chain activities produces challenges, and said it offers policies to meet these. The organisation noted that its Programme for International Student Assessment, known as PISA, assesses the skills of 15-year-old students in reading, mathematics and science as core domains. The articles give no further figures, dates or names beyond these. The OECD is responsible for the work described, and its statements were paraphrased in the articles rather than attributed to a named individual. The organisation framed the findings around applying effective governance to harness the benefits of AI and mitigate its risks.

It presented the changing world of work as a result of new technologies, new forms of work, greening, demographic change and globalisation. It did not say in the articles what specific measures it recommends or who should carry them out. The context given is that AI adoption is spreading quickly across OECD countries while gaps remain among businesses and generations. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the OECD's stated focus on governance and on attracting better-quality investment. No further steps, deadlines or responses are reported.

stories.Headline: Google CEO Sundar Pichai unveils eight AI and hardware releases in five days
stories.Summary:
Google CEO Sundar Pichai announced eight major AI and hardware releases over five days from Monday to Thursday in November 2026. These updates included two new TPU systems, two Gemini 4 models, three DeepMind projects, a developer API, and smart glasses. The blitz targeted AI researchers, businesses, and developers with enhanced capabilities for complex coding, cyber defence, and rapid execution. Gemini 4 Hydrogen launched on Thursday, while Gemini 4 Carbon became available on Tuesday for paying developers and AI Ultra subscribers. Pre-orders for Android XR audio glasses also began on Thursday, with shipments expected to arrive during the holiday season.

The TPU 8tx system handles encrypted data for governments, while the TPU 8i Max combines two chips for AI agents. Gemini 4 Carbon costs two dollars per million input tokens and ten dollars per million output tokens for complex tasks. The Gemini Decisions API costs ten cents per million input tokens and provides yes or no responses via an AI Studio endpoint. Gemini 4 Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times quicker than Gemini 3.8 Flash and offers four reasoning depths for diverse agentic workflows. Samsung and Google developed thirty Intelligent Eyewear models, including sixteen Gentle Monster and fourteen Warby Parker designs, for a December 10 launch.

Sundar Pichai detailed the product releases, while Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president at Google DeepMind, described the new Hydrogen model's speed. Kavukcuoglu stated that Hydrogen is built for rapid execution of everyday work, such as writing code and running various tests. He noted that Hydrogen is better at following guidance and calling tools to get reliable outputs with less back and forth. The company claimed that Hydrogen is two times less likely to circumvent permission boundaries than the previous Gemini 3.8 Flash model. DeepMind reported that Gemini Robotics 2.5 improves tool handling, resulting in job completion rates that are 20 to 30 per cent quicker.

The new smart glasses affect users in South Korea and the United States, where they support translation and meeting summaries. These glasses, weighing 41 grams, feature a 12 megapixel HDR camera, two open ear speakers, and four microphones for the wearer. Users can photograph whiteboards to save summaries to Samsung Notes, while the battery provides nine hours of use on one charge. Academics can access the AlphaGenome 2 API for free, though companies must join a private preview for this science release. The AlphaProof Code project verified Signal's one to one messaging encryption code in four weeks and found no new flaws.

Google previously launched Gemini 4 Argon two weeks before Carbon, and Gemini 3.8 Flash was released in September to power Search features. The Intelligent Eyewear was showcased at Google I/O in May and Galaxy Unpacked in July before the full lineup was revealed. These glasses use the Qualcomm Snapdragon AR1 Gen 1 platform and offload some processing tasks to a connected Galaxy smartphone. AlphaGenome 2 investigates how DNA changes affect cell types to help trace disease origins, but it is not for diagnosis. The eighth generation chip family now expands to four systems with the addition of the 8tx and 8i Max.

The Intelligent Eyewear will launch in the United States and South Korea on December 10, though only Gentle Monster models hit Korea. Google continues to work on safety and security for Hydrogen, specifically focusing on jailbreak resistance to improve the model's overall reliability. The articles leave open whether the AlphaGenome 2 private preview will expand or if other countries will receive the glasses. It remains unclear if the Gemini Decisions API will add written output or if the free tier has specific usage limits. The text does not state if other hardware partners beyond Samsung, Warby Parker, and Gentle Monster will join the project.

stories.Headline: Hochul announces a new AI research institute at Binghamton University
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul declared earlier this week that New York State will lead the nation in artificial intelligence science and safety, speaking from Binghamton University about a brand new AI research institute located there. The institute is intended to create an environment where data can be studied and scrutinized, and according to the governor it will also monitor the possible dangers that artificial intelligence may present. The center will bring together roughly 80 scientists and researchers whom the state hopes will be able to harness the developing technology for the public good. SUNY Binghamton received 30 million dollars from private donors to establish the center, which the reporting describes as the largest academic gift in the school's history.

The institute's stated purpose is to give the state a place where data can be examined closely while possible dangers of artificial intelligence are watched, and the governor framed the center as part of a broader effort to take back control of the shared future. She said that between the state's data center moratorium, its AI safety laws and this first of its kind research center, New York is taking back control of its shared future and its right to shape AI's role in that future. She also said that once again New York is showing the rest of the nation that the state does have a say, and that it can build a world where technology serves the public interest and not the other way around. The reporting does not say what specific safety rules the institute would follow or when it would begin its work.

Hochul is the official responsible for the announcement, having made the declaration from Binghamton University earlier in the week, and the 30 million dollars in private donations came from donors to SUNY Binghamton rather than from the state itself. In her remarks she presented the research center as one piece of a larger push alongside the data center moratorium and the state's AI safety laws, which she said together amount to taking back control of the future. The articles do not name any of the private donors and do not describe how the roughly 80 scientists and researchers will be selected or when they will arrive. No further steps beyond the announcement are described in the reporting.

stories.Headline: Common Sense Media asks bankruptcy court to protect children's chat data in any Character.ai sale
stories.Summary:
Common Sense Media sent a letter dated November 12, 2026, to Judge Brendan L. Shannon of the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware about Character.ai's bankruptcy, case 26-11603. The clerk received it at 9:59 a.m. on November 13, 2026, and it appeared on the public docket on November 16 as Docket No. 167. The group shipped it by FedEx from its Washington, DC office on November 12, addressed to the judge. The letter asks the court to protect all conversational data in any sale, require a privacy program and demand effective age checks. It is six pages long, and two attached AI risk assessments bring the filing to 84 pages.

The letter asks that any sale include robust privacy protections for all conversational data, a commitment to a comprehensive privacy program and effective age-assurance measures. It repeats the request in its closing paragraph and adds that the court should consider the promises made to children by Character.AI. Footnote 13 says all conversational data deserves protection in the sale, because it is not clear whether age assurance was ever effective. The letter says users under 13 were technically restricted to comply with federal privacy laws, but age determination relied on self-attestation. It says users under 18 could use the service during the assessments and up until November 25, 202, with the final digit of the year missing in the filed copy.

The letter is signed by Amina Fazlullah, Head of Tech Policy Advocacy, Ariel Fox Johnson, Senior Advisor for Data Privacy, and Brenna Leasor, Tech Policy Advisor. It says even if personal identifiers like names are removed, conversations alone could reveal who children are. It quotes Daniel J. Solove's paper of October 19, 2026, that AI's power to generate inferences creates an enormous problem for privacy law. It says the data could be used by marketers targeting children known to have proclivities for gambling, or to charge higher rates, or by criminal actors to sextort or blackmail children. It describes a child who uses a family pet's name in a password and warns the data could become part of a digital dossier.

The letter says the Federal Trade Commission took action over 25 years ago when ToySmart went bankrupt and tried to sell its data, including children's names, birthdays and addresses, at auction, citing the FTC's settlement announcement of July 21, 2000. It says its testing showed Character.ai reassured children repeatedly that conversations were confidential, quoting one chatbot: "Anything you share here stays just between you and me. That's a promise." It does not say which test account received that reply, when, or whether the character was company-built or user-created. The chief executive's first-day declaration says Character spent several months beginning in October 2025 restricting users under 18 from open-ended chats and eventually eliminated that access. The Kentucky complaint cited by the states put US accounts at more than 21.6 million by March 13, 2025, of which more than 2.1 million declared an age under 18.

Both appendices carry a last updated date of April 10, 2025, and an overall rating of "Unacceptable." Appendix A says Character.ai is a social AI companion platform that, despite some guardrails for teens, should not be used by anyone under age 18, and scores it against eight principles. It describes a December 2024 incident in which the company said a refresh of featured Characters temporarily made parts of users' account pages publicly visible, and estimates suggest tens of thousands of users could have had their info viewable. It notes at least one hack of a social AI companion. In voice mode, testers found conversations that seemed entirely without the guardrails on teen accounts, and these speech exchanges were captured in text transcription and saved with all the text chats.

The letter does not describe itself as an objection and does not cite a section of the Bankruptcy Code, and the docket lists it as a response. It does not propose specific terms, and the judge decides what any sale order will contain. The letter says the sale of children's information in an AI world is exponentially more troubling than the ToySmart case. On October 14, 39 states and the District of Columbia said minors had used the platform without adequate age checks and asked for age assurance not relying only on self-declared birthdates. Character.ai disclosed $8 million in monthly losses. The articles leave open whether any buyer could keep the children in those logs unnamed.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google ties school search access to AI use as educators raise concerns
stories.Summary:
Google has told schools that if they decline to use its artificial intelligence tools, their students will lose standard browser-based search access entirely. The company's policy shift, reported by Fox 44 and others, follows months of friction between the tech firm and educators. Google automatically turned on its Gemini chatbot in August for millions of young users in Google Classroom, a platform that had previously been limited to users 18 and older. Critics and child advocacy groups have pushed back, saying the policy penalizes districts trying to protect students and pressures them into relying on AI.

Under the revised framework, Gemini, Gemini Notebook, and Google Search remain inactive by default for K-12 student accounts. School administrators can switch individual applications on or off. However, because modern web search is closely tied to AI functions, districts that opt out of AI would also lose Google Search. Given that Google holds the largest share of the educational technology market, the announcement drew immediate criticism. Some observers have also raised antitrust concerns about a dominant provider conditioning basic research access on AI adoption.

Google's Vice President and General Manager of Education, Chris Phillips, responded in a blog post that schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and that administrators should have controls to manage their approach. The company says it is working to make its search tools more suitable for classroom use. Phillips's statement stresses institutional choice, though the policy as described still links the two services. Google's reach in schools is substantial, with Google Classroom used by more than 100 million students and teachers alongside school-provided Chromebooks.

The controversy comes as artificial intelligence spreads through everyday digital services, and Canadian educators have voiced similar concerns about student privacy and the ability to evaluate tools separately. Those educators question whether schools should have to accept AI features to keep access to a widely used search engine. The reporting points to broader debates over transparency and the influence technology providers hold over classroom tools. The articles do not say whether Google will change the policy or how districts will respond beyond the criticism already voiced.

stories.Summary:
Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, the law firm known as HSF Kramer, has hired a legal engineering team to strengthen its artificial intelligence capabilities, according to the headline. The articles provided do not give the date of the hire, the size of the team, the names of its members or where the team came from. The move fits a wider hiring trend that a Firm Prospects report documented, finding that 46 lawyers left Am Law 200 firms for AI companies in the first half of 2026, including 15 who moved into legal engineer roles. The same articles do not say whether any of those 15 lawyers joined HSF Kramer.

The hire points to legal engineering as a growing career path at the intersection of law and AI. Irene Liu, executive director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, told the ABA Journal that the number of legal engineering jobs available right now is quite amazing and that demand for lawyers in different business capacities is opening interesting career pathways. Stanford Law School is launching a Legal Engineering Academy, a two-week residential program set for summer 2027, which Liu is co-leading. More than 2,000 people have signed up to be notified when applications open, and organizers are targeting a first class of about 40.

Liu and Adam Sterling, a Stanford associate dean, are the people the articles identify as speaking about the trend. Sterling said the transformation can be scary but can also mean more opportunities to do different things, a remark paraphrased here rather than quoted at length. The articles do not include any statement from HSF Kramer or from the legal engineering team it hired, so what the firm or the team said about the move is not known. No numbers specific to the HSF Kramer hire, such as team size or start date, appear in the source material.

The context is a legal market in which AI companies are recruiting lawyers away from large firms at a notable pace, and law schools are preparing students for legal engineering roles. The articles say nothing about what happens next at HSF Kramer, such as further hires or how the team will be used. What is known is that the firm has brought in a legal engineering team, that legal engineering hiring is rising across the profession and that Stanford plans to train about 40 people in its first academy class in summer 2027. The Congress government in Karnataka announced the introduction of Artificial Intelligence, Python Programming, Data Analytics and other trending IT courses in schools across the state. The courses will be initially introduced in Class 9 across 1,800 government high schools from the 2026-27 academic year.

The prescribed Class IX syllabus introduces students to modern artificial intelligence concepts through hands-on modules and practical mathematical applications. The curriculum covers understanding how intelligent systems operate, with foundational exposure to modern generative AI tools, and learning core coding syntax in Python alongside data collection, organisation and pattern analysis. It also covers exploring how machines interpret visual inputs and process human language, and connecting classroom mathematics, specifically Statistics, Probability, Linear Algebra and Calculus, to real world AI model optimization and predictive outcomes. The courses include AI fundamentals, Python Programming, Data Analytics, Computer Vision, Natural Language Processing and Generative AI. stories.Headline: Fed chair Kevin Warsh says AI could speed innovation and growth but warns of job losses and stock declines
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke on Monday about how artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in faster economic growth. He delivered these remarks during a one-day conference on AI and productivity held at the San Francisco branch of the Fed. Warsh acknowledged that the technology carries risks, including widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market. He noted that these negative outcomes could happen if expected returns from huge AI infrastructure investments do not materialize. The Chairman focused on the potential for super intelligence to supercharge idea generation and sustain higher long-run growth.

The Fed uses the term super intelligence because of an executive order issued by President Donald Trump for federal agencies. Warsh previously spoke at a news conference in Washington on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, regarding the economy and the Federal Reserve. Meta data centers operated near Social Circle, Georgia, on September 5, 2026, as part of the broader AI infrastructure buildout. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed to evaluate various economic impacts. One specific task force was created to evaluate AI and its impact on the efficiency of the overall economy.

Chairman Warsh stated that great opportunities rarely come risk free and that overlooked risks can be highly disruptive and costly. He suggested that if idea generation broadens, economic growth could be sustained at levels substantially higher than the long-run average. Warsh previously touted AI as a technology that could boost efficiency, allowing the economy to grow without worsening inflation. He warned that falling equity valuations after significant capital investment could lead to an economic slowdown and higher unemployment. The Chairman did not comment on interest rate steps or recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month.

Many Fed colleagues believe the buildout of data centers is accelerating price increases for electricity, copper, electronic components, and computer chips. These costs have lifted prices for computers and smartphones, with smartphone prices rising last month at the fastest pace ever. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said that permanently higher productivity growth could increase firms' demand for funding and raise rates. Some rate-setting committee members signaled support for additional interest rate hikes at the next Federal Reserve meeting in December. These policymakers expressed concern that the demand for AI infrastructure is fanning inflation and raising costs for many consumers.

Warsh has long argued that AI could significantly boost economic efficiency, which might eventually enable the Fed to lower interest rates. The current situation involves a conflict between Warsh's optimistic outlook and the concerns of his colleagues regarding rising price levels. Government data from last week confirmed that inflation accelerated, prompting several policymakers to seek further hikes to stabilize the economy. The Fed is now monitoring how the speed of innovation changes the method of idea generation across various industries. This background highlights a divide within the Federal Reserve regarding the inflationary nature of the current AI investment boom.

Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how the impact of artificial intelligence may play out in the future economy. The Federal Reserve will meet in December, where some members may push for the additional interest rate hikes they signaled. The articles do not state whether Warsh will change his position on inflation or address it in his future speeches. It remains open whether the expected returns from AI infrastructure investments will actually materialize or lead to a market crash. The reports leave undecided if AI will truly lead to permanently higher productivity or cause a notable rise in unemployment.

stories.Headline: US government tightens AI chip export rules to limit China's access
stories.Summary:
The United States government tightened rules for exporting artificial intelligence chips on Friday, November 16, 2026, to limit China's access. This policy move caused Micron stock to fall by 6 percent, with shares sliding as much as 7.8 percent in early trading. Other semiconductor companies including SK Hynix, AMD, and Broadcom also saw their stock prices decline during the same trading session. The Commerce Department issued an interim final rule to stop the flow of computing power and advanced chips to China. This action occurred as investors repriced their exposure to a shifting policy environment regarding the sale of advanced technology.

The rule requires export licenses for servers and AI chips sent to data centers in Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. It targets companies in high-risk countries, specifically China, Russia, and Iran, and rescinds the previous Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule. The regulation takes effect immediately, though it includes a 90-day transition period for companies to adjust to the new requirements. Additionally, four bills are circulating, including the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, the Match Act, and the Remote Access Security Act. These proposals aim to track processor locations, limit equipment sales, and stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers.

The Department of Commerce, the National Security Council, and the Treasury Department are responsible for the new interim final rule. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced criticism for delaying enforcement on indirect shipments, and lawmakers are now pressing him for answers. House Speaker Mike Johnson stated on November 12 that a developing consensus exists in Congress to limit chip exports to China. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott and House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast have both sought testimony from former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Lawmakers are also scrutinizing Megaspeed, a Singapore company suspected of smuggling restricted Nvidia chips into China.

Investors are affected because licensing requirements add paperwork, cause delays, and create risks of denials for previously simple international sales. Cloud providers are impacted because the Remote Access Security Act targets the renting of data centers to reach restricted hardware. Nvidia has verbally told its cloud clients to cap their business with Chinese firms at 49 percent of their services. Micron faces additional pressure from a federal court allowing an antitrust lawsuit regarding DRAM price-fixing to proceed against it. This lawsuit also names Samsung and SK Hynix, although the court has not yet found any of these companies liable.

Washington has long used export controls on advanced chips as a tool to limit the cutting-edge AI capabilities of China. Previous efforts focused on where physical chips were shipped, but the new rule focuses on where computing power ends up. Nvidia previously spent years lobbying against these curbs, but its lobbying power weakened after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO. In April 2025, Nvidia took a 5.5 billion dollar charge, and AMD warned of a hit of 800 million dollars. Taiwanese prosecutors also raided Nvidia offices on July 28 and detained an employee during a widening AI chip smuggling probe.

Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent successor both inside and outside the company. Republicans want to attach the new chip restrictions to the annual defense authorization bill, which is considered a must-pass measure. Democrats have signaled they will take broader action after they take the House majority in January 2027. The articles leave open the final date for Jensen Huang's testimony and the specific costs of the new tracking mandates. No official vote has been scheduled for the chip language within the defense bill, leaving the final legislative outcome uncertain.

stories.Headline: US authorities ground flights as Microsoft outage and technical failures spark system stability fears
stories.Summary:
US authorities ordered every plane across the country to land immediately on Friday, November 14, 2026. This nationwide ground stop occurred alongside a major Microsoft outage and chaos in Silicon Valley. These events happened during a week that included reports of an AI billionaire's affair. The billionaire was allegedly involved with a suspected Chinese spy, which sparked significant tech turbulence. These combined disruptions left millions of people wondering if interconnected technology systems were beginning to unravel.

The ground stop lasted more than four hours and affected thousands of downed jetliners across the United States. A technology upgrade on the air traffic control system overloaded antiquated equipment, causing intermittent communications and radar gaps. Microsoft reported a network capacity upgrade issue that affected many millions of people around the world. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy requested tens of billions in more funding to upgrade the outdated system. This follows a previous funding approval of 2.5 billion dollars by Congress for the same overhaul.

Administration officials stated that the air traffic control problems were caused by prosaic technical failures. Bryan Bedford, the administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, said schedules should be normal by late Sunday. Microsoft stated on Saturday that its services were fully restored after the network capacity issue surfaced. Both the FAA and Microsoft said there were no signs that malicious activity caused the troubles. These agencies denied that any cyberattack or malicious actor was behind the various technical failures.

Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, felt that the weird events could cripple an economy. Maxine Gustafson, a 34-year-old physician assistant from Minneapolis, said the mishaps made her feel afraid and helpless. Tori Perkins, a 34-year-old from Hawaii, said she did not necessarily believe what the government says. Passengers at San Diego International Airport saw 11 of 62 flights canceled or delayed on Saturday morning. Other affected people included workers cast adrift by the outage and travelers stranded at various airports.

The articles mention a cruise ship that overturned in New Orleans after a tanker slammed into it. Suspicious drones were reported over a US air base in Britain on the same Friday. A bomb was also found near an ethanol plant in Ohio during this period of chaos. The White House has been pushing for 60 billion more dollars to complete the system work. These events occurred while some people watched planes land from the Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center.

Air travel was already smoother by Saturday morning as the FAA worked to restore normal flight schedules. The White House continues to seek additional funding to ease concerns and complete the air traffic overhaul. Stephen King tweeted a joke that aliens had landed to explain the ground stop and avoid panic. The articles leave open whether the public will trust the official government explanations for these failures. They also leave open if further funding will be granted to fix the outdated national infrastructure.
