stories.Headline: Penn State researchers build AI that explains manufacturing fixes to engineers
stories.Summary:
A team led by Penn State researchers, funded by the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, is building a neurosymbolic intelligent system that pairs a neural network learning from industrial data with knowledge graphs of engineering rules. The work was published on November 16, 2026, by Tucker Leighty-Phillips of Penn State University. The system is meant to flag manufacturing problems and explain its recommendations to plant engineers. The Genesis Mission is a national effort led by the U.S. Department of Energy to use AI to accelerate scientific discovery and innovation. The team's aim is to combine data-driven learning with human-like reasoning.

The system will identify manufacturing issues through pattern recognition and symbolic reasoning, and use engineering and physics knowledge to understand and resolve problems. Operators will see what the neural system flags and decide whether to agree or override it with symbolic knowledge and reasoning assistance. The system will talk with engineers, draw out hidden constraints and work with the optimization models plants already use, updating recommendations as floor conditions change. A knowledge graph stores expert knowledge as a web of connected facts, linking items such as a weld defect, a machine setting or an assembly line step to the others they affect. Porosity in a weld can be caused by a travel speed that is too fast, and engineers can add new rules to the graph as they learn them.

Soundar Kumara, Allen E. Pearce and Allen M. Pearce Professor of Industrial Engineering and principal investigator, said the team is building a neurosymbolic intelligence with an explanation capability that will make the future of the global manufacturing landscape different and truly useful. He said neurosymbolic manufacturing intelligence will open new avenues and revitalize manufacturing by providing better explanations for the inferences made. He said the major focus is building neurosymbolic architecture that integrates neural inference with symbolic reasoning. He said the team is building neural reasoning connected with knowledge graphs for two case studies, one from General Motors and another from a small and medium-sized manufacturer in Pennsylvania. He said the architecture will be adaptable enough for other manufacturing applications.

Anirudh Subramanyam, Charles and Enid Schneider Early Career Assistant Professor of Industrial Engineering, said optimization models are very good at finding the best plan under the rules you give them. He said the trouble on a real assembly line is that many of the most important rules have never been written down, as they only live in the heads of the engineers who run it. He said the team wants a system that learns those rules from engineers' feedback and can tell them not just what to change, but which constraint forced its hand. Rebecca Napolitano, co-principal investigator, associate professor of architectural engineering and associate director of the Digital Twin Hub, said the physics and engineering knowledge built into the symbolic side gives a way to test the AI, not just train it. She said that when the system makes a recommendation, the operator can see what it is based on and how confident it is.

The team includes collaborators from multiple Penn State units, industry, a national lab and commonwealth groups, including the Pennsylvania Technical Assistance Program (PennTAP) and Team Pennsylvania Foundation. Los Alamos National Laboratory will provide foundational expertise on neurosymbolic intelligence. Kumara said PennTAP and Team Pennsylvania Foundation work directly with manufacturers across the state, which gives a practical path into the shops that need this most. He said PennTAP offers no-cost energy assessments for companies, so they will measure energy usage at the shop before and after the tools are brought in. He said Team Pennsylvania Foundation will support the project by finding other in-state manufacturers and connecting them.

The researchers are building and testing their approach in two real-world case studies: welding quality inspection at a Pennsylvania manufacturer and assembly line rebalancing with General Motors. The researchers intentionally selected both a small and large manufacturer to test their approach, stating that if the model works at both scales, it should work for all enterprises of different scales. Currently, weld inspection relies on a person looking at the weld, which is getting harder as experienced welders retire, the researchers said. Penn State students are training neural models to spot defects like cracks, porosity and undercut, and are building knowledge graphs from real-world welding rules and standards. For example, if the system spots porosity in a weld image, it can use its welding rules to trace the likely cause to a setting such as electrode travel speed or voltage and suggest an adjustment for the welder to check.

For the General Motors case study, the researchers are applying neurosymbolic intelligence to rebalance assembly lines, where work is split into small tasks across a sequence of workstations. When the product mix shifts or the line must speed up, those tasks must be redistributed, and because tasks depend on one another, moving them can set off a chain of further moves down the line. Plants plan these changes with optimization models, but those models are limited by their hardcoded rules, and their recommendations can be hard for line engineers to interpret. In the team's approach, an optimization model proposes each plan while a neural layer learns from engineers' feedback, and when an engineer rejects a plan, for example because a needed tool sits at only one station, the system automatically infers the unwritten rule, adds it to the optimization model and proposes a new plan. Anirudh Subramanyam is leading the optimization effort with Seog-Chan Oh of General Motors, while Kamesh Madduri, associate professor of computer science and engineering, is leading development of the dynamic knowledge graph.

The researchers are also exploring federated learning, where models improve by learning across several companies without any of them having to share their data. Kumara said small manufacturers usually don't have enough data on their own to train a good AI model, and they also really don't want to hand their production data to a big company or a competitor. Federated learning lets each shop's model learn on its own data and only share what the model learned, not the raw data itself, allowing them to build a better model while ensuring their data stays in-house, the researchers explained. The project also draws on the interdisciplinary research community fostered by Penn State's Digital Twin Hub, a joint initiative of the Cocoziello Institute for Real Estate Innovation and the Institute for Computational and Data Sciences (ICDS). Jessica Menold, co-principal investigator and associate professor of mechanical engineering and industrial engineering, directs the Hub, which connects researchers working across manufacturing, infrastructure, healthcare and other domains to advance digital twin research and applications.

Menold said the challenges of developing digital twins often transcend individual disciplines and industries. She said the project demonstrates the value of bringing together expertise in AI, engineering, advanced manufacturing and human-centered design to advance digital twin research and address real-world manufacturing challenges. She said that by integrating deep learning, engineering knowledge and human expertise, we can move beyond simply modeling physical systems to understanding, predicting and improving their behavior. The researchers said it is equally important to ensure that these increasingly sophisticated systems remain transparent, allowing engineers to understand and critically evaluate the reasoning behind AI-generated recommendations. Other Penn State personnel on the project are Paul Griffin, Lucas Professor in Industrial Engineering; Guha Manogharan, professor of mechanical engineering; Ilya Kovalenko, assistant professor of mechanical engineering; and Tanna Pugh, director of PennTAP.

In addition to Seog-Chan Oh, other external co-principal investigators are Abby Smith of Team Pennsylvania Foundation and William Peck of Los Alamos National Laboratory. Graduate students include Vinay Saji Mathew, Chen Zhou and Xiaowen You, all from industrial engineering. Xiaowen You, doctoral student in industrial engineering, is advised by Soundar Kumara. The article was last updated November 16, 2026, and contact is the College of Engineering Media Relations at communications@engr.psu.edu. The article carries tags including Research, Science and Technology, University Park, Engineering, architectural engineering, industrial and manufacturing engineering, mechanical engineering and Artificial Intelligence.

stories.Headline: Riham Hashi launches Novara Strategies to help companies navigate AI governance and regulation
stories.Summary:
Riham Hashi, a 2026 graduate of Penn Carey Law’s Master in Law program, launched Novara Strategies in April 2025, a boutique consulting firm that helps companies navigate regulation, technology policy and artificial intelligence governance. She had worked in state policy and management roles focused on community-based initiatives and public policy implementation, and she noticed gaps between policy intent and real-world execution. She also worked on the Postsecondary Student Basic Needs Act, which passed in Washington State in May 2023. Soon after launching her firm, she entered the Master in Law program to build the legal expertise her clients needed. Hashi said the program was a deliberate step to strengthen the legal and regulatory foundation she was already building, and that she wanted a stronger framework in regulatory law and to think more precisely about legal structure and compliance, especially in artificial intelligence.

Through the curriculum she gained skills in legal reasoning, building compliance programs and regulatory interpretation. She first noticed a change in her U.S. Law and Legal Methods course, which she called foundational to how she analyzes legal issues for clients, and she said it changed how she reads and structures information and helped her approach statutes and case law with greater discipline and clarity. She also found immediate professional relevance in her Corporate Governance and Compliance and Intellectual Property Law for Strategists, Innovators, and Owners of IP Assets courses, and she said it was easy to connect classroom learning to real-life work. Hashi valued learning from faculty who are actively practicing in the fields they teach, and she pointed to her Corporate Governance and Compliance professor, Andrew Kandel, as an example of that practitioner-driven perspective. She said he is actively doing the work and that it is helpful to learn from someone directly in the field.

She also credited the program’s flexibility as a major advantage for professionals whose work intersects with the law, saying students can come from any field and mold the program to fit what they think is important to their work. She encouraged prospective students to take advantage of the larger Penn ecosystem and to enter the program with a clear sense of how they want to use the degree. For Hashi, the degree provided more than legal literacy, offering a structured framework for understanding governance, compliance and organizational decision-making at a deeper level. That framework now informs the work she is building through Novara Strategies and her broader approach to AI governance and regulatory strategy.

stories.Headline: Fraud experts say AI makes impersonation scams more believable and harder to detect
stories.Summary:
Scammers are finding new ways to impersonate people and organizations that victims trust, fraud experts warn, and these scams can begin across phone calls, texts, email, messaging apps and social media. Artificial intelligence is making these tactics more believable and harder to detect, according to the articles. Impersonation scams happen when someone pretends to be a trusted person or organization, such as a government agency, law enforcement, a bank, a tech support provider or even a family member. The scams work because they create a sense of urgency and rely on trust to push people to act quickly. In some cases criminals now use AI to generate realistic messages, real-time videos or even mimic a person's voice, which can make a scam feel more urgent and personal.

The articles describe a five-step anatomy of a scam: contact from someone claiming to be a trusted source, trust built by a believable message, urgency from a claimed problem or emergency, a request to send money or share information, and extraction of money or sensitive information. They list five ways to protect yourself, starting with verifying the request through a trusted contact method such as a known phone number or official website rather than information in the message. People should not rely on caller ID or voice alone, because phone numbers and messages can be altered, faked or manipulated and caller ID can show an institution's name that is not real. Readers are told to slow down and ask questions, since a legitimate person or organization will not rush them into immediate action. The articles also advise caution about sharing personal information in response to unexpected requests and talking to someone trusted before acting, because a second opinion can help spot red flags.

Joshua Del Valle, executive director of enterprise fraud at PNC Bank, said the technology may be new but the strategy behind these scams is not. He said fraudsters want to build trust, create pressure and keep people from pausing long enough to question the request. He advised verifying the request through a contact method you already know and trust instead of relying on how convincing a message, voice or video appears. The articles say scammers may pose as familiar or authoritative sources, with common examples including calls claiming to be from a bank, a government agency or a relative in distress. They note that people impersonating law enforcement or bank employees often tell victims to mention nothing to bank employees during a withdrawal transaction because those employees are supposedly compromised.

The articles say contact can happen in multiple ways, with calls, texts, email and social media messages all used together. They say technology is making scams more convincing, with messages that may be more polished and personalized and timed to feel legitimate. Pressure is a key tactic, and scammers often push for immediate action or ask people not to involve others. The articles state that impersonation scams continue to evolve, but the underlying tactics remain the same: gaining trust and pushing people to act quickly. They say slowing down and verifying before responding can help people avoid making a payment or sharing information based on a false request.

The articles were published on November 16, 2026, by the Mesabi Tribune at 12:15 and by the Watauga Democrat at 11:15. Both carry the headline asking who is really on the other end and how to recognize impersonation and AI-driven scams. The Mesabi Tribune is based at 704 7th Avenue in Virginia, Minnesota, and the Watauga Democrat is part of Mountain Times Publications, which the article says has 8 full-time reporters and editors covering the High Country. The Watauga Democrat asks readers to support local journalism with a contribution. The Mesabi Tribune offers a Day Pass for $1.99 and runs a $15,000 Free Rent or Mortgage Sweepstakes.

For more information on best practices to help prevent fraud, the articles point readers to PNC's Security and Privacy Center. The articles leave open who specifically is behind these scams and how often they succeed. They do not say whether any particular victim, loss amount or case is involved. They do not give a date for when the AI tactics first appeared or how widely they are used. They do not say what PNC or any other organization is doing beyond offering the guidance and the Security and Privacy Center.

stories.Headline: Asian investors sell off AI stocks ahead of Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO
stories.Summary:
Investors in Asia reduced their exposure to artificial intelligence stocks on Sunday, November 15, 2026, as a market selloff resumed. This caution follows the resignation of Nvidia chief Jensen Huang last week after revelations of extramarital affairs. Nvidia is scheduled to report its earnings on Tuesday during a crucial week for the tech boom. Anthropic will price its initial public offering on Wednesday and debut shares on the Nasdaq on Thursday. These events are testing a fragile market sentiment that has already seen significant volatility.

The Taiex index in Taiwan plunged more than 4 percent, while indexes in Japan and South Korea also slumped. Nasdaq 100 futures fell 0.5 percent after the cash index dropped 1.2 percent on Friday. Nvidia has lost 1.9 trillion dollars in market capitalisation since early October according to LSEG data. Interim CEO Colette Kress, the former chief financial officer, must now attempt to shore up investor confidence. European futures in Britain and Germany rose slightly due to a lower concentration of AI shares.

Interim CEO Colette Kress is responsible for managing the company during this leadership crisis and upcoming earnings report. The Financial Times reports that Jensen Huang has discussed a possible comeback with his confidants. Another report from the Financial Times says Nvidia approached Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas for the job. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News on Sunday that the company needs to hire from outside. Elon Musk stated on X on Saturday that Nvidia would lose critical deals without Huang.

Investors in Asia and the United States are affected by the current instability in the semiconductor market. Market participants are also watching the Federal Reserve and inflationary pressures affecting December rate hike bets. Retail sales data on Tuesday will provide insight into the resilience of the United States consumer. Earnings from Walmart, Target, Home Depot, and Lowe's will further reveal the state of the consumer. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will speak at a public forum in San Francisco on Monday.

Nvidia was the signature stock in a tech-led bull market that lasted for four years. Concerns about the sustainability of debt-fuelled AI buildouts grew starting in early October. Democrats won the US midterm elections earlier this month, which threatened more regulations on data-centre expansion. The Federal Reserve has issued hawkish comments that raised market bets of a half-point rate hike to 8 percent. The minutes of the October policy meeting are scheduled for release on Wednesday.

The market will wait to see if Colette Kress can stabilize investor confidence on Tuesday. Investors will observe the Anthropic IPO pricing on Wednesday and the subsequent Nasdaq debut on Thursday. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will discuss how artificial intelligence will reshape the United States economy. The articles leave open whether Jensen Huang will actually return to lead the company. It remains unclear how the new tech boom will evolve and on what specific timetable.

stories.Headline: Caltech dean says students adopt AI faster than admissions offices update rules
stories.Summary:
Students are increasingly using artificial intelligence in their college applications, and admissions offices across the country are rushing to update their guidelines in response, according to CNN reporting published on November 15, 2026. Kate Gilbertson, who graduated from UC Berkeley in 2025 and now edits college applications full time, said she has lately received many drafts that lack the usual quirks of teenage writing. ChatGPT has been out for just four years, yet AI has already reshaped the entire admissions process from top to bottom, and more high schoolers are turning to chatbots instead of college counselors who often charge thousands of dollars. As the January 1 deadline for the Common App approaches, colleges are also testing AI evaluations of their own to sift through thousands, if not tens of thousands, of applications.

Each admissions office's guidelines look a little different. CalTech, which narrowed thousands of applicants to fewer than 450 admitted students last year, said replacing a student's unique voice with AI content is unethical but generating questions to kick start brainstorming is acceptable. The University of Pennsylvania warned against AI use for letters of recommendation written by counselors and teachers. Virginia Tech, which received a record 57,622 first-year applications for 2025, is testing AI to keep up with mass application volume, while UNC-Chapel Hill reversed its decision to auto-score essays after a spokesperson said widespread AI-assisted writing diminished the usefulness of AI essay ratings. Tulane no longer requires a "Why Tulane?" essay, and spokesperson Michael Strecker confirmed that concerns about AI played a role in that decision.

Ashley Pallie, CalTech's dean of undergraduate admissions, said students are moving faster than admissions offices and that an AI bot could not replace professional essay readers anytime soon. She said you cannot develop a perfect formula to choose the right students and you need humans reading the humans who submitted applications, though CalTech does use an AI that reads students' scientific research and asks questions faculty later review. Sophie Sajnani, who founded a boutique consulting firm after graduating in 2025, discourages students from using AI to brainstorm but does not mind when it writes for them, saying her AI-native students have trained chatbots to sound like them. Anisah Ali, a high school junior in Washington, told CNN she sees AI as a way to open up ideas rather than cheat the process.

The articles describe AI as leveling the field for students without counselors, since it helps them find suitable schools at the start of the process. Pallie said she sees a distant future where essays play a smaller role, and in her ideal world everyone would do an interview of some sort, conducted by a human. The reporting does not say what further steps colleges plan beyond the guideline updates and experiments already under way.

stories.Headline: TSMC creates 500 million dollar fund for chip startups and suppliers
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company launched a new investment fund of 500 million dollars on November 16, 2026, to support promising chip startups. This initiative aims to strengthen the broader semiconductor ecosystem and back emerging companies that could become future tech giants like Nvidia or Broadcom. The world's largest contract chipmaker seeks to expand its role beyond the manufacturing of advanced processors during the current artificial intelligence boom. This new venture fund targets chip startups, suppliers, and other upstream partners to help them grow within the global semiconductor industry. The company announced these plans during the Nikkei Forum Global Management Dialogue 2026, which took place in the city of Tokyo.

The fund requires a 500 million dollar investment to support suppliers of chipmaking equipment, advanced materials, chemicals, and various intellectual property. TSMC also plans to invest up to 500 million dollars each into two major AI model developers known as OpenAI and Anthropic. These specific AI companies are currently exploring the use of custom chips to power their future computing needs and technical requirements. This strategy marks a significant change for TSMC, as the company has not previously invested in its own suppliers of materials. The total investment commitment for the company could now reach 1.7 billion dollars including the existing fund and new investment arm.

Kevin Zhang is the senior vice president and deputy co-chief operating officer who explained the company's strategy to Nikkei Asia. Zhang stated that TSMC intends to formalize its investment mechanism and extend its scope beyond the needs of its immediate customers. He explained that investing in Anthropic or OpenAI creates a reinforcing loop to build a richer, healthier, and bigger semiconductor ecosystem. Zhang noted that the company wants to support the future's Nvidia in addition to supporting the current version of the company. He also mentioned that the returns from the company's earlier investment fund had been exceptional for the semiconductor manufacturing giant.

The new fund will affect promising chip startups and suppliers who can now receive financial backing from the world's largest chipmaker. AI model developers like OpenAI and Anthropic are specifically affected as they seek custom chips to power their future computing needs. These firms are part of a broader strategy to ensure the semiconductor ecosystem remains healthy and grows during the AI boom. Other affected parties include suppliers of chemicals and advanced materials who now have access to TSMC's new investment arm activities. The initiative seeks to identify and support the next chip titans that could eventually rival the scale of Broadcom or Nvidia.

TSMC previously operated a 200 million dollar emerging fund that was launched in 2021 to help startups develop their new products. That earlier fund allowed startups to develop products using the advanced chip manufacturing technology provided by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. The current 500 million dollar fund is significantly larger than that 2021 fund which focused on the development of new products. The company is now seeing insatiable demand for chips, which has driven the need to broaden its overall semiconductor ecosystem. This background of success with earlier funds has led the company to increase its total investment commitment to 1.7 billion.

TSMC will now move forward with investing in AI firms and suppliers to create a more robust and reinforcing industry loop. The company will continue to back emerging chip companies that have the potential to become the next major global tech giants. TSMC indicated that it could expand its investment activities even further in the future if the company finds it is needed. The articles leave open exactly how many new startups will receive funding from the 500 million dollar venture capital fund. It remains unclear which specific suppliers of chemicals or materials will be the first to receive these new corporate investments.

stories.Headline: Caribbean AI Takes Center Stage on Wall Street as Future Caribbean Names Its Top Startups
stories.Summary:
Future Caribbean named Caribbean Grid AI, Neptune Analytics and Miracle as the standout companies of its investor showcase at the New York Stock Exchange on Friday evening, November 13, 2026. The event was co-hosted by Future Caribbean founder Lily Dash, with Silicon Valley venture capitalist Bill Tai joining virtually. The invitation-only evening brought 16 finalist founder teams before investors, family offices, diplomats and enterprise leaders. The showcase was the final stage of a programme launched in May at IDB Invest Sustainability Week in Barbados. More than 450 builders from 39 countries took part, with finalists selected through more than 2,000 reviews and over 600 one-to-one advisory sessions.

The programme was supported by a network of more than 200 advisors and judges and more than 48 partner organizations. The evening opened with remarks from Brian Baumann, Global Head of Technology Ecosystems at the NYSE, followed by a virtual address from Minister Williams. Williams noted that 56 Jamaican builders took part in the programme and eight Jamaican teams reached the finals. The showcase was supported by sponsors Andrik Capital, Invest Barbados and Polymath Research, event partner Lingnum Security Limited, and Book Better as official travel sponsor. The programme itself ran on Buildathon-in-a-Box, Future Caribbean's agentic platform, which coordinated around 1,200 participants and more than 600 one-to-one advisory calls.

Fayval Williams, Jamaica's Minister of Finance and the Public Service, told the room that the Caribbean should not watch the AI transformation happen but help shape it. Williams told the finalists, "You made us proud. Extremely proud." She said the companies show that when you build carefully, for real users and to last, a solution that makes it in the Caribbean can make it anywhere. She said Jamaica wants to work with serious partners on practical problems like these. Lily Dash, Founder of Future Caribbean, said Caribbean founders showed investors, diplomats and enterprise leaders at the New York Stock Exchange that category-defining companies can come from anywhere.

Dash said the winners stood out, but every team on that stage is building technology that solves real problems at home and can serve customers around the world. She said Future Caribbean is now focused on turning these conversations into investment, partnerships and revenue. Bill Tai described how a single Caribbean nation can serve as a testbed to get a product running before it is replicated across the region. He pointed to a moment when agentic AI is allowing companies with a handful of employees to build at global scale. Senior diplomatic and institutional leaders in attendance included Aubrey Webson, Antigua and Barbuda's Ambassador to the United Nations, and Oliver Mair, Jamaica's Consul General in New York.

Representatives of the Consulate General of The Bahamas, Invest Barbados and UNDP also attended. On the investor side, Brian Feuer, former Global Head of Portfolio Management at McKinsey, was joined by Steven Grin of Lateral Frontiers VC, Krishna Singh of GTCapital and Sergio Fernández de Córdova, Chairman of the PVBLIC Foundation. Intel was represented by Managing Director Mark Castleman and NVIDIA by Principal Solutions Architect Anton Alexander and scientist Camir Ricketts. OCEANIX co-founder and CEO Itai Madamombe and World Identity Network founder Mariana Dahan, who previously led the World Bank's Identification for Development agenda, brought expertise in ocean infrastructure and digital identity. Cultural figures in the room ranged from Barbadian singer-songwriter JusJay to Shelley Worrell, founder of Brooklyn's Little Caribbean.

Two of the three winners are tackling the Caribbean's energy problem, while the third is taking on one of its most stretched health services. When Barbados Light & Power set Caribbean Grid AI a forecasting challenge, the Barbados-based team beat the utility's benchmark by 12%. Founded by data analyst Andrew Narine, the platform draws on ten years of local solar and wind data to help grid operators decide when to store, dispatch, hold or curtail renewable power. The utility is now reviewing it as Barbados works toward its renewable energy targets. Caribbean power producers spend around US$8.5 billion a year on imported fuel, and roughly US$4 billion of it escapes as waste heat.

Trinidad and Tobago's Neptune Analytics, founded by Simon Neptune, is turning that loss into electricity by capturing heat from sources as low as 60°C, well below the 200°C most existing systems require. The company has already secured a non-binding letter of intent for 20 megawatts of capacity at a power plant in Tobago. Miracle began with an injury: occupational therapist Brenda Luo hurt her hand and could not get therapy at her local clinic. Her answer turns an ordinary mirror into an AR-guided, AI-coached rehab session that flags pain and logs progress for clinicians. Early testing in Alberta recorded 100% task completion at one site, and for the Caribbean, where rehab specialists are scarce, it means a single therapist can support far more patients at home.

All three winners will walk away with consulting hours from EY-Parthenon, giving them access to one of the world's leading strategy advisory teams as they take their products to market. Jamaica's Project Lighthouse, co-founded by Sammarieo Brown, is building a relief platform backed by a catastrophe bond that would pay citizens directly rather than routing funds through government. Field Watch AI, founded by Onassis Nottage, proposed a satellite and sensor pilot to monitor hurricane shelters in The Bahamas in real time. stories.Headline: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says AI will automate much of its customer service
stories.Summary:
Verizon CEO Dan Schulman said in a Fortune interview published on November 16, 2026, that AI will automate much of Verizon's customer service. Schulman spoke with Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell on the new episode of Fortune 500: Titans and Disruptors of Industry. He took the CEO seat about a year earlier, after Verizon's board asked him several times and he said no several times. His wife convinced him to take the job, and he left retirement on his Montana ranch, where he has 900 head of cattle. He is now a year into a three-year overhaul of a company he calls a "big, lumbering giant."

Schulman said Verizon had been losing market share for five years or so and had gone from first in market capitalization in its industry to last. He said Verizon had the lowest P/E, which he described as what the Street thinks of future growth potential. He said Verizon has 150 million lines and the largest customer base. He said the company had processes requiring something like 35 signatures before moving forward, and that he blew that up, saying surely no more than three or four people need to sign. He said he told employees at his first all-hands meeting that layoffs were likely and that Verizon needed to spend billions of dollars investing back into the business.

Schulman said culture is the single most important thing in any transformation. He said Verizon had been playing not to lose instead of playing to win, with engineering at the center of the culture instead of the customer. He said the culture was very bureaucratic, very hierarchical, almost like the military, and very siloed, and that it was risk-averse and afraid of failing. He said he is a one on the integrity of financial results, cybersecurity and compliance, but an eight or a nine on trying new things. He said he got thousands of emails after the all-hands meeting from employees glad he laid out the truth.

Schulman said he thought AGI was three, four or five years away but now thinks most experts see it as soon as a year away, with the most skeptical at three years. He said quantum hits commercially probably in 2028 or 2029, and that humanoid robotics will be pretty darn good by 2035 at the latest. He said 85% of models today are done through recursive self-improvement, which he described as AI building the next model of itself. He said Verizon increased phone net adds ninefold from a year earlier while cutting acquisition costs by 41%. He said he is preparing for Elon Musk to become a bigger competitor and for SpaceX to deliver on its ambitions.

Lucas Perez Echeimberg wrote in a Deseret News guest opinion published November 15, 2026, that poor service isn't an AI problem. He is a Brazilian tax lawyer with a graduate degree in tax law from the Pontifical Catholic University of São Paulo and a student in Avila University Arizona's Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence, and he lives in Utah. He wrote that on January 21, 2025, President Donald Trump presented a joint venture of up to $500 billion in AI infrastructure formed by OpenAI, Oracle and SoftBank. He wrote that on October 30, 2026, Bloomberg reported America's tech giants are funding about $750 billion in AI spending this year, paid for by their advertising, consumer and retail businesses.

He wrote that Salesforce, a leading U.S. software company that also sells AI agents, surveyed 3,075 customer service professionals worldwide. Echeimberg wrote that the survey found adoption of AI agents in customer service rose from 39% to 66% between 2025 and 2026. He wrote that after adopting them, companies reported customer satisfaction was the most improved metric, ahead of rep productivity, average handle time, customer retention and first-response time. He wrote that Brazil's recent Decree No. 13,135, in force since November 2, allows AI but requires a live human by phone from 8 a.m.

to 8 p.m., seven days a week, and the option to reach a person at every step. He wrote that Connecticut's new AI law, SB 5, exempts customer-service bots, and that Congress is weighing the Keep Call Centers in America Act, which would require transfer to a U.S.-based human on request. He wrote that companies should have the freedom to decide how they use AI, and that lawmakers should look at how well companies serve their customers. Schulman said he did not want to come back into the CEO job, calling such jobs all-consuming at 10 to 14 hours a day.

He said he was the lead independent director of Verizon's board and that the board probably should have acted sooner. He said he came in with a little bit of a bad attitude but a year later is absolutely loving the job and is pretty hopeful about the future. He said Verizon is positioning its fiber network and facilities to capitalize on the AI infrastructure buildout, and he sees satellite service as a complement to Verizon's network rather than a replacement. Echeimberg wrote that AI can be regulated as long as the rules follow certain principles while still allowing nations some flexibility for the sake of their technological progress, and he cited the philosopher Luciano Florid in 2019.

stories.Headline: Higgsfield releases AI Ad Generator for small businesses to create video adverts without studios
stories.Summary:
Higgsfield released an AI Ad Generator to help small businesses create video adverts without using a professional studio. This software allows owners in Harare, Bulawayo, and Mutare to produce content for social media. The tool turns product links or photos into finished videos without a filming crew. It targets firms selling clothes, hair products, hardware, school supplies, and various services. This shift moves production from traditional studios directly into a web browser.

The tool requires only a browser and a product description, not a server or special hardware. Users can upload five images or a link to extract names and descriptions. It offers over 40 avatars and nine modes, including UGC, Tutorial, Product Review, and Unboxing. Other modes are TV Spot, Hyper Motion, Wild Card, and two Virtual Try On options. Seedance 2.0 provides native audio and lip sync for 9:16, 16:9, and 1:1 shapes.

Higgsfield claims the process takes about two minutes from a product link to a final video. The company states the tool writes scripts, directs shots, and delivers the final cut. It says avatars can speak multiple languages, though English is the default setting. The provider notes that no design or editing experience is needed to use the suite. They suggest the tool acts as a drafting partner rather than an autopilot.

Small business owners are affected because traditional production is often too expensive or time consuming. These owners often lack the skills to write scripts, set up lighting, or edit video. Some diaspora entrepreneurs use the tool to reach customers both at home and abroad. Local users must ensure that generated scenes and accents sound credible to their audiences. They are warned not to present digital avatars as real customers giving reviews.

Interest grew after Zimbabwe launched its National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in March 2026. The government urged the private sector to invest in technology and partner with start ups. Officials planned to offer incentives to businesses that integrate AI into their operations. Many firms previously relied on single photos because they lacked cameras, presenters, and quiet locations. This background makes marketing a practical starting point where the cost of mistakes is low.

Users should next test several modes for one product to see which fits their customers. They must check that prices, features, and offers shown in the adverts are true. Businesses should track views, replies, and sales to measure the success of the clips. The articles leave the specific supported languages and the current pricing plans open. stories.Headline: Physicist Nathaniel Craig and GPT-6 Astra propose a lattice definition of the Standard Model
stories.Summary:
Physicist Nathaniel Craig, a visiting scientist at OpenAI, worked with GPT-6 Astra on a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model, as described in a guest post on OpenAI's science blog dated November 15, 2026. Craig leads the particle theory group at the University of California, Santa Barbara, and is a permanent member of its Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics. In an October preprint prepared with the aid of GPT-6 Astra, Craig proposed a candidate definition on a lattice, a grid representing spacetime. Craig had a strategy for tackling the problem but had not been able to prove it worked in all the cases it needed to cover. Astra helped turn that strategy into a construction and took the lead in developing the detailed proof.

The Standard Model describes the known elementary particles and three of the four fundamental forces: the strong force, the weak force, and electromagnetism. Its success rests on agreement between theoretical calculations and experiments across eighteen orders of magnitude, from the low energies of hydrogen's 21-centimeter radio emission to the high energies of collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. For more than fifty years a foundational problem has remained: how to give the full theory a nonperturbative definition that does not treat its interactions as small corrections. Perturbation theory has let physicists predict the strength of the electron's magnetism to within a few parts in a trillion. For the full Standard Model in continuous spacetime, there is no nonperturbative definition, or even an understanding of whether the interacting theory is mathematically well defined.

Craig wrote that a promising alternative is to discretize spacetime into a grid of points known as a lattice, whose spacing defines the shortest distance the theory can resolve. Studying a finite grid allows a rigorous nonperturbative definition of the theory at a given spacing and enables calculations on a computer without perturbation theory. This approach, lattice field theory, has led to remarkable progress in understanding the strong force, including a quantitative understanding of the proton's mass from first principles. Craig explained that the Standard Model is a chiral theory, meaning it looks different under reflection in space, because the weak force treats left- and right-handed fermions differently.

He wrote that putting chiral theories on a lattice is profoundly challenging, since the most natural rules give a left-handed fermion a right-handed partner you never asked for, a problem called doubling. Craig described an analogy with light, in which a box with ordinary mirrors turns left-circular light into right-circular light, much as doublers appear when a left-handed fermion is put on the lattice. He wrote that chiral mirrors made of special films whose molecules line up in layers can send left-handed light back left-handed and let right-handed light pass through. Such chiral mirrors have been around for more than a decade, and the phenomenon even occurs in nature, in the shiny shells of some scarab beetles.

Decades ago, Paul Ginsparg and Nobel laureate Ken Wilson worked out the lattice rules analogous to the requirement that chiral mirrors reverse the rotation of the electric field upon reflection. Rajamani Narayanan and Herbert Neuberger built the analog of the chiral mirrors by finding the necessary definition of fundamental particles on the lattice, known as overlap fermions. Martin Lüscher showed how to tell the difference between left-handed and right-handed overlap fermions on the lattice, while Yoshio Kikukawa and collaborators explored how this might be used to describe weak interactions in the Standard Model. Craig wrote that one piece was still missing, which he identified as getting the phase right.

He explained the optical phase by imagining water waves rolling past the pilings of a dock, and the relative phase of two waves determining how much they add or cancel at the same point. In a box with chiral mirrors, left-circular light bounces back and forth, and after a lap the returning light meets fresh light from the laser going in the same direction. If their electric fields are in step, the light builds up inside the box, and if the fields are half a cycle apart, the returning light cancels some of the fresh light. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Uber exits Nigeria and launches London robotaxis with Wayve as drivers describe falling pay
stories.Summary:
On 2 September, Uber confirmed it was discontinuing its operations in Nigeria after 12 years in one of Africa's biggest markets, and it announced a similar exercise in Uganda. Uber said the decision followed a review of its business priorities and investment focus across Africa. The next day, 3 September, Uber and British AI company Wayve launched supervised autonomous ride-hailing services in London, matching passengers with electric vehicles equipped with Wayve's AI Driver technology. The vehicles initially operated with licensed safety drivers onboard, following global restructuring plans that included cutting about 3,300 jobs. Isiaka Agbaje, 42, a cab driver at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos, said the ride-hailing business no longer pays his bills.

The move redirected savings and investments into autonomous vehicles and robotaxi partnerships, and Uber did not officially link its exit from the Nigerian market to investment in AI efficiency. Premium Times gathered responses from nearly a dozen cab drivers operating in Lagos, Nigeria's commercial nerve centre, Abuja and other parts of the country. Samuel Adeoti put Uber's commission at 35 per cent and gave a hypothetical example of a ₦10,000 trip, from which he said Uber deducted ₦3,500, leaving ₦6,500 with the driver. After spending about ₦5,000 on fuel, he said a driver would have just ₦1,500 left to cover other costs including car maintenance and dealings with the task force, police and road safety. In 2023, shortly after being sworn in, President Bola Tinubu introduced sweeping reforms in Nigeria's foreign exchange market and the downstream petroleum sector, abolishing what the government termed a wasteful subsidy regime and harmonising the foreign exchange market.

Lanre Mustapha, an ex-Uber driver, said the company failed to adequately address drivers' complaints about fares and commissions amid sky-high domestic prices. He said drivers had protested against low fares about six months before Uber left Nigeria, but the company failed to address their concerns. Mustapha said he migrated to InDrive and described uncertainty over account suspensions there as a major challenge, saying workers can wake up to find themselves permanently blocked without stated reasons. John Promise, 39, another driver on the platform, said drivers remained because they had no better options and did not want to lose access to their customers. Innocent Ogwuche, another ex-Uber driver, said he initially had a positive experience because of the app and safety features, but things changed when fuel prices increased and automated fares failed to keep pace with operating costs.

Ogwuche said Uber is not the one fuelling the car or doing the maintenance, and he lamented inadequate compensation for trips delayed by traffic. He said he repeatedly faced technical problems while accessing his driver account, which contributed to his decision to leave the platform. Abubakar Aliyu, a cab driver based in Abuja, said a union, the Amalgamated Union of App-Based Transport Workers of Nigeria (AUTTWON), represents ride-hailing and app-based transport drivers such as those on Bolt and InDrive. He said the union uses strikes, fare boycotts and court actions to push back against algorithmic control, but platforms often treat workers as independent contractors rather than employees. Aliyu said platforms use legal technicalities and grey areas to avoid collective bargaining agreements and demands for better service conditions, adding that the union is engaging rather slowly and faces challenges.

Earlier this year, the World Bank released a report titled World Development Report 2026: The Promise of Artificial Intelligence, which assesses how AI impacts 5.6 billion people in low- and middle-income countries. The report showed that AI offers a rare path to accelerate growth at a time when global development progress has dipped to its weakest pace in 75 years, and it can help bridge chronic gaps in health, agricultural guidance for farmers and basic administrative support for governments. It urged policymakers to follow a structured three-step approach: adopt existing AI tools, tailor the tools to local realities and develop the technology. The report cautioned that traditional work faces targeted white-collar disruption, entry-level hiring freezes and widening productivity gaps, and it warned that economic benefits from AI tend to flow toward business and capital owners rather than wage workers. It said mass automation is less immediate in developing economies, where only 4.5 per cent of jobs are highly exposed compared to 14.2 per cent in wealthy nations.

On 22 October, Uber announced a separate expansion of its AI adoption, making ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees globally after an initial pilot involving 1,000 workers. Through initiatives like Uber AI Solutions and Digital Tasks, Uber also lets drivers and contractors earn money by labelling data, recording voice prompts and evaluating AI responses during downtime. Digital labour sociologist Antonio Casilli describes this move as a "Great Digital Labour Convergence", adding that merging physical gig work with micro-task data labelling normalises underpaid, algorithmically managed work across more industries while threatening traditional employment protections. He argued that platforms serve as testing grounds where industrialists experiment with ideas they plan to roll out across all labour markets, and that even traditionally stable professions have begun to absorb gig-like features such as flexible scheduling, task-based pay, algorithmic oversight and precarious autonomy. In their book, 'Notes Towards a Digital Worker's Enquiry', Julie Chen, a professor of communications and digital labour, and other scholars examined how previously viewed "unorganizable" digital and precarious workforces are building collective resistance and identifying tactical chokepoints within platform capitalism.

stories.Headline: Downing Street aide reads ChatGPT feedback on Burnham speech draft on train
stories.Summary:
An unnamed Downing Street speechwriter was photographed on Friday reading ChatGPT’s suggestions for making the prime minister’s speech more emotive, according to the Mail on Sunday. The aide to Andy Burnham was seen on the 5.03pm train from London Euston to Holyhead as Burnham and his team headed to the Welsh Labour conference with a bottle of bubbly. The pictures were taken while the aide sipped prosecco and read the AI chatbot’s feedback on a passage criticising the legacy of Margaret Thatcher. An image of the aide’s phone screen showed ChatGPT commenting on lines about Thatcher’s impact on working men’s clubs, choirs and other social infrastructure in the 1980s. Burnham later delivered the speech at the Welsh Labour Conference in Llandudno, in northern Wales, and did not use the specific passage seen in the pictures.

The chatbot said it preferred the second passage because it moves from the miners to their families to the wider community, showing how industrial work created bonds beyond the workplace. In the speech, Burnham said Thatcher shattered the way of life for communities up and down Britain with mines closed, factories closed and steelworks silenced. He also said cost of living is the top issue in Wales, as it is in all parts of the UK. Burnham spoke of the workplaces that created a way of life, the social infrastructure taken for granted, the working men’s clubs, the sports teams, the choirs and the trade unions, adding that people came together and looked out for each other. Elsewhere he said Labour had lost power in Wales after elections earlier this year, that the party may have lost sight of the principles that drove devolution, and that for the first time in its history Labour is not leading the Welsh Government.

A No 10 spokesperson said the PM writes most of his own speeches and that an aide sought feedback on a speech draft that had already been written. The Express reported the spokesperson saying the PM writes most of his own speeches and this one was no exception. Reform UK chairman Lee Anderson told the Mail on Sunday that it must be thirsty work writing speeches for Burnham. Anderson said his bubbly-drinking socialists have no plan to tackle the cost-of-living crisis and that AI Andy’s man-of-the-people act has been exposed as a sham. He added that Burnham is an artificial prime minister who does not have the faintest clue what he believes or what he is doing.

The use of ChatGPT and other AI chatbots by politicians and their aides has drawn plenty of attention since the tech first emerged earlier this decade. Addressing the House of Commons last year, Conservative MP Tom Tugendhat blasted colleagues for supposedly using AI to write their own speeches, saying the phrase I rise to speak is a giveaway. Tugendhat said all they were hearing was the ChatGPT generated press releases. He said ChatGPT knows you’re there, but that is an Americanism we don’t use, and told colleagues to keep using it because it makes clear the place has become absurd. The Express reported that the AI tool suggested using an emotive passage describing working men’s clubs, choirs and other social infrastructure lost as Britain moved away from its industrial base.

The photographs were taken on Friday as Burnham and his team travelled to the Welsh Labour conference, and the speech was delivered on Saturday. The Mail on Sunday published the pictures of the aide’s phone screen showing ChatGPT’s feedback on the Thatcher passage. The articles do not say whether the aide faced any disciplinary action or whether Downing Street investigated the matter further. They do not name the speechwriter or say how the photographs were obtained. They also do not say whether Burnham commented on the photographs himself.

Many publicly traded Japanese companies reported higher profits for the first half of the current business year ending in March. These financial gains occurred during the period from April to September and were driven by the ongoing artificial intelligence boom. Firms within the manufacturing sector performed particularly well as they capitalized on the robust demand for new technology. Several of these organizations have already revised their full-year earnings forecasts upward to reflect this growth. The current economic shift requires these companies to adapt their production and financial planning to meet the surging demand for AI.

This trend changes the outlook for the manufacturing sector by increasing the expected revenue for the remainder of the fiscal year. Every firm that closes its books in March must now account for these unexpected gains in their official reports. The surge in profits indicates a broader transition toward integrating artificial intelligence across various industrial applications. Yoshimitsu Goto, who serves as the Senior Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of SoftBank Group, spoke about these developments.

He addressed the current business climate during an online news conference held on Tuesday to discuss the financial landscape. While the specific details of his remarks were not fully detailed, his presence highlighted the importance of the AI boom. He represents a major player in the technology sector that is closely monitoring these market shifts. The broader context involves a period of significant growth for Japanese firms despite growing uncertainty in the global market.

These companies are leveraging the AI boom to strengthen their positions against international competitors in the tech space. Future reports will likely determine if this profit trend continues through the end of the business year. stories.Headline: Armin Ashenberg argues universities must teach graduates to collaborate with AI as automation reshapes the job market
stories.Summary:
Dr Armin D Ashenberg of the School of Law at Western Sydney University wrote an opinion piece first published with full links on The Conversation. The piece was also published by Western Sydney University on 16 November 2026. It addresses concerns about artificial intelligence taking people's jobs and reducing job opportunities for university graduates. AI software companies such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic are pursuing AI systems capable of matching or exceeding human performance across a broad range of intellectual tasks. The article asks what this means for graduates and universities and which jobs are most at risk.

A federal government report published in July rated jobs typically involving cognitive tasks as those with the highest exposure to AI automation, including accountants, clerks and receptionists. Jobs rated as lowest exposure tended to require more physical work, such as tradies, carers and truck drivers. The report found that as of February this year AI had not had significant impacts on the Australian job market, including graduate opportunities. This month the Reserve Bank of Australia noted some signs younger workers in more AI-exposed industries are struggling to find work in Australia. The number of graduate jobs in some law firms has been slashed, with low-level tasks passed onto AI, and consulting firms have also cut graduate roles in recent years but claim it is not because of AI.

Just last week Qantas announced it will outsource 850 jobs to India while investing more in AI. A 2024 study compared the reasoning skills of humans and AI language models through tests including maths puzzles designed to assess whether people and AI models could recognise that an answer, which seems right at first, is actually wrong. In the example given, a scarf costs 210€ more than a hat, the scarf and the hat cost 220€ in total, and the correct answer for the hat is 5€. Researchers found earlier AI systems performed worse than human participants in the study's reasoning test, while more recent AI models performed better. An OpenAI model recently disproved a longstanding conjecture in geometry dating back to 1946.

Ashenberg's own research analysed AI's responses on university criminal law exams in 2023 and 2025, finding average exam scores improved from 52.5% in 2023 to 76.3% in 2025. Unlike the 2023 study, the 2025 models on average performed better than an average university student on critical thinking capabilities. These were specific tests and do not prove AI could displace humans and take over an entire profession, but the results challenge the assumption AI weaknesses will remain unchanged. Robotaxis carry passengers in a growing number of cities, delivery robots bring meals to customers and autonomous excavators dig on construction sites. In a 2026 pilot study health-care professionals, mostly nurses, accepted half the deliberately wrong AI recommendations and passed over about one in six correct ones.

In a study looking at how the UK public uses AI for medical advice, researchers found people sometimes left out important details when consulting chatbots, so the chatbots sometimes mixed useful suggestions with misleading ones. The article is part of a series on how AI is reshaping higher education, taking a deeper look into how AI has disrupted degrees, how universities are responding and what the technology means for the sector's future. The article states that if a sufficiently capable AI could control reliable, affordable robots then electricians and plumbers could also face competition. It adds that despite significant progress in robots' ability to carry out complex physical tasks it is still unclear how soon they will be able to do more of the work tradies do. For now, students who choose vocational pathways such as apprenticeships may face a lower risk of AI-related job disruption.

The article argues the possibility of humans working with AI should be central to how universities prepare students for the workforce, because if a worker can't improve the quality or efficiency of AI's output an employer may have little economic reason to involve them. It says graduates may need to understand what a good result looks like when using AI, recognise when AI falls short, and have the knowledge and skills to improve AI's output. It says they also need to learn how to collaborate with AI, how to direct it, question its output and persist until the result is better than what it produced initially. It states universities can't simply replace disciplinary knowledge with AI skills, and students will need the knowledge and skills their degrees have always required as well as the ability to collaborate effectively with AI. It concludes that a technology designed to make our lives easier may actually require us to work harder to stay relevant in the job market.

stories.Headline: Young South Koreans use AI to create fake funeral portraits as a prank
stories.Summary:
Young South Koreans are using generative artificial intelligence to create fake funeral portraits of themselves or their friends as a joke. This social media trend was reported on November 15, 2026, as a growing practice among the youth in Seoul. The prank involves posting these AI images on Instagram accompanied by memorial messages to trick people into thinking they died. Many of these posts are designed to look like genuine death announcements to confuse the people who see them. This trend has prompted various news reports to call for tighter regulation of the online platforms where they appear.

The posts feature black and white images styled as funeral portraits with phrases like Rest in peace or You will always be remembered. Some images include fabricated dates of death and dates of birth, along with white chrysanthemums and black ribbons for added realism. This specific practice has recently gained popularity among teenagers and people in their 20s as a prank among close friends. The images are shared on Instagram, which is the primary platform where this surge of AI generated content is occurring. These visual elements make the fake portraits very difficult to distinguish from real announcements of a person's passing.

Kim Si-deok is a professor in the department of funeral services at Eulji University who spoke to the South Korean media. He stated that younger generations are increasingly taking the significance of death and funeral traditions lightly through this specific social trend. The professor warned that this behavior trivialises death and urged online platforms to take steps to prevent such content from spreading. Meta, the parent company of Instagram, responded by saying it removes or restricts content that violates its community standards. The company told a local news outlet that it will continue working with outside organisations to maintain a safe environment.

Some people who are aware of the prank ask what food they should prepare for the fake memorial service in comments. Others are unaware that the posts are fake and offer sincere condolences, saying it is heartbreaking to see someone die young. Experts are affected by this trend and have called for stronger action from social media platforms to stop the practice. Meta noted that users can report manipulated images of private individuals, including minors, that are shared without their own consent. The company claims it promptly removes such content following a review to protect the users on its social platform.

The articles provide background on how generative AI is being used to create these deceptive images for social media entertainment. This trend is part of a broader context of AI use in South Korea, including fake chats and exam cheating. One mentioned case involved a man making over 100 prank calls to police to be sent to a jail. Another instance involved an actor named Lee Yi kyung whose lewd chats were created by an accuser using AI tools. These examples show a pattern of using artificial intelligence for deception or pranks within the South Korean society.

Meta will continue to review and remove manipulated images of private individuals that are reported by users on the Instagram platform. The company intends to keep working with relevant outside organisations to ensure that the social media environment remains safe. The articles leave open whether the calls for tighter regulation of online platforms will lead to new laws or rules. It is unclear if the trend among teenagers and people in their 20s will decrease after these expert warnings. The reports do not state if any specific legal actions will be taken against those posting the fake portraits.

stories.Headline: Google agrees to pay $10 million for Spirit Airlines corporate data
stories.Summary:
Google agreed to pay $10 million for bankrupt Spirit Airlines’ corporate data, covering some 31 years of internal workflows, Cedar News reported on 2026-11-15. Cedar News said a new market is taking shape around one of businesses’ most overlooked assets, their internal data. The Cedar News item appeared under the headline that frontier labs are buying up internal company data to train AI. Cedar News said the marketplace is booming, despite privacy concerns. The potential payouts are substantial, Cedar News said.

Bain & Company estimated spending of up to US$6.5tn to build nearly 150GW of new compute capacity by 2030. Bain expected 20, 30% growth in data centre critical capacity over the next five years. Hyperscalers’ data centre CapEx could top US$1tn by 2028, Bain said. The number of semiconductor companies manufacturing the most advanced logic node fell 84%, from 25 companies in 2002, 2003 to 4 companies from 2020-2026. Global data centre electricity demand is estimated to more than double from an estimated 589TWh in 2026 to 1,228TWh in 2030, and North America’s virtual power plant market is 37.5GW.

Adam Mayer, Technical Product Marketing Director at Qlik, wrote in TechRadar on 13 November 2026 that data privacy is becoming harder to manage as businesses give AI applications and agents access to more internal systems. Mayer said much of the focus has been on the risk of AI models surfacing sensitive or confidential information in their responses, but the privacy challenge starts earlier. He said organizations also need to understand what data AI systems can access in the first place, where that data comes from and how it is being used. Mayer said 95% of enterprises have delayed or cancelled AI projects because of infrastructure and data governance challenges. He said businesses need to get the foundations right before privacy risks become impossible to contain.

Mayer said data privacy is not just a legal or compliance concern and should matter to everyone who touches data within an organization. He said the consequences of getting it wrong are growing, from exposing sensitive information to damaging customer trust and brand reputation. Mayer said poorly classified, duplicated or outdated data can carry existing privacy problems into AI applications, turning weaknesses previously contained within individual systems into much wider risks. He said agentic AI raises the stakes further because agents can increasingly surface and act on information across multiple parts of the business. Mayer said personally identifiable information such as names, addresses or financial details should be clearly labelled so it can be spotted before it is moved.

Mayer said identifying sensitive data is only the first step in managing the privacy challenge. He said businesses also need to track where it moves, particularly when information is copied from live systems into testing or development environments which may not have the same security controls in place. He said sensitive information should remain within the live systems where it is needed wherever possible. Mayer said removing or masking identifying details can reduce the risk of unnecessary exposure if data does need to be used elsewhere. Bain said building AI-ready data centres is proving as much a test of supply chains and power infrastructure as it is of capital.

Bain’s figures were drawn from the December Week 1 edition of Data Centre Magazine, which sets out the scale of the challenge from the spending required to deliver nearly 150GW of new compute capacity by 2030 to the shrinking number of manufacturers able to produce the most advanced chips. Bain’s figures also point to sharply rising electricity demand and a growing virtual power plant market in North America. Cedar News said the potential payouts are substantial, evidenced by Google’s agreement to pay $10 million for Spirit Airlines’ corporate data. TechRadar published Mayer’s opinion piece on 13 November 2026 under the title that AI privacy starts with your data. Data Centre Magazine published its Bain statistics article on November 15, 2026.

stories.Headline: Dublin City Council pilots AI flood warning system with EMR Integrated Solutions
stories.Summary:
Dublin City Council will pilot a new artificial intelligence early warning system for major flood events in Dublin City, the Irish Examiner reported on Monday, 16 November, 2026. The project is run in partnership with critical infrastructure specialist EMR Integrated Solutions, which gathered the sensor data used by the model. The pilot is set to run through this autumn and winter, according to the Irish Examiner. Silicon Republic reported that the rollout covers the autumn and winter of late 2026 and early 2027. Trials of the technology using historical events showed potential early warnings of 13 to 21 hours for some mountain rain-driven events.

The AI model draws on ten years' worth of sensor data gathered by EMR Integrated Solutions, including river level readings, rainfall measurements, tide data and data from Met Éireann. The project could warn between 13 and 21 hours ahead of events, which Dublin City Council says will give staff and response teams more time to prepare and act. EMR has operated Dublin City Council's regional flood monitoring system for nine years through outstations in the city and surrounding counties that monitor rainfall, river levels, tide readings and more. EMR was founded in the 1980s and is based in Dunboyne, Co Meath, and works with sectors including water, power, utilities, corporate business, broadcasting and public safety organisations. EMR has an agreement with Dublin City Council to provide engineers to support the council's flood management through associated site work, installations, repairs and instrument calibration.

Minister for Climate, Environment and Energy Darragh O'Brien, TD, welcomed the initiative and said the single most valuable thing we can give people is time. O'Brien said the pilot shows how AI can turn the data we already have into earlier, clearer warnings, helping engineers and emergency services make better decisions when it matters most. He said he very much welcomed the initiative from EMR Integrated Solutions and Dublin City Council and looked forward to seeing the results. Dublin City Council chief executive Richard Shakespeare said the pilot is likely to demonstrate how technology and data can be harnessed to support better decision-making and improve preparedness for flooding events. Shakespeare said the council is committed to further embracing appropriate AI technology that helps protect communities, homes and critical infrastructure as climate change increases the frequency and intensity of severe weather events.

EMR chief commercial officer Mark O'Connor said we know we can't stop the rain, nor can we prevent every flood, but we can potentially give people something they cannot buy, time to prepare and prevent, and time for the council to take action. Dennis Keeley, Dublin City Council's assistant chief executive for climate and urban resilience, said one of the greatest challenges during flooding events is ensuring operational teams have sufficient time to deploy resources, protect critical infrastructure and respond effectively to emerging risks. Keeley said the AI technology could help reduce disruption to communities, minimise damage to public assets and enhance public safety during extreme weather events. According to EMR, a central principle for the pilot system is that all decisions remain with qualified Dublin City Council staff, who can review and interpret alerts generated by the AI model based on its analysis of signals and patterns in the relevant data. EMR said the project aims to allow timely delivery of accurate and relevant information to residents who may be affected, supporting greater awareness, preparedness and community resilience.

Shakespeare said the pilot aligns strongly with the ambitions set out in the Dublin City Council Corporate Plan, particularly the commitment to building a climate-resilient city and delivering high-quality public services through innovation and collaboration. He referred to recent engagements with telemetry and SCADA provider EMR Integrated Solutions. O'Brien said we have seen in the past the devastating effect flooding has on homes, businesses and communities around Dublin. The Irish Examiner reported that trials of the tech show it can give between 13 and 21 hours of early warnings for some mountain rain-driven events. The AI model will rapidly analyse the data sets provided to staff and then give a more reliable warning of conditions which could lead to serious flooding.

The pilot is set to run through this autumn and winter, and Silicon Republic reported the rollout covers the autumn and winter of late 2026 and early 2027. O'Brien said he looked forward to seeing the results of the initiative from EMR Integrated Solutions and Dublin City Council. Shakespeare said the pilot is likely to demonstrate how technology and data can be harnessed to support better decision-making and improve preparedness for flooding events. According to EMR, all decisions remain with qualified Dublin City Council staff, who can review and interpret alerts generated by the AI model. The articles do not state what will happen after the pilot ends or whether the system will be made permanent.

stories.Headline: GIGABYTE launches AI TOP AERO desktop for local AI development and content creation
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE announced the launch of the AI TOP AERO personal AI studio on November 16, 2026, in the city of Taipei. This new desktop computer is powered by the NVIDIA RTX Spark platform to expand the local AI solutions offered by GIGABYTE. The system is designed to bring local AI development, gaming, and content creation directly into personal workspaces for various professional users. It allows users to run larger AI models locally on their own devices without needing to depend on cloud computing services. This product combines a GPU with NVIDIA Blackwell architecture and a compact chassis design to create a powerful and thin PC.

The AI TOP AERO uses the NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X Superchip, which integrates a 20 core NVIDIA Grace CPU and Blackwell GPU. It runs on Windows 11 and offers up to 128 GB of LPDDR5x unified memory and a 4 TB PCIe Gen5 SSD. The compact chassis measures approximately one liter and includes USB Type-C, 10 GbE Ethernet, and Wi-Fi 7 for connecting various external peripherals. It supports NVIDIA DLSS 5 for gaming and uses NVIDIA PAIR to distribute inference tasks across a local network of available devices. The system is built to handle professional workloads and AI inference through a specialized GIGABYTE cooling design for thermal headroom.

GIGABYTE is responsible for the hardware integration and the cooling design that maintains performance during long periods of high professional workloads. The company stated that the AI TOP AERO responds to needs for data privacy, faster response times, and lower usage costs. They explained that the device integrates AI technology into the daily tools, personal data, and existing workflows of the target users. GIGABYTE noted that their hardware experience allows this compact format to provide the necessary performance for prolonged and demanding computing use. The company claims the system provides a fluid experience by integrating various applications, tools, and workflows into one single personal studio.

The product is specifically targeted at developers, creators, and AI users who want to process data and test applications on their devices. Developers can use the NVIDIA CUDA platform to create, prototype, tune, and run the latest open models locally on the system. These users can employ NVIDIA Nemotron compatible models and CUDA accelerated tools to explore local inference and agentic AI application testing. Content creators can use ComfyUI for generative AI workflows, while NVIDIA Broadcast and RTX Video improve the quality of audio and video. Gamers are affected by the inclusion of neural rendering, which provides more detailed lighting and materials in supported games via DLSS 5.

The articles state that generative AI is moving beyond conversational assistants toward AI agents, content generation, and the automation of various workflows. Users are seeking more personal AI computing options to maintain privacy and control over their data while avoiding the costs of cloud. GIGABYTE previously expanded its local AI development options by making the 64 GB unified memory version of the AI TOP ATOM available. The company also received a CES 2027 Innovation Award for its AORUS C510 GLASS INFINITY tower, showing its ongoing focus on hardware. This new studio is an extension of the current range of AI solutions that GIGABYTE provides for the global market.

The AI TOP AERO was scheduled for official release on November 10, 2026, to provide a new option for local AI development. Users can utilize additional compatible tools such as Ollama and LM Studio to create a local AI environment tailored to individual needs. The system allows for continuous agents to be available 24 hours a day while keeping all inference and data on device. The articles leave the specific pricing and the exact availability in different regions open for users to check via local communications. They do not specify the exact cost of the different memory configurations or the specific retail partners for the product.
