stories.Headline: Thirty-one states enact AI election laws while nineteen states have none as of October 2026
stories.Summary:
Thirty-one states enacted laws regulating artificial intelligence in election campaigns by October 2026, according to SciLine. Nineteen states had no such laws on the books by that same date. The United States still has no federal rule written for AI political advertising. These figures frame a debate about how elections affect technology policy. The AI industry has watched this cycle closely.

State laws mostly target deepfakes and require labels on AI-generated content. The Federal Communications Commission banned AI-generated voices in robocalls in 2024 under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act. In 2024, the Federal Election Commission declined to create a dedicated federal rule on deceptive AI campaign advertisements. These rules vary by state, creating a patchwork for campaigns and vendors. No federal statute specifically governs AI in political advertising as of October 2026.

The Federal Election Commission said its existing prohibition on fraudulent misrepresentation is technology neutral. The agency stated that a lie in a campaign ad is a lie regardless of the producer. This choice favors case-by-case enforcement over a bright-line statute. The FCC acted on a delivery channel it already regulates. Neither federal agency has a mandate to police AI-generated video on social platforms.

Campaigns must now track which assets need disclosure in which states to avoid complaints. Broadcasters must decide if they are responsible for missing labels on aired ads. Platforms face costs for moderation at scale because federal rules are thin. AI vendors often adopt the strictest common denominator to avoid tracking thirty-one rulebooks. These actors are affected by the lack of a national definition or disclosure rule.

The articles state that AI election policy often lurches after viral fakes and then stalls. Most state laws target synthetic media rather than general-purpose AI to survive constitutional scrutiny. Some states without laws may rely on older fraud or defamation statutes. Sam Altman told Bloomberg House in January 2024 that America and AI would be fine. Federal power often flows toward national security framing before consumer or election framing.

A single federal standard could eventually replace the current inconsistency with one rule. This federal framework might displace stricter state requirements, which some advocacy groups resist. The record does not show a specific policy change tied to the recent vote. It remains open whether a federal overhaul will occur or if the split persists. stories.Headline: US restricts remote AI compute access for China and other embargoed nations

The Trump administration announced new export controls on Monday to stop companies in China and other restricted nations from remotely accessing AI infrastructure. These rules target the D:5 group of embargoed countries, which includes Russia, Iran, North Korea, China, and 18 other nations. The Commerce Department now requires licenses to export, transfer, or reexport AI chips and servers to any global data center providing compute to these restricted entities. This action follows the resignation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang and reports that a customer named Megaspeed bought thousands of chips to bypass existing laws.

The new regulations apply to any network or data center with a total processing performance over 12 million, which equals roughly 750 Nvidia H200 or H100 chips. Licensing requirements are also now mandatory for advanced semiconductor transfers to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to higher risks of diversion. Existing operators must obtain licenses within 90 days, although the rules do not apply to commercial recommendation systems used for social media or e-commerce. Additionally, the administration rescinded the January 2025 AI Diffusion Rule from the Biden era to remove unnecessary restrictions on allies and American firms.

The Commerce Department stated that these restrictions are a logical extension of current controls designed to undermine the ability of concerning countries to train advanced Super Intelligence models. Officials explained that such computing power could support intelligence or military activities that threaten foreign policy interests or the national security of the United States. The government believes these changes prevent the use of specific items at power levels capable of running advanced models. This move comes as Chinese AI firms reportedly rush to secure overseas computing capacity before further restrictions are implemented.

stories.Headline: Ralf Seifert proposes a five stage model to move procurement teams from AI pilots to autonomy
stories.Summary:
Ralf Seifert published an article on November 16, 2026, regarding the use of artificial intelligence in procurement. He explains that many procurement teams are currently testing AI agents without having a formal plan. The author proposes a five stage maturity model to help these organizations map their journey toward scale. This process aims to move teams from initial pilots to a fully autonomous state of operation. Scaling these tools requires clear ownership, trusted data, governance, and specific organizational skills.

The maturity model consists of five stages called aligned, organized, data ready, augmented, and autonomous. This transformation requires a spend data platform, enterprise resource planning integration, and strict model governance. In October 2026, the software company SAP showcased the autonomous enterprise at its Connect conference. Novartis presented a sourcing assistant pilot co developed with SAP to handle tactical sourcing work. This specific agent promised 35 percent higher productivity and 25 percent faster cycle times.

Ralf Seifert states that endless pilots alone will not build the necessary organizational readiness for scale. He argues that organizations must develop their mindset, skillset, and toolset together to achieve success. The author notes that value does not scale before the first three stages are complete. He suggests that leaders should match the level of autonomy to the specific risk involved. This includes giving agents defined spending limits and access rights while retaining human oversight.

A survey by ProcureAbility in October 2026 found that 68 percent of senior leaders tested AI without plans. Only 8 percent of those same senior procurement leaders had a defined plan for AI implementation. Dirk Holbach, former chief supply chain officer of Henkel Consumer Brands, said the industry is in a hype cycle. Luca Nanni, chief procurement officer at Philip Morris International, said manual spreadsheets prevent AI scaling. Nanni noted that his organization had to redesign its operating model and processes to succeed.

The articles state that the main impediment to scaling AI is a lack of organizational adoption. Success requires an owner, quality data, and guardrails, as well as models that work in daily use. The first three stages of the maturity model deliver little more than basic visibility. Savings leakage, supply risk, and price variance are only tackled once a team reaches Stage 4. Early stage teams often pick use cases from vendor demos and estimate value only once.

The author provides ten questions for leaders covering ambition, leadership, value, ownership, skills, governance, data, scaling, autonomy, and competitiveness. These questions focus on organizational challenges rather than technology because people are more likely to be bottlenecks. Advanced teams rank a portfolio by value and validate their savings with finance departments. The text does not state how many organizations have successfully reached the autonomous stage. It leaves open how long the transition through the five stages typically takes.

stories.Headline: Max Roser finds every high-quality US survey shows more negative than positive views on AI
stories.Summary:
Max Roser of Our World in Data published an article on November 16, 2026, comparing recent high-quality surveys of American views on artificial intelligence. He wrote that he searched for a range of recent high-quality surveys and put them together in one chart. He said he was cautious about surveys because answers can shift when a question is worded slightly differently or when respondents can choose from different options. Every survey he included found that more Americans have a negative view of AI than a positive one. He wrote that he was surprised by how consistent the overall result is.

In Pew's survey, 52% say they are more concerned than excited and 9% are more excited than concerned, a ratio of more than five to one. When Pew first asked this in 2021, the ratio was about two to one. When a middle answer is offered, 37% took it in Pew's recent survey, and in both Pew's and Gallup's surveys only 9% chose a positive view. In the Ipsos survey, 17% said AI is an extremely bad thing for society and just 2% said extremely good. In a Quinnipiac poll in September 2026, 35% said they are somewhat concerned and 38% very concerned that future AI systems could threaten human survival, and 73% believe such a risk exists.

Pew's survey found that 56% of Democrats and 49% of Republicans are more concerned than excited about AI, and in both parties only around one in ten are more excited than concerned. Roser wrote that many find the prospects of AI exciting, but for more Americans the concerns are larger. He wrote that if the industry wants to earn the public's trust, it will have to take these widespread concerns much more seriously than it has so far. Pew's survey covered 3,488 US adults on the American Trends Panel, conducted June 22 to 28, 2026, with November 2021 data from the same panel conducted November 1 to 7, 2021. The Gallup and Bentley University survey covered 3,270 US adults on the Gallup Panel, conducted May 4 to 11, 2026.

The Quinnipiac poll was released March 30, 2026, based on a telephone survey of 1,397 US adults conducted March 19 to 23, 2026. The Annenberg Public Policy Center survey covered 1,320 US adults, conducted June 16 to July 19, 2026. The Ipsos survey for ABC News and The Washington Post covered 2,545 US adults on the Ipsos KnowledgePanel, conducted October 9 to 13, 2026. In the same Ipsos survey, 50% said AI is a good thing for them personally and 49% a bad thing, while 15% said it is extremely bad for them personally against 3% who said extremely good. In Quinnipiac's March 2026 poll, 55% expected AI to do more harm than good in their day-to-day life against 34% who expected more good.

Roser included only surveys based on probability samples, and Quinnipiac called randomly generated landline and cell phone numbers. The other four surveyed members of online panels recruited at random, mostly by mail to randomly selected addresses: Pew's American Trends Panel, the Gallup Panel, the panel used by the Annenberg Public Policy Center, and Ipsos's KnowledgePanel. All five surveys weight their results to match the US adult population and publish the full wording of their questions and their results. Roser did not include polls based on opt-in online panels, citing an opt-in poll that found 20% of Americans under 30 agreed that the Holocaust is a myth, when Pew's probability-based panel found 3%. In 2021, Pew introduced the question with a short definition and referred to artificial intelligence computer programs rather than artificial intelligence (AI), and Pew reports the results as one trend.

The Quinnipiac poll on concern about human survival was a telephone survey of 1,202 US adults conducted September 24 to 27, 2026 using random digit dialing, with live interviewers calling landlines and cell phones. In that poll, 14% were not so concerned, 11% not concerned at all, and 1% did not know or gave no answer. A Quinnipiac release on September 30, 2026 reported that 86% support independent safety standards for AI companies. Pew's September 16, 2026 report by Monica Anderson and William Bishop was titled Democrats are now more worried than Republicans about AI and its impact on jobs. The article leaves open how the industry should address these concerns, beyond Roser's statement that it will have to take them much more seriously than it has so far.

Articles.Title: No matter how you ask, more Americans are negative than positive about AI

stories.Headline: Amazon identifies AI agent campaign stealing API keys from exposed AI applications
stories.Summary:
Amazon's threat intelligence team uncovered a campaign using AI agents to steal API keys from internet-exposed AI applications. These agents hunted for weak spots in apps like LiteLLM, Dify, and One API to extract provider keys. The activity was captured by decoy servers between October 3 and late last week. The team believes separate China-linked groups operated the agents based on time zones and prompts. These actors used stolen keys to power the search for additional keys.

The campaign targeted gateways like Veloera, Sub2API, New API, and LiteLLM, and builders like FastGPT, LobeChat, and Ollama. It also hit RAGFlow, Langflow, Open WebUI, and Dify using a playbook of known entry points. Attackers exploited default master keys in LiteLLM and an authentication bypass in One API family systems. They used server-side request forgery to reach cloud metadata and found secrets in JavaScript and environment files. The agents also targeted managed services and premium AI models.

Amazon's team said they cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents but have moderate confidence they used ARTEX. They stated that AI agents increase the speed and persistence of attackers rather than introducing new techniques. The team noted that agents succeeded where basic security was missing, such as unpatched software or hard-coded credentials. They recommended treating AI apps like production systems and watching for unusual spending. AWS customers who may have been affected were notified.

Cloudflare responders saw ARTEX use a compromised CI/CD token to make 400 database dump requests in one hour. This token had no rate limiting or IP restrictions, which Cloudflare says is a common root cause. Microsoft reported attackers using ARTEX for GitHub secret hunting and described an earlier RAGFlow attack on August 26. The FBI warned that ARTEX has targeted global organizations in many sectors since at least August. South Korean financial institutions lost personal information of 67,000 people in one campaign.

The agents used internet scanning, certificate transparency logs, and GitHub repositories to find leaked keys. They also searched npm, PyPI packages, container image layers, notebooks, and Telegram channels. One separate campaign attempted to use deepfakes to bypass identity checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges. A verification vendor rejected the live deepfake video, though the status of fabricated ID photos is unknown. ARTEX is an open-source penetration testing tool with a commercial version called ARTEX PRO.

The FBI and Amazon suggest rotating exposed credentials and changing default administrator passwords immediately. Cloudflare recommends giving API tokens expiry dates and limiting client IP addresses. Users should check logs for 11 specific IP addresses and over 2,500 addresses linked to ARTEX. The ARTEX developer made the GitHub repository unavailable on October 8, but community forks still exist. The articles leave open whether the database dump requests returned data or if persistence attempts worked.

stories.Headline: APA publishes guidance urging employers to put people at the centre of workplace AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The American Psychological Association published new guidance on 16 November 2026 to help organisations introduce artificial intelligence into the workplace responsibly, warning that unclear policies and conflicting expectations risk undermining employee trust and wellbeing. The guide, titled Deploying AI Into Workplaces: What Leaders Need to Know, sets out seven recommended practices informed by established psychological research and emerging evidence about AI use. It is intended to help employers balance the potential benefits of AI with the need to protect workers, maintain meaningful human oversight and consider how technology changes the design of jobs. The guidance comes amid growing pressure on employees to incorporate AI into their daily activities, often without clear organisational policies governing its use. According to the APA's 2026 Work in America Survey, fewer than 40% of workers for whom the question was applicable knew whether their employer had an official policy on acceptable AI use, pointing to a potential disconnect between the pace of AI adoption and the development of workplace policies to support it.

Among the guide's recommendations are ensuring that safeguards reflect the potential consequences of AI errors, involving employees and others affected by AI systems in decisions about their introduction, and protecting opportunities for workers to develop expertise and learn through experience. The APA also encourages organisations to consider how AI might affect professional judgement, knowledge sharing and the development of skills over time, rather than focusing exclusively on efficiency or productivity gains. Developed with input from specialists in human-technology interaction and several branches of psychology, the guide includes practical examples of effective implementation and warning signs that organisations should recognise. APA CEO Arthur C. Evans Jr. said the rapidly growing use of AI at work is creating new behaviours and social judgments while raising questions about trust, all of which are fundamentally questions of psychology, and he asked whether using AI to write emails should change how someone is judged. He said psychological science can help organisations understand not just what AI tools can do, but how their use affects trust, decision-making and employee well-being, and that the guide gives leaders a practical framework for introducing AI thoughtfully, with people at the centre of the process.

Dennis P. Stolle, executive lead psychologist for applied psychology at APA, said purchasing an AI tool and telling people to use it without further direction is not a sound strategy. He said organisations need to invest in the people who will work with the technology, not just the technology itself, which means giving workers the information they need to judge where AI tools are reliable and where they are not, making sure human oversight is meaningful and rethinking how jobs are designed. Although aimed at employers across sectors, the guidance raises questions relevant to universities, research organisations and scholarly publishers, where AI is increasingly being incorporated into research, editorial, administrative and knowledge-management workflows. For these organisations, the APA's recommendations underline the importance of establishing clear expectations around acceptable AI use while preserving professional expertise, accountability and trust in human decision-making.

stories.Headline: Cloud provider leak exposes personal data of 46,000 TSMC employees
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company confirmed on November 16, 2026, that personal data of current and former employees was leaked online. A threat actor using the alias SmithBianl posted a sample text file on a hacker forum on November 8. This individual claimed the sample came from a larger 6.9GB dataset containing 46,000 employee records. The leaked information was offered for auction with a starting price of 3 BTC, which is roughly $65,000.

The breach requires the company to notify affected staff and provide them with necessary support. The compromised data includes sensitive details such as national ID numbers, banking information, addresses, and contact details. TSMC determined that the leak originated from the system services of a cloud service provider rather than its own internal infrastructure. Consequently, the company has engaged a third-party cybersecurity firm to help manage the ongoing situation.

TSMC stated that its operations and customers remain unaffected by this external security incident. In a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, the company noted there is no evidence that its own systems were compromised. The chipmaker, which produces hardware for Nvidia and Apple, is focusing on supporting the employees whose data was exposed. The company continues to investigate the breach through its partnership with external cybersecurity experts.

stories.Headline: CDW's Hang Tan says CIOs must redesign core workflows so AI improves business performance
stories.Summary:
Hang Tan, chief strategy and transformation officer and executive vice president at CDW, wrote in a Nov 16, 2026 opinion article on cio.com that AI is getting smarter at remarkable speed. He said employees can now draft, analyze, search and automate routine work faster than they could a year ago. He said recent research on the state of AI shows organizations continuing to expand adoption across functions and use cases. He said that in many organizations the business still works the same way, with the same work moving through the same systems. He said AI speeds up a task and the benefit disappears into a process designed for another era.

Tan said CDW works across thousands of customer environments and has made AI assistants available to more than 14,000 coworkers. He said CDW has built more than 12,000 agents and started redesigning core workflows. He said the CIO's challenge is no longer simply enabling access to AI. He said the challenge is helping the business move quickly without creating fragmented technology, uncontrolled cost and risks that IT will ultimately have to manage. He said usage climbed quickly inside CDW but usage alone couldn't tell whether the business was performing better.

Tan said the task is not the real unit of business performance and the workflow is. He said the next phase of AI value creation will come from improving how work moves across the enterprise. He said leaders who see the workflow as the constraint are tempted to apply AI to every step, an instinct that is often a mistake. He said the better approach is to start with the business challenge, not the technology, and define the outcome that matters and work backward. He said not every problem needs an agent and sometimes a simple rule works better and costs less.

Tan said employees experiment and surface opportunities but can only change the tasks they control, not the handoffs before and after them. He said business leaders choose which workflows matter and own the outcomes and have the authority to bring functions together. He said a workflow designed from the top will struggle if the people running it have never used AI or don't trust it. He said CDW needs both broad access so coworkers build fluency and leadership focus on a few core workflows where redesign can change performance. He said neither scales if every team has to solve for tools, data, security and cost on its own.

Tan said the CIO's mandate is to build the enterprise AI foundation quickly enough and make it useful enough that business teams build on it rather than around it. He said that foundation combines approved AI tools, trusted data and business context, connections into enterprise applications and workflows, security and governance, and visibility into performance, cost and value. He said business teams won't wait for IT and will find their own tools and build their own connections if the foundation isn't there. He said the CIO then inherits fragmented data, duplicated spending, inconsistent governance, cyber risk and little visibility into what AI is doing across the company. He said a foundation that is too restrictive or hard to use drives people around it, while one that works becomes the default.

Tan said AI will keep getting more capable and the competitive difference will come from what companies are willing to change around it. He said the measure of that change isn't how much AI a company has deployed but whether the business performs better. He said that is the standard CDW is applying inside the company and the standard he would encourage every CIO to use. He said CIOs should not stop at licenses, usage or hours saved but should ask whether AI has changed an outcome the business cares about. He said companies should build the highway for AI transformation or spend the next several years managing the risks created on the side roads.

Articles.Title: Your AI is smarter. Is your business still working the same way?

stories.Headline: Executives trust AI over their own judgment twice as often as other workers, survey finds
stories.Summary:
New research from Charter's AI Pulse survey of 5,002 full-time U.S. desk workers who use AI on the job found that executives are twice as likely as rank-and-file employees to trust AI over their own judgment, Fortune reported on November 16, 2026. About a third of managers and executives say they trust AI more than their own judgment on work decisions, compared with 16.3% of non-managers, and executives are also more than twice as likely as workers to trust AI over a knowledgeable colleague. The same article notes that Gen Z approaches AI with some skepticism, since 69% of employed Gen Zers in the Voices of Gen Z study from Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation and GSV Ventures say they trust work completed without AI more than AI-assisted work. That study surveyed 1,572 Americans ages 14 to 29, and only 3% of them put the most faith in work produced entirely by AI, even though 51% of Gen Zers use generative AI at least weekly. The survey also found that 81% of executives say they always or usually fact-check AI output before using it, versus 71% of workers, and that executives are 3.3 times as likely as workers to use outputs they doubt.

In Charter's survey, 85% of executives are at least somewhat optimistic about AI's impact on their organization, compared with 56% of employees. The article recalls that in 2025, SAP research shared with Fortune found that 74% of executives trusted AI more for business advice than colleagues or friends. It adds that misplaced trust in AI carries a bigger price at the top, because when an executive leans on a flawed AI answer to decide who gets promoted, where the money goes, or how a team is restructured after a merger, employees absorb the consequences without getting a vote. Brian Elliott, Charter's executive-in-residence, who co-led the AI Pulse research, says where someone sits at the table matters more than the year they were born, and that the survey of over 5,000 AI users at work found sharper divides by career stage than by age. He says AI is great at summaries and high-level answers, which is much of what a leader needs, while workers deal with specifics where AI's gaps show.

He says executives fact-check AI more but are also far more likely to use outputs they doubt, almost certainly because they have less fear that a mistake might cost them their job. In his view the biggest driver may be pressure, since many leaders are expected to move fast and have all the answers, and he says that combination explains how a CFO might drop the CMO's campaign into ChatGPT and quiz her on it, trusting the tool over a peer who knows the context and spent weeks on the work. The article says younger workers' wariness stems from institutions they feel have failed them, from schools to employers, and that Gen Z treats AI as an assistant rather than giving it main character energy. It notes that executives are finalizing next year's budgets and AI strategies now, and that the open question is how many of those calls will rest on a leader's judgment and how many on a chatbot's general answer. It concludes that leaders who treat AI the same way Gen Z does could make 2027 a better year for the employees who live with their decisions.

Articles.Title: Everyone worries Gen Z trusts AI too much. Executives trust it over their own judgment twice as often

stories.Headline: Attackers use AI to bypass security patches and find vulnerability variants
stories.Summary:
This summer, maintainers of the vm2 JavaScript library shipped fixes for 34 sandbox-escape vulnerabilities. Anthropic's Claude co-wrote 19 of these patches, but a security researcher later used an AI agent to bypass one. Shayaun Nejad of Rubrik highlighted these challenges at the [un]prompted AI security conference in San Francisco. He noted that AI-discovered bugs are often rediscovered in new testing runs despite previous fixes. Nejad warned that published patches now serve as blueprints for attackers to find vulnerability variants.

The vm2 library sees 1 million downloads per week, and the P2Patch benchmark tested 101 real vulnerabilities. In 41 of those cases, an AI agent successfully bypassed patches to trigger the same flaw. Off-by-1 Labs at 1Password tested 6,080 patch candidates for six vulnerabilities, finding half left attack paths open. Fudan University researchers in Shanghai analyzed 76 patches from 62 closed-source applications across 25 vendors. Their framework flagged 63 incomplete patches, leading to 19 CVE assignments and 28,100 dollars in bounties.

Shayaun Nejad said variant analysis is a context magnet that pops up frequently. Tim de Waal of OpenAI showed an agent removing stack canaries and missing single-quote bypasses in firmware. Anthropic stated that software security is now limited by how quickly humans verify and patch AI findings. David Molnar of Meta said humans are drowning in reviews because AI code grew over 100 percent. Taesoo Kim of Microsoft warned that AI drastically reduces the time needed for binary-diff analysis.

Bank of America added 1,000 contractors in the second quarter to help 3,000 staff with patching. Meta used AI for 40 percent of critical fixes by July, but exposure time did not decrease. The Microsoft Edge Security team warned that attackers are increasingly using patch-gap abuse to target downstream browsers. Epoch AI researchers used GLM 5.3 to compromise every Firefox release shipped between September 17 and October 26. These researchers spent 1,000 dollars in credits and 12 hours per target without triggering safeguards.

Trail of Bits found one in eight human-written patches failed to resolve 2,265 vulnerabilities over several years. A human and an AI agent both caused a crash in the freenginx web server. Anthropic's Glasswing program found 37,966 vulnerabilities, but VulnCheck found only 217 of 7,349 public flaws were fixed. FIRST projected 66,000 CVEs for this year, but the number is now approaching 100,000. Microsoft's October Patch Tuesday addressed 1,415 vulnerabilities, compared to 180 in October 2025.

Mozilla will stop releasing regression tests associated with security fixes to prevent further patch gap abuse. Attackers now use open-weight models like Qwen, Kimi, and GLM to bypass frontier model guardrails. AI can now create open-source replicas of proprietary products, such as Adobe Photoshop, to aid reverse engineering. Anthropic researchers found a model produced a working Firefox exploit within one hour of a patch landing. The articles leave open how companies will fully automate the review pipeline to replace human-in-the-loop systems.

stories.Headline: German students use AI for homework as PISA finds lowest scores in 25 years
stories.Summary:
Young Germans have used artificial intelligence tools in classrooms for two and a half years. Students use these applications for subjects like math, physics, chemistry, English, and German. Many students use these tools to complete their homework or explain complex topics. Some students use AI during class to read prepared answers to their teachers. This trend has led to a phenomenon known in science as cognitive outsourcing.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani banned AI in public schools up to eighth grade for 2026 and 2027. The KMK has issued vague statements on responsible AI use in Germany since 2024. A 2024 JIM study found 91 percent of Germans aged 12 to 19 use AI. That same study found 74 percent of those students use AI for learning and homework. PISA evaluated 15 year olds from over 90 countries in a September study.

OECD director Andreas Schleicher said learning requires productive cognitive engagement rather than just consuming content. He noted that students using AI chatbots generally receive lower average scores in science. Teacher Julian Hinn said AI can respond better to the needs and language of students. Teacher Franziska Müller said some students can no longer think for themselves due to AI. She believes students read less because they let AI summarize almost everything.

The Brookings Institution argued that AI risks outweigh benefits by eroding critical thinking and memory. Students with knowledge gaps may adopt AI errors and fall further behind their peers. PISA noted that AI can widen the gap for children from less affluent backgrounds. This creates a Matthew effect where early success leads to more future progress. Students who rely on AI may fail exams where no digital aids are allowed.

The PISA study reported that German 15 year olds posted their lowest scores in 25 years. The Brookings study found similar high AI usage figures in Asia, Latin America, and the US. Some students use AI to explain basic concepts better than traditional textbooks can. Teachers are now more motivated to challenge students to maintain their own personal autonomy. One student felt he could not think independently after receiving a poor exam result.

Julian Hinn suggests introducing AI in classes starting from the 10th grade for older students. He encourages his senior students to critically question the quality of AI generated solutions. Franziska Müller bans AI in some class aspects so students focus on thinking independently. The articles leave open how the KMK will move beyond its current vague statements. It remains unclear if other cities will follow the New York ban for younger students.

Articles.Title: AI in German classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

stories.Headline: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw
stories.Summary:
Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw, the founder of Biocon, said on the social media platform X that the recent disruption of Microsoft services could create an opening for the Indian software company Zoho to serve as a backup management information system for Indian businesses, according to TechGig. She made the suggestion as companies were re-evaluating their reliance on global technology providers following the outage. The Microsoft 365 outage affected users in more than 70 countries, including India, according to Downdetector data cited by the report. Microsoft announced on Saturday that its services had been fully restored and that all products were operational, confirming the Microsoft 365 disruption was resolved.

The report said Microsoft's Microsoft 365 suite has more than 450 million commercial users, a figure Bloomberg reported, and the scale of the disruption renewed concerns about the risks of businesses relying heavily on a single technology provider. Zoho already has a significant presence in India's government email infrastructure, with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology stating in December that nearly 12.68 lakh official email accounts across various ministries and departments had migrated to a Zoho-based platform. Approximately 7.45 lakh of those accounts belonged to central government employees, according to the ministry. Union ministers publicly backed domestic products, including Zoho's software and its messaging platform Arattai, as alternatives to foreign technology services in October last year.

Mazumdar-Shaw is the person behind the suggestion, and she posted on X that Zoho could emerge as a backup management information system provider for India Inc given such unforeseen events, the article said. The report did not say whether Zoho or Microsoft responded to her remarks. The articles give no further statements from Microsoft, Zoho or government officials beyond the ministry's December figure and the ministers' earlier public backing of domestic products. The articles also do not say what steps, if any, Indian businesses plan to take in response to the outage or to her suggestion.

Articles.Title: Microsoft outage creates Zoho opportunity for India Inc, says Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw

stories.Headline: Gen Z buyers use AI to shortlist homes and estimate mortgage costs
stories.Summary:
Gen Z consumers are increasingly using artificial intelligence to research homebuying, according to a 2026 Homebuyer Insights Report from Bank of America. These young buyers use the technology to shortlist properties, estimate mortgage payments, and calculate closing costs before contacting agents or lenders. The report found that 32 percent of Gen Z, 28 percent of millennials, and 20 percent of all prospective buyers or homeowners used AI tools in the past year. Most users focused on financial affordability, with 57 percent estimating costs and 55 percent learning about the general homebuying process.

The shift requires real estate firms to scale their technology, though JLL research shows 90 percent of companies are testing AI while only 5 percent have met their goals. More than 60 percent of these firms are unprepared to scale beyond pilots, and only 33 percent of workers feel adequately trained. In early 2026, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac introduced governance frameworks for accountability and human oversight, while MISMO released a voluntary toolkit in June. Additionally, a revised law in Colorado regarding automated decisions is scheduled to take effect on January 1.

Matt Vernon, the head of consumer lending at Bank of America, stated that AI is now a meaningful first step in the journey for buyers. Despite this trend, the report indicates that 55 percent of buyers still prefer humans for touring homes and 54 percent want human legal advice. The Urban Institute noted that AI already assists with underwriting, valuation, and fraud detection to lower costs and speed up servicing. They suggested that lenders should measure success by how many more people become and remain homeowners.

The real estate industry is currently undergoing its largest transformation in a generation, which the World Economic Forum compares to the early days of the internet. Companies with C-suite sponsors for their technology programs are three times more likely to succeed than those without such leadership. The Urban Institute has launched a new initiative on AI in mortgage finance to track these developments. Future success for firms will depend on training their staff and proving measurable results to keep pace with AI-savvy buyers.

Articles.Title: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying

stories.headline_source: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI uses Kimi models to pursue scientific discoveries in biology and chemistry
stories.Summary:
The Beijing-based artificial intelligence start-up known as Moonshot AI recently announced its intention to utilize Kimi models for scientific discovery. This strategic move was highlighted by the company during a keynote address delivered at the Web Summit technology conference in Lisbon late last week. The organization is now competing with rivals from the United States to transform artificial intelligence into a powerful engine for research. By focusing on these goals, the company aims to push the boundaries of what current machine learning models can achieve. This new direction requires the development of more advanced reasoning capabilities to handle complex data in specialized fields.

The company is specifically pushing into the realms of biology, chemistry, and pharmaceutical research to find new breakthroughs. These scientific applications demand a much higher level of intelligence than those used for standard coding tasks. The transition involves moving beyond general purpose AI to create tools that can solve intricate problems in the natural sciences. Giacomo Ficari, who serves as the director of international for Moonshot AI, spoke about the potential of this shift.

He stated that the real excitement for the company lies in the field of science. Ficari explained that while finance and legal applications are at the same intelligence level as coding, science pushes that level even higher. He believes that the ability to reason through scientific problems represents the next major frontier for their technology. More to follow.

Articles.Title: China’s Moonshot AI puts Kimi models into race for science discoveries

stories.headline_source: China’s Moonshot AI puts Kimi models into race for science discoveries

stories.Headline: VA official Zack Schwartz announces homepage redesign to prepare for AI enhancements
stories.Summary:
The Department of Veterans Affairs updated its homepage last week to provide a more simplified experience for users. Zack Schwartz, the principal deputy assistant secretary of the Office of Information and Technology, announced these changes at the VA Modernization Forum on November 13, 2026. The redesign followed a period of extensive veteran testing and the analysis of nearly 90,000 survey responses. This initial update serves as a foundation for further artificial intelligence enhancements planned for the coming months.

The new website features pre-filled forms, natural language searching, magic links, and a single sign-on capability. To improve security, the agency collaborated with global cybersecurity firms to implement a security wrapper similar to those used in commercial banking. The department also partnered with the identity verification service CLEAR last month to help thousands of veterans create accounts via in-person kiosks. Future updates scheduled for January and throughout next year will make the site more compatible with large language models.

Zack Schwartz stated that the office is moving away from science experiments to keep pace with evolving technology. He explained that the agency is studying how large language models navigate the site to build better skills for younger veterans. Schwartz noted that while the financial costs of artificial intelligence remain unknown, the agency is working with America.gov to improve services. He emphasized that success depends on building relationships and listening to criticism rather than simply deploying new technology.

The agency intends to serve as a representative example for other federal offices regarding the use of super intelligence. Schwartz plans to meet with incoming Federal Chief Information Officer Carter Farmer to discuss these advancements in the artificial intelligence space. By automating internal processes, the department hopes to reduce costs and allow staff to focus on critical veteran-facing activities. These incremental changes are designed to deliver consistent results for veterans regardless of which administration is in power.

Articles.Title: VA website gets a redesign with more AI-friendly updates coming, IT official says

stories.headline_source: VA website gets a redesign with more AI-friendly updates coming, IT official says

stories.Headline: Ronen Schwartz says purpose-built storage keeps AI accelerators fully utilized
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud published a blog post on November 16, 2026, titled “Beyond the compute bottleneck: Maximizing the ROI of AI accelerators with purpose-built storage.” Ronen Schwartz, VP of Product Management for Storage at Google Cloud, wrote the post. The post says the infrastructure mandate for enterprise AI has shifted from acquiring accelerators to keeping them fully utilized. It says storage accounts for only a small sliver of total AI spend, but the wrong storage can put committed compute capital at risk. It says insufficient storage throughput has become a primary impediment to AI success across the industry.

The post cites a Gartner prediction that enterprises will deploy over 150,000 agents in the next few years. It says Cloud Storage Rapid delivers up to 15 TB/s of throughput and 20 million queries per second with sub-millisecond latency from a single bucket. It says Rapid Cache delivers up to 2.5 TB/s of aggregate read throughput with no code changes and takes idle cold-start times from hours to minutes. It says Google Cloud Managed Lustre, built in partnership with DDN, provides up to 10 TB/s of throughput per instance. It says many models now process context windows that exceed 100,000 tokens.

Schwartz said organizations are eager to move AI initiatives forward, but preventing idle compute requires a purpose-built approach to data I/O. He said the most common architectural misstep is treating AI as a single, general-purpose workload. He said compute, networking and storage need to be deeply integrated to solve I/O challenges and keep accelerators busy. He said organizations should evaluate token economics rather than just legacy storage metrics. He said AI infrastructure needs enterprise-grade reliability, built-in security and automated cost discipline for optimized TCO.

The post says nine out of the world’s ten leading AI frontier model labs run on Google Cloud infrastructure. It says Google Cloud spent the last two years co-designing its storage architecture with these frontier labs and with Google’s own foundation model teams. It says Salesforce AI Research serves complex agentic inference workloads with up to 40% fewer GPUs. It says Thinking Machines Lab uses Cloud Storage Rapid Cache to stabilize read throughput peaks above 1.8 TB/s and achieve an 89% cache hit ratio. It says Shopify deployed 50+ unique Rapid Caches worldwide, achieving over 2 TB/s peak throughput and up to a 90% latency reduction from baseline.

The post says Atlassian adopted Managed Lustre on Google Kubernetes Engine to turn preemption interruptions into quick five-minute restores, delivering nearly 5x higher throughput and boosting GPU utilization by 70% compared to NVMe-based systems. It says Harmonic relies on Managed Lustre to train mathematical reasoning models, eliminating 50% of experiment interruptions, cutting startup times in half and increasing data retrieval speeds by 15x. It says Colossus is the planet-scale distributed file system powering Google Search, YouTube and Gemini. It says this shared infrastructure supports billions of users daily. It says Managed Lustre’s new Dynamic Tier consolidates hot and cold data into a single namespace, eliminating traditional caching performance cliffs.

The post says Managed Lustre Cloud Storage Mirror automatically synchronizes datasets in the background so they are ready before training begins. It says the post was posted in Storage & Data Transfer and tagged AI infrastructure. It lists related articles, including one introducing Z4M storage-optimized compute for AI/ML and parallel file systems by bob Napaa. It lists another related article on what’s new in AI infrastructure and orchestration in October by Alex Barrett. It lists a related article introducing Google Cloud’s U4 compute for ultra-low latency trading by Disha Chopra and one on Cloud Storage end-to-end checksums by Denis Serenyi.

stories.Headline: Telefonica says digital security now requires protecting trust as AI fuels fraud
stories.Summary:
Digital security is becoming a priority for citizens, businesses, and institutions in the face of rising fraud, identity theft, and content manipulated using artificial intelligence, according to Telefonica on 16 November 2026. Cybercriminals no longer seek only to breach technological systems, and increasingly they attempt to deceive people through fraud, identity theft, manipulated content, or messages designed to appear legitimate. In Spain, computer fraud ranks high among cybercrimes, reflecting the growing importance of techniques designed to manipulate people's trust. AI-based tools enable the generation of text, voice, images, and video with ever-increasing quality, and these same capabilities can be used to personalize deceptions, automate fraud campaigns, or create synthetic content intended to cause confusion. European institutions are promoting measures aimed at strengthening the protection of minors online, advocating for design models that take into account users' ages, privacy, and risk reduction from the very inception of digital platforms.

The article says digital security requires strengthening digital identity, verifying communications and transactions, embedding security by design, and promoting the responsible use of AI. It also poses social and regulatory challenges, such as protecting minors online, and age verification, privacy controls, and the creation of safer digital environments play a prominent role in the debate. The European Union has developed a framework covering operational resilience, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and user protection, including the NIS2 Directive, the DORA Regulation, the Cyber Resilience Regulation, the Artificial Intelligence Regulation, and the Digital Services Regulation. Organizations should strengthen mechanisms for protecting digital identity, improve the verification of transactions and communications, properly manage risks associated with third parties and suppliers, integrate security and privacy into the design of products and services, establish governance frameworks for the responsible use of artificial intelligence, promote training and awareness among employees and users, and periodically review prevention, detection, and response mechanisms. Initiatives focused on the digital provenance of content aim to provide verifiable information about the origin and modifications made to images, videos, or digital documents.

The article states that security is no longer an issue exclusive to technical departments but has become a shared responsibility. It says this evolution involves, to varying degrees and with differing responsibilities, manufacturers, developers, service providers, platforms, and organizations. It says the challenge is not to curb innovation, but to develop mechanisms that allow us to harness the potential of artificial intelligence while maintaining user security and trust. It says technology alone will not solve the problem, and digital trust also requires education, critical thinking, transparency, and the ability to verify information before sharing it or acting on it. It says the common goal is to build digital experiences that protect the most vulnerable users without compromising fundamental rights such as privacy.

The article says digital safety is the set of practices, technologies, and measures designed to protect people, organizations, and digital services from risks such as fraud, loss of privacy, identity theft, content manipulation, or cyberattacks. It says digital safety centers on people and their ability to navigate safely in an increasingly connected environment, unlike traditional cybersecurity, which focuses primarily on systems, networks, and data. It says digital security is a key element of the customer experience, corporate reputation, and trust in digital services, and customer trust becomes a fundamental factor in evaluating service quality and building secure digital experiences. It says the ability to offer secure, transparent, and reliable experiences will be a key factor for organizations, alongside technological innovation and the ability to respond to the needs of an increasingly connected population. It says trust is becoming an essential element for the development and functioning of an increasingly connected world.

The article says every digital interaction begins with an act of trust, and every day we perform dozens of digital actions without even thinking about it. It says for years the main digital threats were associated with malware, vulnerabilities, or unauthorized access, and although these risks still exist, digital fraud has taken center stage. It says in certain cases cybercriminals may try to convince a person to provide information, make a transfer, or hand over their credentials, rather than attempting to bypass technical security mechanisms. It says concepts such as digital identity, verification, reputation, and trust are taking on strategic importance for citizens, businesses, and institutions. It says artificial intelligence is driving some of the most significant technological advances in recent years and is also reshaping the landscape of digital risks.

The article says the history of digital transformation has been marked by technological innovation, but its evolution will also depend on organizations' ability to build and maintain trust. It says digital security is no longer just about protecting systems, and it also involves protecting the trust that enables citizens, businesses, and institutions to interact, share information, and use digital services. It says this approach addresses the challenge of facilitating citizens' access to digital technologies through innovative, secure, and reliable networks and services. It says the digital transformation is accompanied by a profound regulatory evolution, and security extends beyond technical departments. It says ensuring safe, transparent, and reliable digital experiences is essential to harnessing innovation without undermining the trust that underpins the digital economy.

stories.Headline: Trump administration tightens AI chip loophole to block Chinese access via third countries
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration announced on Monday, November 16, 2026, that it is tightening a loophole regarding advanced artificial intelligence chips. This action targets Chinese technology firms that have bypassed United States restrictions by using third countries to access high end semiconductors. The announcement comes just days before President Trump is scheduled to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week. This move follows an international scandal involving Nvidia that led to the resignation of CEO and President Jensen Huang.

The new rule from the Commerce Department requires buyers of advanced semiconductors from specific nations to secure a license for any sale or transfer. This regulation specifically impacts buyers from Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand because they are viewed as having a higher than normal risk of evading sanctions. These measures are set to go into effect in 90 days to stop the use of shell companies and rented computing power. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick will have wide discretion to orally inform companies about stricter export rules if he believes there is an unacceptable risk.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Howard Lutnick on Sunday for failing to properly oversee chip exports to China during a CNBC interview. Bessent stated that the Treasury, State, War, and USTR departments wanted to put a company called Megaspeed on the entity list for months. He noted that President Trump made it clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s to avoid giving the Chinese an advantage. The scandal involves allegations that Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, spied for China while having an affair with Jensen Huang.

President Trump is scheduled to arrive in China on Wednesday to meet with President Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. This first of its kind summit will focus on the reduction of nuclear weapons in addition to the issue of artificial intelligence chips. Democrats are expected to take control of Congress next year and will likely probe the administration's AI policies. Lawmakers have already asked the Commerce Department to preserve all records related to Nvidia as part of this ongoing investigation.

stories.Headline: Travel firms expect AI agent bookings to keep protection as sellers seek machine-readable offers
stories.Summary:
As artificial intelligence agents begin to take on more of the travel booking process, the industry faces a new question about how travelers will be offered protection when an AI assistant is handling the transaction, according to a PhocusWire report published on November 16, 2026. Travel insurance has traditionally been presented during checkout, where sellers can explain coverage, provide required disclosures and obtain consent from the buyer. But as booking shifts toward conversational interfaces, those familiar steps will need to be rethought by the companies involved. New Phocuswright research finds that travel companies generally expect protection to remain part of AI-driven bookings, although their requirements differ from one another.

Only 5% of surveyed companies say they would leave protection out of AI agent booking flows, which means the large majority expect it to stay in place. Travel sellers prioritize machine-readable offers and a clear business case for including protection in those flows. Technology providers, by contrast, are more interested in solutions they can deploy across multiple clients rather than single-purpose tools. The sponsored report examines what it will take to integrate travel protection into AI-driven booking experiences, including the technical, commercial and regulatory considerations involved.

The report also identifies six priorities for companies evaluating protection partners as agentic commerce evolves, though the article does not list them. The research was sponsored by Travel Insured International/C&F, and the full report is available by filling out a form on the PhocusWire site. The article does not name any individual responsible for the findings or attribute any direct statements to a person. It also does not say what happens next beyond the report's release and the six priorities it identifies for companies assessing partners.

Articles.Title: How travel protection needs to adapt as AI agents book at scale

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as AI industry faces potential financial bubble burst
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, November 13, 2026, which has shaken confidence in the center of the artificial intelligence boom. This sudden leadership change occurred while the industry was already struggling with significant financial and political uncertainty. The company named CFO Colette Kress as the interim leader to manage the current vacuum. This event adds an explosive risk to a strained market that may be facing a dot-com style reckoning.

The situation requires a new approach to infrastructure spending, as providers project spending 7 trillion dollars through 2030 against expected revenues of only 3.6 trillion dollars. Anthropic reported an annualized revenue run rate of 81 billion dollars in October, yet its IPO terms imply a valuation below 2 trillion dollars. OpenAI grew third quarter revenue by 50 percent to 10 billion dollars, though its adjusted operating losses reached 10.9 billion dollars. These numbers highlight a gap between the massive costs of expansion and the actual financial returns.

RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas stated that the departure of Huang could trigger a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble. Professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh noted that the turmoil matters if lenders lose confidence that Nvidia will back future projects. Investor Paul Kedrosky explained that the fact that the technology works is exactly what makes a financial bubble possible. MIT professor Ricardo Caballero argued that while AI will be transformative, this does not preclude the existence of a speculative bubble.

The broader context includes rising borrowing costs and a wave of election victories for candidates who are skeptical of artificial intelligence. Bipartisan demands for tighter restrictions on advanced chip exports to China are also mounting following the downfall of Huang. A retreat in investment could become self-reinforcing, turning a simple market correction into a much larger financial reckoning. This cycle could vaporize trillions in investor wealth even if the technology eventually succeeds in transforming the world.

Articles.Title: "No sane person questions whether AI works" — but an AI bubble appears ready to pop.

stories.Headline: Clay raises $115m Series D led by Wellington at a $7.1bn valuation
stories.Summary:
Clay, a New York company that sells data and AI agents to sales and marketing teams, was valued at US$7.1bn after a US$115m Series D round led by Wellington in September 2026, more than double its valuation of US$3.1bn in August 2025. The company was co-founded by Kareem Amin, who is chief executive and who sold his previous start-up Frame to Sailthru in 2012, and by Varun Anand. Clay began as a way to fill spreadsheets with better data, and its waterfall enrichment queries more than 200 data providers one after another, from ZoomInfo to People Data Labs and Hunter, until it finds a match. It now counts OpenAI, Anthropic, Mistral AI and ElevenLabs among more than 17,000 customers, up from 10,000 a year earlier, and 80% of the Forbes AI 50 are Clay customers. Revenue grew fourfold in 2025, and annual recurring revenue was about US$150m in May 2026 according to a Sacra estimate.

A March 2026 pricing overhaul split data credits from Actions and cut data costs by 50% to 90%, a move designed to widen use beyond power users. Clay unifies CRM records from Salesforce and HubSpot with product usage, campaign engagement, calls and emails, then predicts the next best action and helps a team take it, while agents handle account research, lead scoring and pre-call preparation. A September 2026 update added an action that drops enriched records straight into HubSpot lists, and 24 new or updated connectors in September 2026 extended EMEA and APAC data coverage, added Canva for personalised decks and wrote records back to Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks and ClickHouse. Amin now describes the goal as a self-learning revenue engine, and he has said that AI is unleashing the biggest wave of company creation in history. Scotty Huhn, engineering lead at OpenAI, has said of Clay that it allows OpenAI to move fast and drive outsized impact on GTM execution.

Customers report good numbers, with Anthropic tripling its enrichment rate, Mistral AI cutting market mapping and account scoring from two months to ten days, Intercom growing outbound-sourced pipeline by 140% and Pendo reaching 200% quota attainment. ElevenLabs lifted sales-qualified leads by 50% by cutting speed to lead to under five minutes. A new job title, the GTM engineer, has grown up around the product, and Clay is investing in the people who run it through a US$1m scholarship fund that trains GTM engineers, with its ecosystem team saying more than 50,000 people have been trained. At Sculpt 2026, its second annual conference, about 2,000 attendees from 30 countries saw agent-first building, Clay Workflows and an Inbound SDR Agent. The customer list reads like a roll call of the AI industry, with OpenAI, Cursor, Lovable, Notion and Figma using Clay alongside established software firms such as Okta and Rippling.

stories.Headline: Developers use AI tools to build clones of Adobe and Microsoft software
stories.Summary:
A group of developers has used AI-powered software development tools to build feature-exact clones of the Adobe Creative Suite, the Microsoft Office suite and the AutoDesk CAD applications, a collection known as ArtCraft, according to an InfoWorld opinion piece published on November 16, 2026. The piece says the most striking ArtCraft release so far is not a clone of an existing app but a relatively original project called Craft Anything, which it describes as a fancy agent harness for studying existing applications or websites. That tool then prompts a large language model to create your own copy of the studied software, either by reproducing its outward behavior, which the piece calls clean-room cloning, or by disassembling binaries. The writer says you never have to touch a line of code if you don't want to, calling it the no-code dream pushed to the limit.

The piece says the trend is driving development of ever-more-abstracted software tools and transforming existing tools into more abstracted ones, and it is also fostering new generations of developers for whom those tools will be their first contact with programming, and possibly their last. It notes that higher-level languages once replaced machine code, that compilers now write better machine language than people produce by hand, and that higher-level languages are now next in line to be automated away, or so the argument goes. The writer, Serdar Yegulalp, a senior writer at InfoWorld, says he does not think it is a bad idea to have a choice of abstraction levels, but he does think it is a bad idea to believe more abstraction is inevitable or always better. He says the more abstraction we put between ourselves and the work, the harder it is to know what might be wrong or how it might be better.

Yegulalp says we have not begun to understand the psychological impacts of LLM use on veteran programmers and newcomers, and that the non-deterministic output of agents makes it harder for developers to reason about the results of any given prompt. He asks whether an agent that never generates the same code twice is producing a bug or a feature, and he says some people argue there is no point in knowing what is under the hood because the work now happens at a pace and scale only other machines can handle. He calls that argument seductive to developers facing impossible deadlines but says it feels like the same kind of fatalism, and he asks how many of those expectations about velocity are genuine and how much LLM-driven work actually results in features shipped, bugs fixed and value delivered. He says those were already hard questions before LLMs came along, and that as more developers gravitate toward an agent-first way of doing things it will be harder for them to ask such vital questions in the first place.

stories.Headline: JetBrains CEO Kirill Skrygan says policies alone cannot govern AI agents
stories.Summary:
The article, published by InfoWorld on 2026-11-16, describes how AI agents are changing software governance as organizations accelerate AI adoption across software development. It reports that AI systems can act faster than the organizations responsible for them can understand or govern what is happening. It says organizations are thinking about compliance, data privacy, security, and model reliability while boards demand policies and regulators develop frameworks. It states that AI has significantly lowered the barriers to generating code, with assistants suggesting individual functions and coding agents working across repositories, running tests, making changes, and executing multi-step tasks. It says agents can access tools, retrieve data, write code, trigger actions, and coordinate tasks on behalf of users.

The article says the goal is to scale AI across development workflows while ensuring the people responsible for the software can still understand, verify, and stand behind what those systems produce. It says governance becomes murkier when AI agents not only generate code but test it, deploy it, open a pull request, modify multiple files, or interact with other systems. It says the distance between decision and action becomes much shorter, making it harder for humans to retain enough access to understand and monitor each step. It says developers must decide what work to delegate, what context an agent needs, and how to verify the result. It says a developer can delegate a task without delegating responsibility for the outcome.

The article says Kirill Skrygan is CEO of JetBrains, the company behind intelligent software development tools trusted by more than 15 million users and 88 Fortune Global Top 100 companies. It says he leads JetBrains as the company combines its deep expertise in code intelligence with AI to help developers and organizations build. It says most organizations already have policies governing software security, access, and compliance, but policies alone cannot govern AI agents operating across repositories, tools, and development environments. It says organizations must define what agents can access, what actions they can perform, how their work is recorded, and where human approval is required. It says these controls need to be built into the environment where development happens rather than applied after an agent has completed its work.

The article says the first control to consider is traceability, so developers understand what AI has contributed to a codebase. It says AI-generated changes must be tracked and made auditable so teams can read, review, and understand the output. It says if an agent makes changes across multiple files and runs tests, the team should identify exactly what actions were taken, what was changed, which instructions were received, and which tests were run. It says developers are ultimately responsible for software that reaches production, and customers do not care who or what wrote the code. It says accountability ultimately sits with the organization and its engineering team.

The article says the goal should not be to put a human in the loop for every individual action carried out by AI. It says organizations need to clearly define where human judgment is required, for example allowing AI to generate code and run tests automatically while requiring explicit human review for changes to production infrastructure or other critical systems. It says an AI tool that can modify application code does not necessarily need access to production infrastructure, and a coding agent that can run tests does not necessarily need permission to change deployment configuration. It says tokenmaxxing has been one of the defining AI trends of 2026, yet organizations increasingly realize AI activity and AI value are not the same thing. It says measuring usage rates, prompts, and token consumption tells organizations how much AI they are using but not whether AI is delivering better outcomes or creating meaningful business value.

The article says agentic systems can perform long, multi-step workflows and consume significant resources without a developer manually initiating every individual step. It says this is driving interest in what the industry now calls a software harness, a layer of software around AI models that can provide context and give organizations greater control over tasks and token costs. It says what works when one developer is directing one agent becomes harder when multiple agents operate across repositories, teams, and shared systems. It says the most successful organizations will not be those that deploy the largest number of AI agents but the ones able to create the clearest lines of accountability around them. It says the question is not whether organizations will adopt AI agents but how they can remain in control of them.

stories.Headline: India's data protection rules drive cybersecurity demand from May 2027, K7 white paper says
stories.Summary:
India's Digital Personal Data Protection Rules are expected to increase demand for cybersecurity professionals and managed security services, according to a white paper by K7 CyberSecurity reported by TechGig on November 16, 2026. The principal privacy, security and breach-notification obligations under the rules take effect from May 13, 2027, which is the deadline by which companies must strengthen their systems for data protection, risk monitoring and breach response. Businesses are likely to increase investments in access monitoring, data protection, incident response and security operations centres as that date approaches. The K7 white paper is titled "Turning DPDP Compliance into a Security-Led Capability" and highlights the need for organisations to establish stronger monitoring systems.

Rule 6 requires organisations to put in place safeguards covering encryption or masking, access controls, monitoring and review of access, continuity after a security compromise, specified data and log retention, and processor security provisions in contracts. Companies must also protect personal data across business applications, cloud services, devices, portals and third-party suppliers, and must keep evidence that their safeguards are actually working. The DPDP Act sets maximum penalties of ₹250 crore for failure to maintain reasonable security safeguards and ₹200 crore for failure to meet breach-intimation obligations, both subject to inquiry and the statutory process. After a personal data breach, affected individuals and the Data Protection Board must be informed without delay, and an updated detailed report must reach the Board within 72 hours of awareness unless an extension is permitted.

The report says human teams must retain control over legal classification, regulatory communication and disruptive containment decisions, while managed SOC services, including those using AI agents for bounded work, can connect security information across systems and keep records for audits and incident reporting. K7's briefing advises companies to move beyond relying only on security policies or dashboards and to demonstrate whether safeguards were actually effective. The report notes that an integrated security approach helps organisations identify weaknesses, investigate incidents and show compliance, since security controls, current state, incident investigations and retrievable evidence form one operating chain. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the May 13, 2027 start of the principal obligations.

Articles.Title: DPDP rules to boost cybersecurity demand by May 2027

stories.Headline: South Korea bans all electronic devices at 1,312 test sites to stop AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korean education authorities are scrambling to prevent AI-assisted cheating before the national college entrance exam this Thursday. Public outrage grew on Sunday after the top scorer of this year's certified tax accountant exam confessed to using a smartphone, a miniature camera, and generative AI. This individual missed only one of 160 questions in the first round and scored high marks in the second round. Police have opened an investigation into the matter, which follows other cases where four students used AI glasses during school and university tests.

The government will ban all electronic devices from the 1,312 test sites, allowing only scratch pads and writing utensils. Specialized personnel will be dispatched to detect AI-powered glasses that can scan tests and produce answers in seconds. Students caught with smart devices will have their results invalidated and face a ban from the exam next year. Officials are currently moving to extend this penalty to a three year ban for offenders.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook called for the use of all national capabilities to prevent misconduct during this week's exam. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin vowed a zero-tolerance approach and stated that the ministry will actively seek criminal punishment. While some suggest using metal detectors or physical searches, officials say these are realistically difficult to implement. Floor leader Chun Ha-ram of the New Reform Party suggested postponing the exam to ensure systematic preventive measures.

The College Scholastic Ability Test, known as Suneung, is a major life event that determines university placement and future careers. It is considered so critical that military drills and flight schedules are adjusted to avoid disturbing the test takers. A spokesperson for the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union argued that the government should change educational evaluation practices. They believe that relying on proctor vigilance is insufficient in an era where AI can easily find answers.

Articles.Title: S. Korea scrambles to crack down on AI-assisted cheating ahead of nat'l college entrance exam

stories.Headline: Doosan Enerbility shares AI maintenance technologies with domestic power companies
stories.Summary:
Doosan Enerbility shared artificial intelligence-based technologies for operating and maintaining power generation equipment with domestic power companies, the company said on Nov. 15. The company held the 2026 Power Generation Operation Technology Exchange at its headquarters in Changwon, South Gyeongsang Province, according to the report. The two-day event began Nov. 12 and drew about 100 participants, including officials from major domestic power companies and university professors. Doosan Enerbility presented its in-house-developed predictive diagnostics solution Prevision, along with AI-based remote monitoring and non-destructive testing technologies.

The technologies analyze power equipment operating data to detect abnormal signs early and improve maintenance efficiency, the article says. The company also shared cases of operational support using power equipment technical data and AI data development. Participants toured Doosan Enerbility's gas turbine plant and the test center for GUARDIAN, its in-house-developed power equipment control system. Doosan Enerbility plans to strengthen its long-term maintenance and digital solution businesses in line with expanding gas turbine supply.

The articles do not name a specific person as responsible for the event or give direct comments from company officials. The report attributes the announcement to Doosan Enerbility as a company rather than to an individual speaker. No other responsible party or quoted statement is provided in the article. The context given is the company's plan to expand its gas turbine supply and its related maintenance and digital solution businesses.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the stated plan to strengthen those businesses. No further dates, figures or follow-up steps are given in the report. The article does not describe any response from the participating power companies or universities. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Doosan Enerbility Shares AI Operation Tech with Power Firms
