stories.Headline: Prophecy Gov analyzes 10,000 comments and finds 90% of Americans detest data centers
stories.Summary:
A San Francisco-based AI startup called Prophecy Gov analyzed public comments from hundreds of local government meetings across the United States that discussed data center projects, and it launched a website called American Sentiment to display the findings, KQED reported on Nov. 16, 2026. The company said it captured more than 10,000 public comments from recordings of 906 local government meetings across 417 different government entities, a small share of the more than 90,000 local government entities counted in the 2022 census. The analysis found that 90% of Americans detest data centers, while 79% of self-identified union workers supported data center development and 60% of self-identified data center workers opposed data center projects. Commenters mainly spoke about distrust of tech billionaires, a desire for more transparency and fear for the collective climate future, according to the company. Prophecy Gov did not respond to multiple requests for comment from KQED, and the American Sentiment website carries no published methodology, so it is not clear how the company turned spoken comments into a statistical rating.

Jonathan Bash, chief executive of Locunity, a company that uses AI to turn meeting agendas and videos into real-time briefings and alerts, described the general recipe as collecting meeting recordings, using speech-to-text software to create transcripts, then using an AI tool to find comments about data centers, sort them by speaker and label them as pro or anti. Bash said he could not speak to Prophecy Gov's exact tech stack but was certain AI would be used at a minimum for transcription and sentiment analysis, and he cautioned that AI can mishear names and misconstrue sarcasm. He also said city council speaker data tends to overindex toward passionate, hyper-active community members, which he called valuable for an advocate, journalist or political candidate but less useful for predicting elections or reading residents' minds. Kyle Short, a teacher at Gilroy Unified School District who is featured on the American Sentiment website with a 2 out of 5 rating, said he did not know about the project before speaking with KQED but was flattered to be included and found it inspiring that people across the political spectrum have taken issue with how data centers have been rolled out. Short said he learned about the data center issue while trying to stop an ICE processing facility from being built in Gilroy, which in the past year became a potential site for both an ICE detention facility and a data center, and he argued that data center processing power can be used for ICE operations.

Prophecy Gov did not capture public comments from San Francisco or neighboring Oakland, where residents have advocated for a data center moratorium during city council meetings. Eisa Al-Shamma, an organizer with No Data Center Oakland and the Party for Socialism and Liberation, said dozens of residents have gone to Oakland council meetings to protest proposed data center development, and he said his main concern is who controls the data centers and how they are rolled out over the will of the people. Al-Shamma said he did not take issue with the American Sentiment project using AI, arguing that the problem is not the technology itself but how it is used and developed and who holds the levers of power. Members of No Data Center Oakland and dozens of Oakland residents and organizations showed up at the city council last Tuesday before a vote on extending the data center moratorium that passed in October, and the council voted unanimously to extend it through Oct. 5, 2027. Councilmember Carroll Fife, who proposed the moratorium, said she felt it was imperative to take immediate action to protect Oakland residents from what has happened in other parts of the country, calling the measure guardrails against an industry that has steamrolled individuals across the globe.

Articles.Title: Tracking Data Center Drama … With AI? - KQED

stories.Headline: Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin launch Noeri with $110M to build self-improving AI for enterprises
stories.Summary:
Stanford professors Yejin Choi and Carlos Guestrin founded the AI lab Noeri in 2026 to build self-improving AI for enterprises. On November 16, 2026, the Palo Alto company announced it had raised 110 million dollars in new funding. Menlo Ventures led this investment round with participation from Madrona Venture Group, Kindred Ventures, Wing Venture Capital, and NEA. Strategic investors for the new lab also include Snowflake, NVIDIA, and Cisco Investments. The company is currently hiring researchers and engineers for its offices in Zurich and Palo Alto.

The system changes AI from frozen models into living systems that self-organize and self-improve through interactions on the job. Noeri's technology studies an enterprise's own data and workflows to improve the harness, skills, instructions, tools, and underlying parameters. The software works with open-weight and closed models, and customers retain ownership of their data and developed workflows. This approach allows smaller, specialized models to make sustained scientific discovery affordable by reducing the compute needed for search. The lab's mission is to enable a future where plural intelligence, meaning intelligence in the plural, co-evolves with humanity.

Co-founder and co-CEO Yejin Choi stated that the future of AI will be a healthy ecosystem of many diverse intelligences. Co-founder and co-CEO Carlos Guestrin said that specialization can move the curve for companies struggling with model costs and results. Guestrin noted that Noeri builds AI that becomes obsessed with the hardest problems of a company and teaches itself solutions. Venky Ganesan of Menlo Ventures said the founders are rare because they put world-class research to work inside companies. He explained that this combination of research and application is why his firm moved quickly to lead the funding round.

Large companies are affected because they spend heavily on AI but struggle to turn general-purpose models into specific results. These organizations typically must choose between paying more for the most capable models or accepting weaker results from cheaper ones. Noeri's AI acts as a co-discoverer for scientists and engineers working on complex technical systems, proteins, and new molecules. The system ensures every change is explained and sent to a person for approval, similar to a standard code review. This process allows the AI to find new solutions and refine known ones based on actual experience.

The technology is based on joint research by Choi and Guestrin regarding test-time training and on-the-job learning after deployment. Guestrin previously co-founded Turi, which Apple acquired in 2016, and he later led Apple's central machine learning and AI organization. He also co-created XGBoost, a widely used machine learning technology that powers various industries and accelerates scientific discovery. Choi is a MacArthur Fellow and a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Senior Fellow who previously worked at the Allen Institute. Her research on agentic orchestration and pluralistic alignment helps small models outperform frontier models at a fraction of the cost.

Noeri is currently working with a varied group of strategic partners, including some of its investors, to help its technology generalize. The company aims to solve the open research problem of moving past the trade-off between model cost and performance. The lab continues to develop systems that align AI with the full diversity of human needs and values. The articles do not state when the first commercial products will be available to the general public. They also leave open which specific industries will be the first to adopt these self-improving living systems.

stories.Headline: Oren Etzioni argues AI startups mistake fast iteration for fast scaling
stories.Summary:
Oren Etzioni, a longtime artificial intelligence researcher and entrepreneur, published a column on November 15, 2026, arguing that AI startups have fetishized speed and whipped themselves into a frenzy without a clear strategy. He wrote that a feature that took a quarter to build in 2023 takes a mere AI-fueled weekend in 2026, yet many startups run on fear of missing out, caffeine and tokens rather than direction. He compared a startup to a marathon and said a team that tries to sprint the whole way will burn out before the finish line. He noted that he had once sung from the same hymnbook, writing earlier in the year that velocity is the new moat, but that he stopped once everyone got fast.

Etzioni laid out five common arguments for the speed creed and weighed each one. On the closing window, he said that if the frontier labs will close the gap anyway, speed merely buys a nicer funeral, so the argument supports picking a different direction rather than running faster in the same one. On ubiquitous competitors, he said cheap building is exactly why velocity is not a moat, and he cited Peter Thiel's last-mover argument from Zero to One as stronger today than when it was written. On the data flywheel, he said each new model generation resets the flywheel, and that the data that matters is data the labs cannot easily get, such as clinical records, industrial sensor readings and proprietary transactions, which usually comes through trust and partnerships that take time.

On momentum attracting capital and talent, he said a high valuation can box a startup into the growth story that justified it, while raising at a saner pace keeps the option to change direction. He then separated two kinds of speed, saying fast iteration means cheap experiments such as a prototype, a pilot or a feature shipped to 20 users and pulled if it flops, while fast scaling means hiring ahead of revenue, signing multi-year contracts, buying compute and raising at a valuation the company must then grow into. He said iteration should be as fast as possible because each cycle is cheap to undo, but scaling should come more slowly because each step is a major commitment that is hard to unwind. He cited a 2011 study of more than 3,200 high-growth technology startups that blamed premature scaling for about 74% of internet startup failures.

He also invoked Jeff Bezos's 2015 letter to Amazon shareholders, which distinguished one-way doors that are irreversible and deserve deliberation from two-way doors that should be decided fast by a small group, and he said a startup's experiments are two-way doors while a large raise, a long contract or a hiring spree are not. Etzioni quoted Sri Chandrasekar, one of the managing directors at AI House, saying the firm does not hand founders a thesis and expects them to find the right problem, which takes judgment rather than speed, and that building is nearly free now, so founders should run every experiment fast and manually and only build the machine once something works. Etzioni added that finding the right problem takes iteration, acumen and judgment, that speed helps with the first and does little for the other two, and that a hamster on a wheel at 200 mph has plenty of speed and no chance of progress. He closed by noting that even Sam Altman's Startup Playbook, which says he has never seen a slow-moving founder be really successful, also says Y Combinator looks for businesses that get more powerful with scale and that are difficult to copy.

Articles.Title: Etzioni on AI: Startup speed is not a strategy

stories.Headline: YouTube Music's AI DJ drives a WIRED writer to quit AI DJs after mispronouncing Charli XCX
stories.Summary:
Reece Rogers, a senior writer at WIRED who covers software, wrote on November 15, 2026, that YouTube Music's AI DJ feature called Beyond the Beat had driven him to stop using AI DJs altogether. He had enabled the experimental feature through YouTube Labs and left it on for months before a bad experience during a morning workout pushed him to swear off the technology. While listening to a pop divas playlist, the tool interjected for about 30 seconds after a Slayyyter track with a paragraph he described as lengthy platitudes with little substance. The commentary also mispronounced the name of the artist Charli XCX, which he said took him out of the groove and did not feel additive.

The article says YouTube launched its experimental AI DJ in 2025, while Spotify first introduced a similar tool back in 2023 and expanded its AI DJ efforts in November by adding different personalities and more controls over the commentary. Rogers upgraded his Spotify account to the premium tier to try that beta software and played the introduction clips for each of the eight English-language voices in his settings. He found multiple voices leaning on filler words such as you know and like, which gave him what he called the uncanny-valley ick. Spotify's commentary felt tighter and more tolerable than YouTube's, but neither experience was enjoyable enough for him to return, and he noted that both features are optional and avoidable.

Rogers wrote that Spotify claims in its launch blog that 80 percent of listeners come back to DJ week after week, though he said he will not be one of them. He said his rejection is not based on how the voices sound, since both companies' voices are decent and convincingly human, but on the content of the commentary. He cited empty platitudes and the mimicking of human mistakes as what truly turns him off, and concluded that he has heard enough. The article does not say what either company plans to change next.

stories.Headline: Alessi uses AI to turn its design icons into snowy city installations for holiday campaign
stories.Summary:
Italian design firm Alessi used artificial intelligence to create its holiday 2026 digital campaign, which the company told WWD about on Monday. The campaign is called "Happy Holidays to All Dreamers" and is anchored in the concept "Perfect is Boring." Milan-based creative content studio Take Off Production led the direction of the campaign, which featured AI-generated images of Alessi's design icons. These included the Juicy Salif citrus squeezer, designed by Philippe Starck in 1988, and the 9090 coffee-maker, designed by Richard Sapper in 1978. Both objects were transformed into monumental installations displayed in snow-covered city streets from Tokyo to Milan.

Alessi chief executive officer Alberto Camerlengo said that by using artificial intelligence the firm has found a new way to attract and engage a younger audience, in addition to social media. He said the company sees great potential in engaging younger generations through more contemporary, dynamic and digitally native forms of communication. He said Alessi wants to create content that is not simply about showcasing products but about generating curiosity, emotion and conversation around the Alessi universe. Since Camerlengo's appointment in 2024, Alessi has been focused on enchanting new generations, and in 2025 former Benetton designer Andrea Incontri returned with his art direction for the "Alessi Moments" campaign.

Camerlengo said there is also an element of irony and playfulness, which has always been part of Alessi's visual and cultural language. He said the firm wanted to create something visually impactful, unexpected and immediately engaging, particularly in a digital environment. Alessi was founded by Giovanni Alessi Anghini, a sheet metal worker, in the Italian lakeside town of Omegna in 1921. Since then the firm's stylish home decor, tea pots and pans have become ubiquitous in Italian homes as well as around the world. Camerlengo concluded that at Alessi everyday objects often have the ability to become something extraordinary.

The article names several Alessi icons, including the Plissè water boiler by designer Michele de Lucchi and the Cupola coffee-maker designed by Aldo Rossi. It also lists the Menhir coffee-maker by Cypriot-born, London-based designer Michael Anastassiades and the Tore tea kettle by Japanese design Studio Nendo. The article describes these as everyday objects envisaged to echo for decades and even centuries to come. The articles do not say what happens next with the campaign or whether Alessi plans further AI work.

stories.Headline: Jared Bernstein warns Nvidia circular financing and Huang dependence raise AI bubble risk
stories.Summary:
Jared Bernstein wrote in his Substack newsletter on November 15, 2026, that last week's consumer price index came in warmer than expected, while wholesale inflation later in the week matched expectations, and he said markets and Federal Open Market Committee voters believe the situation warrants a rate hike at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting. Market probabilities stand at 89 percent for a quarter-point hike and 11 percent for a half-point hike, and Bernstein said he would go with the quarter-point call. He pointed to tariffs and the war as causes but said the core services line has struck him as a broad category picking up price pressures less clearly tied to those policy mistakes. He also cited elevated operating margins by sector in the Census Quarterly Financial Report as a possible source of underlying price pressures that he would expect to be at least somewhat responsive to rate hikes. He wrote that his head calls for a hike but his heart is not in it, noting that many people are struggling and do not need higher rates, especially in housing where the 30-year fixed mortgage rate is at 7.5 percent.

Bernstein also discussed Nvidia, writing that his first thought when the stock began to tank was that the chips are still the chips and the potentially excessive demand is still the demand. He then raised the extent to which Nvidia used its ample profits to take shares in other tech firms and to fund its buyers, which he called circular financing, citing the Financial Times. He said Jensen Huang's control within Nvidia and over its sizeable investment portfolio means his departure now threatens to unravel a web of financial dependencies binding the AI ecosystem together. Bernstein said Huang was instrumental in spinning that web, which feeds into his and Ryan's financial bubble call.

Bernstein appeared with Paul Krugman and Jason Furman on Krugman's Substack to discuss whether AI is a bubble and what might happen if it pops, and he said he came off most worried, Krugman was in the middle and Furman least so. He said a key reason his and Ryan's forecast is for deeper damage than Furman's is that a stock-market decline would lead to lastingly tighter financial conditions, as happened after the dot-com bubble burst, when the Goldman-Sachs Financial Conditions Index climbed enough to crimp growth, especially in the job market, not peaking until late 2002. He said today's equity market is a lot more pumped-up relative to GDP, and that a higher equity premium rarely moves by itself but shows up in wider credit spreads, tighter lending standards and higher capital costs. He said the bust could be contained, as Furman argues, but he stressed there is a lot more leverage now with poor sightlines into solvency risks, and he raised what he called Huang-systemic risk, the fact that Bank of Nvidia could go down alongside its leader.

stories.Headline: Physicist Vito Servedio finds AI chess engines sustain higher strategic tension than humans after 20 moves
stories.Summary:
A recent paper in APS Open Science, highlighted by Scientific American on November 15, 2026, examines what may make artificial intelligence so effective at chess, a question researchers have pursued since Deep Blue beat the best human player in 1997. The study's senior author, Vito D. P. Servedio, a physicist at the Complexity Science Hub in Vienna, said the paper is probably the closest to understanding what these machines are doing, adding that otherwise it looks like they are playing magic. The researchers collected human versus human games and Stockfish versus Leela games from online databases and measured what they called strategic tension at each point, meaning the number of mutual interactions possible between opposing pieces. Tension is often higher when more moves are possible.

The scientists found that once each player had made 20 moves, the average tension in human games exceeded that of the AI games. Up to that point people tend to rely on memorized tactics and hope complex piece interactions will force human opponents to slip up, but after it human tension drops below that of AI games, which remains high. As terrain becomes more unfamiliar, people may simplify their arrangement of pieces because they cannot hold complicated dynamics and multiple options in their heads. Merim Bilalić, a psychologist at Northumbria University in England who was not involved in the research, said the result makes sense because people need to reduce cognitive load, while engines do not really have that problem. Higher-rated human players maintained greater tension throughout their games, tension was greater in games with more allotted time, higher in classical than in rapid chess and lowest in blitz, and when Stockfish searched deeper trees of possible gameplay, tension increased.

The study did not show that higher tension led to, or came from, greater ability, though higher tension correlated with greater ability in both humans and AI. Servedio said his team's findings may apply to higher-stakes situations such as diplomacy, where AI might reach better outcomes but at the risk of complicating matters. He said this is very dangerous because when you have high tension, systems are very unstable, so just a small error from one of the sides will cause a disaster. Chess continues to be a fruitful model for studying cognition in humans and machines, according to the article.

stories.Headline: University of South Florida researchers develop an AI mosquito trap that identifies species with over 98% accuracy
stories.Summary:
University of South Florida researchers developed an AI mosquito trap that identifies mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing, Fox News reported on November 15, 2026. The technology comes from Digitomy, a startup founded by USF researchers. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan have developed the system through research dating back to 2018. The trap uses built-in cameras and artificial intelligence to identify species that can spread diseases like dengue. Florida is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades.

According to the Florida Department of Health's latest available weekly surveillance report, Hillsborough County recorded 407 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, its largest outbreak on record. Across Florida, officials reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. In October, the Florida Department of Health confirmed Hillsborough County was still responding to an ongoing dengue outbreak. On November 13, Hillsborough County extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito control crews increased aerial and ground treatments. County officials say surveillance continues to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area.

Carney and Chellappan say their system achieved more than 98% accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing. The researchers say the goal is to help mosquito control teams identify caught insects without spending days examining them under a microscope. Digitomy says its system uses AI and cloud computing with the goal of identifying captured species the same day. The company says it can send trap information to a mapping dashboard so teams can see where certain species are appearing. The researchers say the trap can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood.

Former CDC Director Dr. Robert Redfield broke down the risks of transmission and essential prevention measures, according to Fox News. Health officials continue to encourage residents to take precautions against mosquito bites. Hillsborough County mosquito management teams deployed aerial spraying to target the mosquitoes carrying the virus. Traditional mosquito surveillance can take two to three days because specialists often need to examine captured insects under a microscope. There are roughly 3,500 mosquito species worldwide, but only certain species spread particular diseases.

The trap hangs from a low tree branch or sits on the ground, with a light or bait attracting mosquitoes and a small fan pulling them inside. Once insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them, and AI compares the images against a large database. Female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases. Aedes aegypti is the species primarily responsible for spreading dengue in Florida. The trap identifies species capable of carrying disease but does not prove a captured mosquito is infected with dengue.

Health officials would still need laboratory testing to confirm the presence of the virus. Digitomy aims to give mosquito control teams same-day information to help identify where potentially dangerous species are appearing. If several traps detect more Aedes aegypti in one neighborhood, officials could investigate and consider targeted control measures. Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain, and in serious cases can lead to life-threatening complications. The articles do not say when the trap will be deployed or whether it has been tested outside the laboratory.

stories.Headline: Wharton survey finds 79% of Gen Z say AI makes people lazier
stories.Summary:
A Wharton-led survey published earlier this year, conducted with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, found that young people are increasing their use of AI even as they worry it causes lazy thinking. The survey of nearly 2,500 U.S. adults aged 18 to 28 was completed in October 2025. It found that 79% of respondents believed AI makes people lazier, and 62% said they were concerned it makes people less smart. Benjamin Lira Luttges, a postdoctoral scholar at Wharton who led research for the report, told Fortune the findings show deep ambivalence in how Gen Z thinks about using AI. Pew Research Center data published in June found that 66% of people ages 18 to 29 have ever used an AI chatbot such as ChatGPT, up from 55% in 2024.

The Pew data also showed that 37% of those young adults believed AI's impact on them over the next 20 years would be negative, the most pessimistic attitude of any age group surveyed. Nearly one-fifth of Gen Z is worried about AI displacing them at work, yet they lead the workplace in AI adoption. Lira Luttges speculated that the biggest mental factor behind Gen Z's attitudes is a bias toward immediate gratification, more prominent in younger, developing minds. He said there is a legitimate tradeoff between the benefits and costs of using AI, and that our brains are wired to prefer smaller, immediate rewards over long-term, delayed rewards. He noted that workers, particularly young ones, might consider getting tasks done efficiently as more important than an employer's wishes, especially if the risk of getting caught is slow.

Lira Luttges said young people lead the adoption of new technologies, and things often seen as fringe are adopted by young people and eventually become mainstream. He said that looking at Gen Z is a way of looking toward the future of work. He also said anyone, not just Gen Z, could fall victim to the better-than-average effect, a statistically impossible phenomenon of most people believing they are above average at a task. He said Gen Z survey respondents may see themselves as AI power-users, believing AI could atrophy other people's critical thought but not their own.

The report authors argued that employers should not ban AI but rather embrace ambivalence toward it. According to the survey, respondents who reported using AI more frequently worried less about its impact on intelligence and motivation, indicating AI anxiety may resolve over time. Mark Beasley, a professor and director at North Carolina State University's Poole College of Management, told Fortune that a critical thinking gap, not an AI skills gap, will pose a serious threat to organizational pipelines and business operations. Beasley said the threat AI poses to entry-level jobs could mean insufficient training and experience for middle- and eventually upper-tier positions in the near future.

He said the biggest risk organizations face is just being stagnant. Lira Luttges said that as long as workplaces are intentional about how they implement AI, the technology won't have a significant impact on critical thinking. Lira Luttges said that for every task there are two kinds of effort, one germane to the task that gets translated into learning, and another that is just friction and doesn't teach you anything. He added that you should outsource the crap, not the craft.

Last year, researchers from Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University revealed evidence about AI's impact on thinking, finding that among more than 300 knowledge workers, leaning too much on AI tools like ChatGPT was associated with diminished critical thinking skills. MIT-led research mirrored those results and suggested that even using AI for low-stakes tasks such as proofreading can lead to significant negative outcomes in high-stakes contexts like writing legal documents. A version of the Fortune story was published on Fortune.com on Jan. 30, 2026. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Alexa von Tobel says AI will make entrepreneurship the everyday job of the future
stories.Summary:
Alexa von Tobel, a serial founder who left Harvard Business School in 2008 to start the online financial planning firm LearnVest and later sold it to Northwestern Mutual in 2015, said on CNBC's Changemakers podcast that entrepreneurship will become the everyday job of the future. She told Julia Boorstin that she believes every person in America will be empowered to be entrepreneurial because of artificial intelligence. Von Tobel, who co-founded the venture capital firm Inspired Capital with former U.S. Commerce Secretary Penny Pritzker in 2019, said she reviews as many as 100 business pitches a week. She said anyone with any skill set can turn it into a business because of AI, and she described entrepreneurship as a commitment that will become low-stakes.

Von Tobel said Inspired Capital, which backs startups that could be worth $10 billion or more, has invested in ShopMy, a platform that lets creators earn commissions by sharing product recommendations and uses AI matching to connect brands with creators. She said platforms like ShopMy offer people more ways to build income around what they already know, with flexibility for those balancing work with family or caregiving. She also suggested entrepreneurship could serve as a fallback for people between jobs, letting them earn money while they retrain or look for their next role. She stressed that AI will enable businesses but the founder must always have the final say, adding that it is still her judgment making the final call.

On the data side, Liya Palagashvili, a labor economist and director of the Labor Policy Project at George Mason University's Mercatus Center, recently told CNBC that her preliminary research shows new business formation is rising among owners who do not expect to hire employees. In industries highly exposed to AI, business applications without early signs of hiring rose 26.8% from the first quarter of 2024 through the first quarter of 2026. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on David Senra's Founders podcast that we are about to see the greatest boom in people starting smaller businesses that we have ever seen. Von Tobel said her own fundraising for LearnVest taught her that some investors advising her had never built a company, a gap that shaped her idea for Inspired Capital.

Von Tobel said she meets with as many as 100 companies a week but may ultimately invest in fewer than eight firms a year, and she looks for founders with a distinct view of their industry and what it could become. She said those founders will have thought deeply about what the world should look like in five, 10 or 20 years. Her interest in financial literacy came from her own early life, after her father died when she was 14 and her mother, a nurse practitioner, had to navigate the family's finances alone. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the podcast episode and the research cited.

stories.Headline: Ashish Manne presents Nucleus cancer AI platform at Berlin oncology congress
stories.Summary:
Ashish Manne, an associate professor at Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center-James Cancer Hospital and Solove Research Institute, said on LinkedIn that he was traveling to Berlin, Germany, to present Nucleus, a clinician-facing AI-powered platform, at the ESMO AI and Digital Oncology Congress 2026. He said that a couple of years earlier, as AI began gaining momentum in healthcare, he and colleagues started thinking about how to translate its potential into meaningful improvements in everyday clinical practice. He noted that while AI holds tremendous promise, integrating it seamlessly into clinical workflows and demonstrating its practical value remain important challenges. That led the team to Nucleus, which he described as a ground-up, cancer-specific, institution-centered clinical intelligence platform designed to turn vast amounts of underutilized patient data into meaningful insights at the point of care.

Starting with pancreatic cancer, Nucleus helps clinicians identify comparable patients, understand their treatment journeys and outcomes, and visualize treatment-related toxicities, all within the routine clinical workflow, according to Manne. He said the goal is to make the collective clinical experience of an institution accessible when caring for the next patient. He said the team recently completed its first round of clinical pilot testing with support from Pannaga Malalur, Arjun Mittra and Shafia Rahman, and is now advancing toward a more comprehensive platform incorporating longitudinal treatment and toxicity intelligence. Manne said he is proud to lead the initiative through a collaboration between Ohio State, its comprehensive cancer center and Microsoft, alongside a multidisciplinary team.

The ESMO AI and Digital Oncology Congress 2026 is an international congress organized by the European Society for Medical Oncology, focusing on the application of artificial intelligence and digital technologies in oncology. According to the article, the congress brings attention to the growing role of AI and digital innovation in the field and provides a dedicated setting for exploring developments at the intersection of technology and cancer care. It highlights the importance of digital oncology as an evolving area within modern cancer research and clinical practice. Manne said he was looking forward to sharing the work and connecting with colleagues shaping the future of AI in oncology.

stories.Headline: OpenAI promotes its Codex tool at TwitchCon as attendees criticize the booth
stories.Summary:
OpenAI promoted its Codex coding tool during a hackathon at TwitchCon in San Diego on November 15, 2026. The company set up a prominent booth on the expo floor to reach personalities, fans, and industry experts. Many attendees reacted negatively to the presence of the company that created the ChatGPT artificial intelligence tool. Some users described the activation as stupid, bland, boring, and tone deaf during the annual convention. One Twitch user shared a forum link on X to call for an end to AI partnerships.

The Codex tool promotion occurred while AI was largely absent from the official programming of the San Diego event. The controversy follows a move by Twitch to allow streamers to opt out of AI training by Amazon. This opt-out feature was introduced a few months before the November 2026 convention to address user data concerns. Streamers argued that the system should have been opt-in because they never consented to having their content scraped. The parent company Amazon did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding its current AI training practices.

Twitch CEO Dan Clancy told NBC News that being automatically opted in does not mean data was already scraped. He stated that the toggle serves as a preventive measure in case Amazon plans to train AI on content. Chief Product Officer Mike Minton said the option was important even though it drove conversations about creator fears. Minton declined to discuss past events because streamers have filed lawsuits that resulted in ongoing litigation. Both executives claimed that most other services do not provide users with any option to opt out of training.

Attendee Chloe Van Ryn, 31, from Arizona, said AI could be useful for accessibility, moderator tools, and pinpointing new users. She expressed suspicion about the opt-out toggle and compared AI scraping to the destruction of scanned books. A user named Rummeko stated he is not a fan of AI and called the scraping process disrespectful. Rummeko suggested that creators who want to use AI should find other people who specifically use those tools. These streamers fear that generative AI could replace human creativity and threaten the jobs of creative workers.

The articles state that AI remains a divisive issue among streamers who are split on experimenting with new tools. Some users find value in speech-to-text, auto-captioning, and clipping tools as long as they do not generate content. The tension stems from a belief that AI companies are taking creative work without proper consent from the authors. This environment led to the creation of community forums where users organize against the influence of AI companies. The conflict highlights a broader struggle between technological advancement and the protection of human creative rights.

It remains unclear if Amazon has already used Twitch content to train its various artificial intelligence models. The articles leave open whether Twitch will change its opt-out system to an opt-in system for its users. There is no information on whether OpenAI will change its promotional approach at future streaming industry events. The outcome of the ongoing litigation filed by streamers against the platform is not yet known to the public. The articles do not state if Twitch will end its partnerships with AI companies following the community outcry.

stories.Headline: Morphisec warns AI tools spread unmanaged Node runtimes across endpoints
stories.Summary:
Morphisec published a blog post on 15 November 2026 arguing that AI tools have turned Node.js from a developer toolchain into an unmanaged runtime spread across corporate endpoints, with a single laptop running a couple of AI tools easily carrying four or five independent Node runtimes. The post says coding agents install through npm, their MCP servers launch through npx, and desktop AI apps and editors ship Node inside their own binaries, so the copies arrive through different doors and are updated by different mechanisms or by none. It lists five sources: a system install for npm-based agent CLIs in Program Files, version managers such as nvm-windows, fnm and Volta in the user profile, MCP servers and tools launched with npx from the npm cache, Electron-based AI apps and editors with Node embedded in their binaries, and single-file agent binaries built with Bun or Node single-executable builds. Only the first looks like software IT manages, and the rest are invisible to an inventory that reads the installed-programs list.

The post says four habits keep those copies vulnerable even after a Node fix ships: tooling documents "Node 18 or newer" as a floor even though Node 18 and Node 20 are end of life and receive no security fixes, npm update -g refreshes the agent package but not the node.exe underneath it, embedded runtimes are patched only when a vendor rebuilds and few release notes say which Node version a build contains, and a working copy gives nobody a reason to touch the version manager. It says Node.js now ships a security release every few months and each one is supposed to end with every copy updated, which on an AI-era endpoint means first finding copies nobody knew were there. It argues an agent's Node talks to whatever the agent decides to reach based on what it reads, such as a link in a README, an issue comment, a docs page or a result from an MCP tool, making prompt injection a delivery mechanism for runtime bugs in the HTTP client, TLS verification, decompression and parsing code. It says a configuration line such as npx -y some-server@latest downloads an unpinned package from the public registry and executes it with the user's full privileges each time the agent starts, with no installer and no approval process, and that MCP servers listening on a local HTTP port can be reached by any local process, with the MCP specification itself warning about DNS rebinding.

A compromised agent runtime runs as the user and can read the model API token, git credentials, cloud CLI profiles, registry tokens and SSH keys in that profile, plus MCP servers' own SaaS tokens. The post is attributed to Morphisec, a security vendor whose blog carries it, and it presents the argument in the author's own voice rather than quoting a named researcher or official. It does not name any specific vulnerability, attacker, victim or incident, and it gives no dates for the Node security releases beyond saying they ship every few months. It does not say what any vendor, developer or standards body has done in response, and it offers no remediation steps beyond the implied need to find and update the hidden copies.

Articles.Title: Every Endpoint Now Runs Node: How AI Tools Multiplied an Unmanaged Runtime

stories.Headline: Nvidia unveils Rubin HPC GPU for agentic AI science workloads
stories.Summary:
Nvidia unveiled a new GPU called Rubin HPC on November 16, 2026, a chip supported by the company's Vera Rubin platform and designed for agentic AI-powered simulation and data processing workloads across science, engineering, and analytics, according to DatacenterDynamics. The chip giant said Rubin HPC will shorten the timeline between exploration and results for the scientists and engineers who use it. The new GPU features more than 50,000 CUDA cores alongside a sparse data acceleration capability that speeds GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation Nvidia NVLink interconnect technology. Nvidia said the chip is meant to support agentic AI-powered simulation and data processing across those fields rather than to serve general computing alone.

Instead of increasing compute capacity alone, Nvidia said the new chip offers a balanced design that scales data movement and compute together, which accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload. Those patterns include sparse matrix operations, stencil computations, sorting and reductions, all of which the company says are common across data analytics, science, and engineering workloads. The sparse data acceleration capability works with the seventh-generation NVLink interconnect to speed GPU-to-GPU connectivity, according to the article. The report gives no pricing, availability date, or performance figures for the chip beyond the core count and interconnect generation.

Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at Nvidia, said that for agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery. He said Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer. The article attributes the balanced design description and the workload examples to Nvidia rather than to independent testing. Buck's comments are the only remarks from a named Nvidia executive that the article includes.

The article places the launch in the context of Nvidia's broader hardware lineup, noting separately that HPE has expanded its Private Cloud AI solution to support mixed Nvidia hardware clusters and launched a Vera CPU rack. It also lists unrelated items, including a University of Münster deployment of Zutacore waterless two-phase liquid cooling and a third-quarter 2026 global data center market report. The article does not say when Rubin HPC will ship, what it will cost, or which customers have committed to using it. No further details on availability or adoption are given.

stories.Headline: Samba CEO Ashwin Navin says AI agents can deliver programmatic advertising's promised efficiency
stories.Summary:
Ashwin Navin, co-founder and chief executive of Samba, used a video interview with Beet.TV and the company's Samba Summit customer event to argue that AI agents can deliver the media efficiency programmatic advertising long promised but rarely produced. He told Beet.TV chief executive Andy Plesser that buyers were promised efficiency and instead got what he described as a massive tax of layers of technology and middlemen. At the summit Samba demonstrated an end-to-end agentic workflow covering media planning, media buying and analytics, according to Navin. He said agentic technology presents a better future and that what programmatic was supposed to deliver will come to fruition thanks to agents.

Navin said media buying and selling involve many manual tasks that his company would gladly hand to agents, but he added that humans should stay in the loop for decisions, applying judgment, creativity and strategy. He argued that AI needs something to reference when deciding how to optimize for a client's objective, and he predicted measurement will have another golden moment like the one that made deduplication important as platforms proliferated. Samba wants to power agentic media buying and analytics that use real data rather than hallucinations, and Navin said every decision loop must be anchored in real deterministic data. He described an ontological knowledge graph of signals on what people watch, stream and scroll across many countries, and Samba acquired the generative AI advertising platform Bestever AI in June, saying the deal would speed its agentic roadmap including autonomous analytics and real-time campaign optimization.

Gartner forecasts that by 2028 more than 70% of global ad spend and 80% of U.S. ad spend will flow through self-serve platforms where AI materially influences media buying, cost and outcomes. McKinsey found that 42% of advertisers cite reliance on black-box optimization systems as a key risk, while cross-platform measurement rose to 72% as a marketer priority from 64% in the IAB's 2026 Outlook Study. Navin said the largest media companies have never needed much help, but the next tier down will have a great moment in the sun and will be easier to buy than in the past. He said he was excited that data can provide transparency into the marketplace where the value is, and the interview was published as part of a DMS by LUMA 2026 series.

Articles.Title: Samba’s Navin Bets AI Agents Can Finally Collect on Programmatic’s Unpaid Promise

stories.Headline: Micron beats EPS estimates for eight straight quarters as CEO Sanjay Mehrotra expects stronger fiscal 2027
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology has beaten EPS estimates for eight consecutive quarters, and CEO Sanjay Mehrotra said Micron delivered record fiscal 2026 results and expects an even stronger fiscal 2027. The consensus price target is $1,561.91, implying 100.68% upside from $778.31, and analysts expect fiscal 2027 EPS of $176.5017, up from $155.7946 90 days ago. A Bernstein memory hierarchy chart built on October pricing estimates places conventional DRAM at about $25 per GB and HBM at about $20 per GB. Micron shares are up 172.91% year-to-date, even after falling 14.86% over the past month. Micron currently trades at 4x fiscal 2027 estimates, and at $1,600 it would trade at just 9x.

Micron says HBM uses about three times the wafer capacity of a similar amount of conventional DRAM, and that ratio could rise toward four times for newer generations. Management said it really does not have line of sight to when supply and demand balance. Micron's Idaho fab expects its first wafer output in mid-calendar 2027, with significant volume following a few quarters later. More than 75% of fiscal 2027 shipments are already committed, and Micron has 26 strategic customer agreements that run through 2030.

Most of Micron's calendar 2027 HBM supply is covered at prices above 2026 levels. Fiscal Q1 2027 guidance calls for $61.5 billion in revenue and $38.15 in EPS, after last quarter delivered $54.23 billion and $33.42. Micron posted a non-GAAP gross margin of 87.0%, up from 45.7% a year earlier. Management says agentic AI, with AI agents running on regular CPUs, is helping push server unit growth in the high teens.

Getting to $1,600 would take a 105.57% gain, and since 2000 Micron has topped that in three full calendar years: 300% in 2009, 243% in 2013, and 240% in 2025. Micron has a beta of 2.398. Memory is still a cyclical business, and rivals could add capacity while high prices could cool demand. The shortage now reaches well beyond high-end AI chips.

The article was published on Yahoo Finance on November 15, 2026, by Rich Duprey. The article states that Micron could hit $1,600 in 2027, a 106% gain, as analysts already forecast about 101% upside to a $1,562 consensus target. The article leaves open whether Micron will reach $1,600. More to follow.

Articles.Title: DRAM Just Got More Expensive Than AI Memory. Here’s Why Micron Could Soar in 2027

stories.Headline: Embodied AI governance must address physical risks beyond screens, article argues
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Fair Observer on 15 November 2026, argues that AI governance must move beyond screens to address embodied AI in vehicles, warehouses, hospitals, performance venues, stores and homes. It says AI is helping machines perceive surroundings, choose actions and move through spaces shared with people. It cites the OECD’s updated definition of an AI system, which recognizes that AI outputs can influence physical as well as virtual environments. It warns that a machine misreading a person’s movement can strike them and that a late driver takeover request can turn a software failure into a collision. It says a service robot failing in a home or care setting may put a vulnerable person at risk.

The article says embodied AI combines software with sensors, mechanical parts, connectivity and a changing environment, and that a system can pass laboratory tests yet fail in the real world. It cites the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s work on autonomous-systems assurance, saying autonomous systems may face an enormous range of operating conditions that make complete testing coverage a major challenge. It cites the NIST AI Risk Management Framework’s four functions, govern, map, measure and manage, and its treatment of safety, security, accountability, transparency, privacy and fairness as connected characteristics. It cites the European Union’s Machinery Regulation on software and machine-learning components performing safety functions and the EU’s updated product-liability rules covering software and AI systems. It also cites the United Nations regulation on automated lane-keeping systems, with requirements on driver availability, takeover requests, cybersecurity, software updates and data storage, and ISO 13482 on hazards of personal-care robots.

The article says developers and operators should identify foreseeable hazards, test realistic conditions, define safe operating limits and prepare for failures before deployment. It says every physical AI system should have a clear statement of where, when and under what conditions it may operate, covering terrain, lighting, weather, network availability, crowd density and user capability. It says these limits should be communicated to buyers and operators in plain language rather than buried in technical documentation. It says a machine exceeding tested limits should slow down, enter a safe state or request qualified human assistance. It says the responsible person needs training, enough information to recognize a problem, authority to intervene and a stop or override mechanism that works under pressure.

The article says workers should be able to report dangerous behavior without retaliation and that consumers and patients should know when a machine is making or carrying out a consequential decision. It says embodied AI systems should create secure, proportionate records of critical decisions, sensor failures, overrides, updates and emergency stops, and that serious patterns should trigger investigation before the next failure becomes an injury. It says recordkeeping must respect privacy and aim at enough reliable evidence to reconstruct what happened, improve the system and establish accountability. It says governance should identify each party’s duties before harm occurs, since a manufacturer, model supplier, integrator, owner and update provider may all be involved. It says contracts should not let the most powerful organizations push every risk onto small businesses, workers or consumers.

The article says safety reviews should include privacy, accessibility, bias, consent and human dignity because systems in homes, care settings and workplaces may collect intimate information about routines, health, emotions and relationships. It says people should not lose the right to human contact, explanation or appeal simply because a robotic service is efficient. The author says he has spent more than 41 years in music and the creative industries and that physical AI will reach concert halls, touring operations, studios, festivals and media production. It says independent venues, artists and small production businesses need practical procurement checklists, clear insurance terms, accessible training, incident-reporting procedures and honest information about a system’s limitations. It says safety and privacy cannot become premium features available only to organizations with large compliance budgets.

The article says society should not wait for a spectacular accident before establishing expectations for embodied AI and that developers and operators can act now by testing under realistic conditions, publishing limits, training responsible people, maintaining genuine stop mechanisms, documenting incidents and assigning accountability throughout the lifecycle. It says progress should be measured not by how human a robot appears but by whether humans remain protected, informed and able to obtain recourse. It says governance that is clear, practical and centered on people creates the trust responsible innovation needs. It says AI is leaving the screen and safeguards must be ready to meet it in the physical world. It says the views expressed are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Fair Observer’s editorial policy.

Articles.Title: AI Governance Must Leave the Screen and Enter the Physical World

stories.headline_source: AI Governance Must Leave the Screen and Enter the Physical World

stories.Headline: Anthropic posts $16.96 billion quarterly revenue as token prices fall
stories.Summary:
Anthropic reported third-quarter revenue of $16.96 billion, up 47% from the second quarter, according to Yardeni Research, which said falling AI token prices need not hurt AI providers. The usage-weighted Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index, tracking what customers pay per million tokens, fell more than 40% between June 30 and early October. Yardeni said the decline reflects price competition and a shift in usage toward cheaper models. Anthropic priced its newest premium model, Fable 5.2, at $8 for input and $40 for output, down from $10 and $50 for Fable 5.1. Google's first-party models were processing nearly 32 billion tokens per minute by its October 28 earnings call, up 40% in a quarter and more than fourfold from a year earlier.

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue rose 1,127% from a year earlier, outpacing a 382% rise in its compute and infrastructure expenses. Quarter to quarter, profit fell: Anthropic swung from a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter to a $567 million operating loss in the third, citing $5 billion of costly short-term compute and a $2.0 billion non-cash donation-matching charge. Excluding that charge alone would leave an operating profit, though the charge may recur. Compute and infrastructure, including training, took about 58% of revenue, versus 48% in the second quarter. DRAM contract prices rose nearly 80% in the second quarter and 40% in the third, TrendForce reported.

Median on-demand GPU rental prices rose 9% from a year earlier, and H100 prices 24.7%, according to GetDeploying's November 9 tracker. AWS raised prices on most new Nvidia Capacity Block reservations from October 7, with increases of at least 15% on seven instance types, according to TIKR. SemiAnalysis measured roughly 14 times more throughput from one Nvidia chip generation on software improvements alone. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 cut customer costs per task by about 40% compared with Opus 5.

Anthropic's repeat customers generated about nine times their year-earlier quarterly revenue in aggregate. Yardeni said it is unknown whether repeat customers would keep spending in a recession, and that the test is rising profits, not rising volumes of tokens sold. Anthropic plans to go public, Yahoo Finance reported 20 days earlier, at a time when AI tokens have never been cheaper. Fortune reported two months earlier on the latest crack in the thesis for the trillion-dollar AI boom, that tokens are getting cheaper.

Decrypt reported 11 days earlier that Anthropic's AI is getting cheaper to use and that this is becoming a problem for its business. TIKR reported two days earlier that AI token prices fell almost 15% last month, which it called good news for Amazon. Yahoo Finance reported a month earlier that Anthropic revealed the Haiku 5.5 model as the AI pricing war intensified. Barrons.com reported 30 days earlier that Anthropic might be worth only $1.5 trillion and that this is not a disaster for the AI trade.

Yahoo Finance reported a month earlier that Anthropic's third-quarter revenue climbed to $16.8 billion. BeInCrypto reported five months earlier that OpenAI's price war with Anthropic could undermine its IPO. Investopedia reported 18 days earlier on how the company behind Claude makes money, and Quartz reported two months earlier that OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic in business AI spending, per Ramp data. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Why falling AI token prices aren’t the negative for AI providers one might assume

stories.Headline: OpenAI signs six-year deal with TensorWave for 457MW of AMD-powered AI capacity
stories.Summary:
On November 16, 2026, the artificial intelligence laboratory OpenAI signed a contract with the neocloud provider TensorWave for 457MW of capacity. This six-year agreement involves the provision of IT capacity powered by AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs across several different data center locations. The project will utilize Helios rack-scale systems and will be operated as dedicated, single-tenant capacity specifically for OpenAI. Operations are expected to begin during the first half of 2027 and should be fully deployed by early 2028.

The Helios racks, which launched in July, integrate AMD Instinct MI455X GPUs, 6th Gen AMD Epyc Venice server CPUs, AMD ROCm software, and AMD Pensando networking. A single rack provides 31 terabytes of HBM4 memory, 1.7 petabytes per second of memory bandwidth, 2.9 exaflops peak FP4, and 1.4 exaflops peak FP8. AMD claims these systems offer 15 percent more peak FP4 performance and 50 percent more high-bandwidth memory capacity than the Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 rack. Additionally, AMD asserts the hardware delivers 50 percent more scale-out bandwidth, six percent more HBM bandwidth, and 30 percent more tokens per dollar.

Piotr Tomasik, the president and co-founder of TensorWave, stated that the ability to reliably deliver hundreds of megawatts of compute will distinguish companies supporting frontier AI. He noted that this deployment proves AMD infrastructure can operate at the scale and reliability required by the most demanding AI firms. Uday Ruddarraju, the CTO for compute at OpenAI, explained that expanding access to large-scale compute is critical for building more capable models. He added that this agreement advances a previously announced partnership with AMD to help scale AI for more people and organizations globally.

This represents the largest deployment contract for TensorWave to date, following a 350 million dollar Series B funding round in June 2026. TensorWave claims to have secured 2GW of long-term data center capacity across the United States. In January 2026, the company also signed a 20MW capacity agreement with TecFusions for data centers located in Arizona and Pennsylvania. TecFusions recently ended its relationship with Fermi's Project Matador earlier this month.

Articles.Title: OpenAI signs on for 457MW AI capacity with TensorWave

stories.Headline: Broadcom projects AI revenue reaching 230 billion dollars by 2028
stories.Summary:
Broadcom projected its artificial intelligence revenue will reach 230 billion dollars by fiscal 2028. This announcement came during a report published on November 15, 2026, by Anders Bylund. The company is a chip giant that provides tools for the AI gold rush. Broadcom reported AI semiconductor revenue of 16.7 billion dollars in the third quarter of 2026. This figure represents a 221 percent increase compared to the previous year.

CEO Hock Tan raised the fiscal 2026 AI revenue guidance to 58 billion dollars. He further projected 115 billion dollars for 2027 and 230 billion dollars for 2028. These goals involve custom AI accelerators co-developed with Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and Anthropic. Broadcom also sells Tomahawk Ethernet switches for use in AI data centers. The company had a market cap of 1.65 trillion dollars on November 13.

Hock Tan provided forward-looking visibility that is rare within the semiconductor industry. He indicated that growth is supported by partnerships with frontier labs for custom accelerators. Broadcom management positions the company as a provider of both processing and transfer tools. The company offers a reliable dividend of 2.60 dollars to its investors. It currently trades at a forward price to earnings ratio of roughly 18.

Credo Technology Group is a networking expert affected by the growth of AI data clusters. Its products include active electric cables and serializer deserializer data converter modules. The company reported first quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of 479 million dollars. This amount more than doubled year over year for the networking firm. Credo has now delivered seven consecutive quarters of triple-digit revenue growth.

Broadcom has trailing sales of 89.1 billion dollars and a net income of 38.3 billion dollars. Its free cash flow of 39.4 billion dollars is comparable to Iceland or Bolivia. Credo has trailing revenues of 1.6 billion dollars and a 25 billion dollar market cap. Credo trailing sales rose 869 percent over the last three years. Broadcom also makes SerDes modules, from which Credo likely collects royalties.

Credo expects its optical segment to generate over 600 million dollars in sales this fiscal year. This growth is driven by silicon photonics, Zero-Flap Optics, and optical digital signal processors. Broadcom remains a choice for conservative investors due to its industrial scale. Credo is presented as a high-growth option for those seeking explosive upside. The articles leave open which company is the better overall AI networking buy.

Articles.Title: Is Credo Technology a Better AI Networking Buy Than Broadcom?

stories.Headline: Howard Lutnick pushes to loosen AI chip restrictions while his former firm finances Asian data centers
stories.Summary:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pushed to loosen restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips, according to a New York Times investigation published Sunday. He did this while his former Wall Street firm helped arrange financing for Asian data centers that could benefit from these decisions. The report raises conflict of interest questions because Lutnick led the investment firm Cantor Fitzgerald for more than three decades. His sons, Brandon and Kyle, now lead the firm while Lutnick serves in the administration of President Donald Trump. The investigation suggests a potential clash between his regulatory duties and his family business interests.

Cantor Fitzgerald worked with companies developing data centers in Southeast Asia, including facilities designed to provide computing power to Chinese customers. One Malaysian data center, known as A201, is expected to open next year with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia servers. Cantor served as a financing or placement agent for companies including Bitdeer Technologies Group and Gorilla Technology Group. Lutnick reportedly resisted efforts by other senior administration officials to strengthen restrictions on Nvidia chip shipments to Asia. He also repeatedly delayed efforts to restrict companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China, according to Axios.

The Commerce Department maintained that Lutnick fully divested his financial interests in Cantor and has had no discussions with the firm. Department officials defended their enforcement record and denied directing staff to avoid investigating particular companies. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly criticized the failure to blacklist Megaspeed, a Singapore based company suspected of helping China. The White House has expressed confidence in Lutnick despite the mounting questions over the decisions made by his department. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment on the reports regarding its business dealings and financing arrangements.

Senator Elizabeth Warren and Senator Ron Wyden demanded information about a loan from cryptocurrency company Tether to a trust for Lutnick's children. This loan was reportedly secured by assets including more than half of the equity in Cantor Fitzgerald. Other Democrats have demanded stronger enforcement of chip exports, while some Republican lawmakers questioned if technology is reaching China. The report notes that Commerce approved Nvidia export licenses involving Chinese companies with links to military contractors or sanctioned entities. These issues come amid a broader controversy involving former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang.

Cantor Fitzgerald attracted attention in July 2025 for offering to purchase potential tariff refund claims for 20 to 30 percent of their value. This arrangement allowed investors to profit if courts overturned tariffs, while Lutnick was a vocal advocate for those same tariffs. In March, Bloomberg reported that Tether provided a loan of an undisclosed amount to the trust benefiting Lutnick's four children. This loan occurred around the time the children acquired the ownership stake in the investment firm. These previous disclosures added to the current scrutiny of the business dealings under the leadership of Brandon and Kyle.

Lawmakers are now intensifying their scrutiny of how the Commerce Department handles the export of advanced chips to Asia. The administration continues to face questions about whether U.S. technology is reaching Chinese interests through third party data centers. It remains unclear if the business dealings of Cantor Fitzgerald influenced the specific policy decisions made by Secretary Lutnick. The New York Times stated it found no evidence that the firm's dealings influenced the secretary's official actions. The articles leave open whether further investigations will be launched into the Tether loan or the A201 project.

Articles.Title: NYT: Lutnick Eased AI Chip Restrictions While Firm Helped Finance Asian Data Centers

stories.headline_source: NYT: Lutnick Eased AI Chip Restrictions While Firm Helped Finance Asian Data Centers

stories.Headline: Economist John Quiggin argues Australian corporate layoffs do not signal an AI job apocalypse
stories.Summary:
Several major Australian companies including NAB, Qantas, Canva, and Atlassian announced large-scale job losses around November 15, 2026. While some of these organizations explicitly blamed artificial intelligence for the cuts, the actual role of the technology remains unclear. This wave of layoffs follows four years of intense hype and excitement since the initial launch of ChatGPT. Many observers are now questioning if these events signal a broader job apocalypse driven by automation.

The situation requires a closer look at the specific changes occurring within these different corporate business models. Qantas plans to outsource 850 Australian jobs to India as part of an overhaul that the company describes as AI-driven. NAB has denied that artificial intelligence played any role in its recent decision to sack employees. Canva faces vulnerability because users can now generate simple graphic designs in seconds using various AI tools. Atlassian is also under challenge, though its project management software is considered harder for AI to replicate.

John Quiggin, a professor at the University of Queensland’s school of economics, argues that the evidence does not support a job apocalypse. He suggests that Qantas is using AI as a cover to muddy the waters regarding simple offshoring. Quiggin believes NAB is simply following a long-term pattern of hiring and sacking workers based on profitability. He notes that productivity growth remains very low despite the massive investments in data centers and infrastructure. The author claims that the current trend mirrors the dotcom era of the 1990s.

The broader context involves a stock market boom based on future demand that has not yet emerged. Hyperscalers like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and Alphabet face competition from cheaper open-weight models such as Mistral and DeepSeek. These competing models from France and China invest far less money while remaining only a year behind the leaders. Quiggin suggests that large language models might become essential utilities like email rather than sources of profit. Consequently, the most significant apocalypse may eventually occur in the stock market instead of the jobs market.

Articles.Title: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin

stories.headline_source: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin

stories.Headline: Mount Saint Mary’s and St. Catherine use $5 million federal grant to expand ethical AI education
stories.Summary:
Mount Saint Mary’s University in Los Angeles and St. Catherine University in Minnesota received a nearly $5 million federal grant for a five-year effort to expand the ethical use of artificial intelligence in higher education, the schools announced Monday. The $4,998,260 grant will fund a project called “AI in the Service of Students and Mission” from October through September 2031, according to the schools. Mount Saint Mary’s, the only women’s university in Los Angeles, will partner with St. Catherine, another women’s university founded by the Sisters of St. Joseph of Carondelet. The funding comes through the Title III Strengthening Institutions Program, a federal initiative administered by the U.S. Department of Labor’s Employment and Training Administration on behalf of the U.S. Department of Education, officials said.

The universities said the project will focus on integrating AI literacy and ethical considerations into courses, creating shared faculty training and developing jointly governed technology infrastructure. Students will be taught to use AI tools, assess AI-generated information, recognize misinformation and apply the technology responsibly in academic and professional settings, according to the schools. The partnership will also establish policies intended to prioritize human oversight, data protection, transparency and responsible use of AI platforms. Mount Saint Mary’s will serve as the fiscal agent for the partnership.

Adam Weyhaupt, Mount Saint Mary’s provost and senior vice president for academic affairs, said the grant represents an extraordinary opportunity for the two schools to reimagine how they prepare students for a future shaped by artificial intelligence. He said their goal is not simply to teach students about AI but to empower them to use it in ways that advance knowledge, strengthen communities and contribute to the common good. St. Catherine Provost and Senior Vice President Denise Baird said the collaboration will pair technological innovation with the liberal arts. She said students will develop the capacity for critical analysis needed to become discerning, ethical and effective users of AI while graduating as leaders ready to meet future workforce demands in meaningful ways.

The universities said they will measure the project’s results through course-completion and student-retention data, AI-literacy gains, faculty participation in training and the implementation of shared academic and technology resources.

Articles.Title: Mount Saint Mary’s to Expand Ethical AI Education with Federal Grant

stories.headline_source: Mount Saint Mary’s to Expand Ethical AI Education with Federal Grant

stories.Headline: MicroVision integrates its IRIS lidar into Kodiak AI's sixth-generation autonomous trucking platform
stories.Summary:
MicroVision, Inc. announced on November 16, 2026 a partnership with Kodiak AI, Inc. involving the integration of MicroVision's IRIS long-range lidar sensor into Kodiak's autonomous driving solution. MicroVision is based in Orlando, FL and Kodiak AI is based in Mountain View, CA. MicroVision trades on Nasdaq under MVIS and Kodiak AI trades on Nasdaq under KDK. The announcement was issued by Newswire.com at 13:00 UTC on November 16, 2026. MicroVision described itself as a leader in advanced perception solutions and Kodiak AI as a leading provider of Physical AI-powered autonomous vehicle technology.

MicroVision's IRIS lidar is currently integrated into Kodiak's sixth-generation autonomous platform. Kodiak will use that platform to launch its unsupervised driverless long-haul commercial service by the end of 2026. IRIS lidar supports Kodiak's plans for scaling long-haul deployments throughout 2027. MicroVision's lidar provides long-range perception with reliable detection beyond 250 meters. Kodiak's technology was already deployed in 37 trucks as of Nov. 3 in a customer-owned-and-operated fleet the release calls the largest of its kind in the world.

Kodiak's autonomous driving system relies on a modular SensorPod architecture that integrates lidar, cameras, and radar into a compact, serviceable unit designed for rapid deployment and uptime. Jamie Hoffacker, Senior Vice President of Hardware at Kodiak, said the key to deploying driverless trucks at scale is ensuring every component performs in the real world, not just in controlled environments. Hoffacker said MicroVision's lidar has demonstrated the performance and robustness required to support Kodiak's commercial operations today. Hoffacker said the lidar plays an important role in enabling the Kodiak Driver. Glen DeVos, MicroVision CEO, said this is not a pilot and is a commercial operation running every day.

DeVos said Kodiak has built one of the most advanced autonomous trucking platforms in operation today. DeVos said the partnership reflects what it takes to move from autonomy as a concept to autonomy at scale. Field validation across Kodiak's commercial operations demonstrated IRIS performance under extreme vibration, dust, weather, and lighting conditions. That validation provided the durability and reliability required for 24/7 driverless operation. Kodiak's platform continues to expand across long-haul freight, industrial trucking, and defense.

Kodiak's commercial deployment in the Permian Basin is supported by a binding 100-truck order from Atlas Energy Solutions. Fleet scaling is expected through 2026 and beyond. MicroVision's next-generation HALO lidar platform is aligned with Kodiak's future system architecture. Kodiak in 2024 became the first company to deploy driverless technology in customer-owned driverless semi-trucks. Commercial partners and customers include Atlas Energy Solutions, IKEA, Bridgestone, Werner Enterprises, C.R. England, General Dynamics Land Systems, and Roehl Transport.

MicroVision said its engineering centers are in the U.S. and Germany. Kodiak commercializes its technology through a Driver-as-a-Service business model and strategic partnerships. The release lists forward-looking statements including Kodiak's expectations regarding the timing of launching driverless trucks for long-haul highways operations. The release also lists Kodiak's expectations regarding the timing of completion of work on its highway launch safety case. The release does not give the date of the launch within the end of 2026 or the terms of the partnership.
