stories.Headline: Horizon3.ai launches Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab and names Z. Berkay Celik as its director
stories.Summary:
Horizon3.ai announced on Thursday that it has established the Adversarial Intelligence Frontier Lab, a research facility that will investigate how artificial intelligence can help cybersecurity teams find weaknesses in computer networks, respond to intrusions and evaluate defensive measures in live environments. The AI-native proactive security company said the lab will draw on data from its NodeZero security tests to study the safe and effective use of autonomous offensive and defensive agents. Z. Berkay Celik, an associate professor of computer science at Purdue University, will serve as the lab's inaugural director. Celik co-directs the Purdue Security Laboratory and has worked with universities, companies and government agencies on research efforts, studying how complex software and systems can be compromised.

A central research priority for the lab is establishing safeguards for autonomous security agents, including methods for evaluating their performance, restricting their activities and reversing actions when necessary. Another initiative involves creating customer-specific cyberworld models that give red team and blue team agents a shared source of operational context and memory. Researchers will also investigate how advanced AI models could speed up vulnerability discovery and how malicious actors might coordinate groups of AI agents to conduct attacks. The lab will further examine whether offensive and defensive agents working together can shorten the process of exploiting a weakness, deploying a patch and confirming that it works.

The research will extend to critical infrastructure through Horizon3.ai's Cyber Resilience Centers of Excellence, which will operate under the lab and apply findings to industries where cyber disruptions could affect national security or economic activity. Horizon3.ai plans to base its research on evidence gathered from actual security assessments rather than relying primarily on digital twins or sensor telemetry, which the company says are common in existing AI security research. Its customer base includes more than 7,000 organizations, ranging from federal agencies and local hospitals to large banks and advanced manufacturers, and these customers conduct hundreds of thousands of NodeZero tests on production systems. According to Horizon3.ai, those tests generate an estimated 30 billion tokens of labeled, anonymized attack-and-defense data each day, documenting configurations of services behind customer firewalls, commands executed during attacks, their outcomes and the reactions of defensive security tools.

Snehal Antani, the company's CEO and co-founder, said Horizon3.ai has spent years collecting the attack-and-defense data required to research these systems. In August, Stephen Gates, a principal security subject matter expert at Horizon3.ai, said autonomous, proactive security testing could help agencies identify and prioritize the risks that pose the greatest threat, writing that NodeZero carries out real attacks using the same tactics adversaries use and is designed to run safely in production environments. In May 2025, Horizon3.ai received Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program High Authorization for NodeZero Federal, which provides autonomous penetration testing that meets government security and compliance requirements. The company also partnered with Intelligent Waves in 2024 to offer penetration testing to the Department of War and the intelligence community through Shadow, powered by NodeZero, an offering designed to run real-time network security assessments and verify fixes immediately.

Articles.Title: Horizon3.ai to Advance AI Cybersecurity Research With New Lab

stories.Headline: FuelCell Energy joins federal StabilityMax program to test fuel cells for AI data centers
stories.Summary:
FuelCell Energy, a fuel cell company headquartered on Great Pasture Road in Danbury near the Bethel border, will take part in a three-year federally funded program to test whether fuel cells can provide electricity to data centers where there are rapid fluctuations in power consumption. The company announced the project in a release dated Nov 13, 2026, reported by staff writer Rob Ryser. The program is known as StabilityMax. Under the project, FuelCell Energy will develop a fuel cell test facility in Danbury, creating a national laboratory-supported testbed for evaluating integrated power solutions for AI data centers. The federal government wants to know whether fuel cells, which already power commercial and industrial facilities, can handle the heavy demands of artificial intelligence data centers.

The project runs three years and is led by the U.S. Department of Energy's National Laboratories of the Rockies. FuelCell Energy reported 425 employees worldwide last year, most of them at the company's Danbury headquarters and its Torrington manufacturing plant. FuelCell planned to keep its staffing levels the same. Details about the StabilityMax grant program, such as how much federal money is involved, were not disclosed. The pairing of fuel cells with data centers made news in October when a developer proposed to reinvigorate a 1.3-million-square-foot office structure in Danbury by bringing in a data center and using fuel cells to power it.

Mayor Roberto Alves said Thursday that FuelCell Energy's participation in the national research effort is a strong example of the innovation and expertise rooted in Danbury. Alves said he was pleased to see a Danbury company working with leading national labs on the challenge and looked forward to learning what the project demonstrates about performance, cost and the effects on the electric grid. Kathleen Blomquist, the company's director of communications, said the project isn't about testing whether fuel cells can power data centers because they can. Blomquist said the question is how to optimize a fuel cell-based power system for the rapidly changing demands of AI infrastructure, including how fuel cells, batteries, power electronics and advanced controls work together as computing loads fluctuate. Zhiwen Ma, a principal investigator at the National Laboratories of the Rockies, said fuel cells combined with data centers provide unique solutions to meet the power demands of AI infrastructure.

Ma said that through the project, NLR will help demonstrate how integrated fuel cell systems can rapidly respond to data center power needs while limiting impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers. Shankar Achanta, chief product and technology officer at FuelCell, said the insights gained through the work will help optimize system designs, validate performance under real-world conditions, and support future deployment of fuel cell-based solutions for digital infrastructure. The company's release said that as AI adoption accelerates, data centers are driving unprecedented demand for electricity and creating rapid fluctuations in power consumption. A data center is an umbrella term for computer processing plants that support all the ways artificial intelligence is used today. Public concern about energy usage by data centers has made headlines across Connecticut and the region.

A fuel cell makes electricity from fuel and air, eliminating the need to burn fuel. The company's headquarters sits on the city's east end. A FuelCell Energy power plant stands on Triangle Street in Danbury. The three-year project isn't as much about testing whether fuel cells work but about applying the technology to the next level. The federal government also wants the work to limit impacts to the utility grid and ratepayers.

The articles do not say when the three-year project begins or ends. The articles do not disclose how much federal money is involved in the StabilityMax grant program. The articles do not say what results the test facility is expected to produce or when. The articles do not say whether the October proposal for the 1.3-million-square-foot Danbury office structure is connected to the StabilityMax project. The articles do not say what the national laboratory-supported testbed will cost or who beyond FuelCell Energy will run it.

Articles.Title: Can fuel cells meet the power demands of AI data centers? Feds invest in Danbury company to find out - Stamford Advocate

The piece said only that Findlay still plans AI rules and that a proposal is expected soon, so the changes the rules would bring remain unknown from the article. The context is thin, because the article did not explain why Findlay wants AI rules or what prompted the plan. It did not say what happens next beyond the expectation of a proposal soon. stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a Nasdaq debut to raise over 90 billion dollars
stories.Summary:
Nathan Chen left the Beijing based company Moonshot AI last month. He joined Discovery Loop, which is a new AI start-up based in Palo Alto. This move happened while Silicon Valley feared China was gaining ground in AI. The United States AI economy is currently in crisis due to turmoil. A scandal at Nvidia cost former chief executive Jensen Huang his job.

Anthropic plans a Nasdaq debut this week to raise over 90 billion dollars. Google and Microsoft are investors in this sale of stock for the firm. Z.ai raised 558 million dollars in January on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. It later raised 9 billion dollars through two more offerings of shares. Alibaba lowered membership fees from 28 yuan to .0015 cents using Li Jiaqi.

Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. Alice Huang was a top executive at the Singapore based firm Megaspeed. U.S. officials investigated Megaspeed for illegally funneling Nvidia chips into China. Lawmakers now plan to tighten chip export restrictions in a defense package. They want to close loopholes used by Chinese firms to get chips.

Kendra Schaefer says Chinese firms have not tried to beat U.S. intelligence. Martin Chorzempa says there is zero evidence AI is spreading faster in China. Unitree CEO Wang Xingxing praised the OpenAI ChatGPT-6 Astra model for humanoid robots. Lao Gan Ma faced boycotts after reports that AI caused hundreds of layoffs. The company denied these claims about workers losing their jobs to technology.

The Communist Party wants AI to fix mounting economic challenges in China. Beijing aims to spread AI through every aspect of society by 2035. The government bans AI content that distorts history or manipulates public opinion. New guidelines from last month provide job training for workers displaced by AI. Regulators may now block AI ventures that cause large scale job losses.

American firms enjoy more capital and better infrastructure than their Chinese rivals. Chinese companies focus on lower cost products rather than cutting edge intelligence. The U.S. government continues to restrict the export of advanced Nvidia chips. It remains unclear if China will block American AI models from operating. The articles leave open if the two countries are in a race.

stories.Headline: Warsh opens first task force hearing on AI and the US job market
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh started a landmark hearing on Monday, November 16, 2026. He led the first meeting of a task force examining artificial intelligence. The session focused on how this technology could reshape the US job market. Warsh explored whether AI will fuel growth or disrupt employment. The event took place at the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference.

The San Francisco Federal Reserve hosted the conference for the newly formed task force. Warsh established five task forces, including this one, to help the Fed set policy. He assembled Marc Andreessen of Andreessen Horowitz, Microsoft CEO Asha Sharma, and Stanford professor Charles Jones. Jones is currently on leave from Anthropic to serve on this specific team. These task force heads operate independently to provide candid feedback to policymakers.

Warsh stated that the widespread adoption of this technology will have a significant economic impact. He noted that these changes will have important implications for future monetary policy. The Chairman said policymakers must be mindful that great opportunities rarely come without risk. He described his goal as humble, which is simply to ask the right questions. Warsh believes that overlooked risks could be highly disruptive and economically costly.

Warsh questioned if the democratization of specialized knowledge will raise general standards of living. He asked if AI will make it harder or easier to achieve price stability. The Chairman wants to know the near, medium, and long term implications for jobs. He is concerned about whether AI will drive productivity gains for the US. These answers will matter greatly for the dual mandate of the Federal Reserve.

Warsh referred to AI as super intelligence, or SI, during the landmark hearing. He compared it to electricity and the internal combustion engine, but noted a difference. He said SI might change the speed of innovation by automating the creation of ideas. This could sustain growth at levels substantially higher than the long run average. He believes this innovation differs from general purpose technologies of the past.

One scenario involves broad economic gains and inflation adjusted GDP growth above the average. Another scenario suggests widespread automation could push the unemployment rate higher through job displacement. A third scenario involves a stock market bust and economic slowdown if AI disappoints. Warsh intends to interrogate the reality of these possibilities by listening to field experts. The articles leave open when the AI surge will start or eventually taper.

Articles.Title: Warsh kicks off first task force hearing on how AI could fuel growth or disrupt jobs

stories.headline_source: Warsh kicks off first task force hearing on how AI could fuel growth or disrupt jobs

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid investigation into relationship with suspected Chinese agent
stories.Summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned on November 15, 2026, following an investigation into his personal relationship with a Chinese businesswoman. Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean cloud company Megaspeed, was suspected by United States intelligence of working for Beijing. The investigation focused on whether Megaspeed helped divert advanced Nvidia processors to China, which would violate strict export controls. This situation highlights the vulnerability of national security when strategic power is concentrated within private technology corporations.

The controversy involves the distribution of graphics processing units that are essential for military research and artificial intelligence. A Reuters report from November 13 identified over $3 billion in Chinese computing projects that utilized these restricted processors. These findings suggest that Chinese firms may bypass direct chip export bans by using overseas data centers. The United States government has spent years tightening restrictions to prevent China from gaining a technological advantage in AI.

Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that the Justice Department has not concluded that Alice Huang was a spy. There is currently no public evidence that Nvidia's proprietary information or national security secrets were compromised. Beijing has rejected all espionage allegations, and the relationship may have been a personal affair without intelligence dimensions. Officials are now questioning how to safeguard a technological ecosystem where private interests often conflict with national security priorities.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal agencies to call AI super intelligence as local leaders debate rebranding
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order in September mandating that artificial intelligence be known as “super intelligence,” arguing that AI makes the technology sound fake. The order applies only to federal agencies and departments, and some have already adopted the term. The effort has some state and local leaders wondering if they should follow the federal government’s lead. Speakers at the Public Technology Institute’s GOVIT Leadership Summit and Symposium in Minneapolis this week said deemphasizing AI as a term might be an interesting path forward. They also said government leaders should spend more time selling the technology and its benefits to the public, regardless of what it is called.

The order argues that so-called “SI” better reflects the technology’s immense capabilities. State and local leaders are reckoning with AI’s impacts on the government workforce, the future of work, service delivery and the backlash against data centers. Last week voters in numerous localities rejected ballot initiatives related to data centers, which provide the infrastructure AI operates on but have been blamed for rising energy costs and other impacts on local communities. Williamsburg, Virginia CIO Mark Barham said the government there has taken to calling data centers “co-location facilities.” Barham said he knows that if leaders disclose they are meeting with data center vendors, “alarm bells go off” in the community.

John Matelski, chief information officer at the National Association of Counties, said during a panel discussion that AI was here 50 years ago and was just called machine learning or something else. Matelski said he has looked at this not as artificial intelligence, more as augmented intelligence. He said he has never liked the term “artificial intelligence.” PTI Senior Fellow Alan Shark suggested on stage that leaders instead be “talking about office automation.” Shark said leaders should “talk about solutions and leave out the word ‘AI’ because that’s a variable.”

Shark said there are two universes, one internal where government must use a language its people understand, and the external one where he sees AI as a negative term. He said people have a right to be fearful, citing AI escaping, destroying systems, apologizing that it destroyed a system, and admitting it failed to follow its own instructions. Amy Cheney, Bloomington, Minnesota’s CIO, said her city has seen a dramatic uptick in people using AI to submit requests under the Freedom of Information Act. Cheney said requesters are using AI against the city to create really complicated requests that staff cannot keep up with, and the city is looking at how to automate that process.

Ben Bowen, vice president of U.S. sales at software company Claro Enterprise Solutions, said you can call it AI, super intelligence or whatever you like, but it is efficiency that it is going to help create. Bowen said he does not want to say there is one broad stroke, don’t say the word “AI,” but it is maybe how to create efficiency within the worlds everyone lives in today. For some time, government leaders at the state and local level have argued that messaging around AI should focus on how it helps make employees’ work easier and more efficient. Those who work for small and rural governments have said previously that the technology has given them “breathing room.” Others argued that focusing on AI’s benefits will help sell it more to the public.

Cheney said a lot of work lies ahead on FOIA requests, and that automation is the key, and getting staff to recognize AI is not going away. She said the city has to figure out ways of being smarter and how it is addressing the demands it is seeing now. Matelski said government must recognize that the technology is here to stay and embrace it carefully, with boundaries on it. The articles leave open whether state and local governments will follow the federal government’s lead on the rebrand. The articles also leave open how the automation of FOIA processes will proceed.

Articles.Title: Does state-and-local AI need a rebrand? - Route Fifty

stories.Headline: Math Ph.D. students find most peers less likely to stay in math after AI advances
stories.Summary:
Three math Ph.D. students, Anna Brandenberger, Hanna Mularczyk and Dora Woodruff, launched an online Google Forms survey after AI cracked problems that mathematicians had chased for decades, and the survey spread quickly through word of mouth and department mailing lists. Woodruff said they needed something that features the voices of graduate students and postdocs as well. The results, described in a preprint paper, drew 268 responses from nearly 60 institutions and paint a stark picture of a community in limbo. Respondents are largely frustrated and anxious that AI is taking the field for a ride, yet they are divided on what to do about it. Seven in 10 respondents say they are now less likely to remain in math, with broad consensus that AI will make tenure-track jobs harder to get.

Two-thirds report feeling less motivated to work on their research, with the growing possibility of a large language model beating them to their goals. About half are optimistic about AI's potential for mathematics, while a third oppose its use, either outright or for creative mathematical work. Among the optimists, four out of five say they are excited about AI in theory but strongly opposed to how things are unfolding in practice, and just 13 percent of all respondents are happy with the current trajectory. Woodruff said people have told her things like "I feel useless," and she noted that math is a lot of people's identities, not just their jobs. Some, she said, feel that not only does their work not matter, but their minds and their creativity do not matter.

She summed up what many early-career colleagues are thinking: in one year or two years, she does not know if she is going to have a job or funding. Even among the respondents who do use AI, which is nearly all of them, many describe feeling pressured to use it to keep pace, resulting in a generation reluctantly mastering the very technology they fear could make them obsolete. Woodruff cautioned that the voluntary survey is not representative of all young mathematicians, and nearly all of its responses arrived before OpenAI published AI-assisted solutions to hundreds of open problems in October. She said the survey shows that this headline-making year for math has come at a huge cost. She also said that a lot of people outside of math are looking at what is happening in math now, and that so far the field is not doing a particularly inspiring job.

stories.Headline: UN chief Guterres warns autonomous weapons cross a moral red line as Geneva talks open
stories.Summary:
Negotiations on possible rules for lethal autonomous weapons, often called killer robots, are underway at the United Nations in Geneva, where the conference on Certain Conventional Weapons meets only once every five years. Supporters of controls say this week's meeting is the last best chance to agree rules before it is too late, as warfare technology has advanced rapidly in recent years. Some experts warn the world is just months away from having weapons that can choose targets and decide to kill on their own. AI-assisted weapons have already been used in Ukraine and Gaza, though those are still controlled remotely by humans.

Humanitarian organizations say the decision to kill, and responsibility for it, must stay in human hands, and the United Nations, the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Pope have all called for legally binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned that letting fully autonomous weapons kill would cross a moral red line. The Red Cross worries that autonomous weapons cannot fully respect the Geneva Conventions, because war is chaotic and situations change rapidly, and soldiers who are wounded or surrendering can no longer be targeted. Legal adviser Georgia Haines said the risk is that such weapons cannot understand contextual signals the way a human does, so misidentification of a target is highly likely.

Human rights groups warn that the technology behind AI-assisted weapons is becoming cheaper and easier to use, and that greater military adoption raises the danger of proliferation and use by terrorist groups or repressive regimes. At least 50 countries, including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany, are calling for a strict timetable to agree binding rules. The United States, Russia and Israel have indicated they will oppose legally binding rules, with Washington proposing a five-year timetable to draft non-binding guidelines instead. Under President Trump, doubts about international law have grown, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned against quoting laws to men with swords.

U.N. negotiations on limiting specific weapons are supposed to be conducted by consensus, which was achieved in 1995 for a ban on blinding lasers but has proved elusive since. With landmines, countries frustrated by delay took negotiations outside the U.N. process to create the Ottawa Convention. This week there may be a compromise: a longer or even open-ended negotiating period to come up with rules that individual states can adopt as binding or non-binding. For diplomats supporting such a solution it is a way to ensure at least some progress, while campaigners see it as less than ideal, with one likening it to kicking a very dangerous can down the road.

Articles.Title: U.N. talks seek to rein in 'killer robots' as fears over AI weapons grow

stories.Headline: Dreamteam raises $53M to build AI-native CRM and signs over 100 customers
stories.Summary:
Dreamteam, a San Francisco-based startup founded in 2025 by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million in seed and Series A funding to build an AI-native CRM aimed at challenging Salesforce and HubSpot. The seed round was led by Together Fund and the Series A by Accel, with participation from Premji Invest, though the company declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation. The company was co-founded by CEO Anand Venkatraman, Senthil Kanthaswamy, who spent more than nine years at Freshworks and most recently served as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy, who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks. Venkatraman said he encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including stints at Salesforce and Freshworks, because salespeople spent considerable time updating records while managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business.

Dreamteam's CRM is built around what it calls the Company Brain, which acts as virtual memory by pulling together information from emails, meetings and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers. The startup has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling, with most paying for the service, and it has replaced established platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare company DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers. The advertising sales team at media streaming company Plex chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, and Plex co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski called its ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company a game changer.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but said their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software, describing the shift as an electric-car moment for systems of record. Kanthaswamy said startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI, since rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time. The venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz argued in a blog post earlier this year that existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a new generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them. Dreamteam plans to expand beyond sales into onboarding, customer support and upselling, and it already offers a feature called Magic Apps that lets users create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions without writing code. The startup employs more than 35 people, with engineering based in Chennai and go-to-market operations in the United States, and Kanthaswamy said it aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose current revenue.

Articles.Title: Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

stories.Headline: Mayo Clinic appoints AI program leader Matthew Callstrom as next CEO
stories.Summary:
The Mayo Clinic Board of Trustees announced this past Friday that Dr. Matthew R. Callstrom, a radiologist who has led the health system's AI program in recent years, will succeed Dr. Gianrico Farrugia as president and chief executive officer in the new year. Callstrom first joined Mayo Clinic more than two decades ago and has held a wide array of leadership roles across clinical practice, research and innovation since 2002. He has served on Mayo Clinic's Board of Governors and Board of Trustees, and most recently was medical director for Mayo Clinic Strategy. He previously served as interim chief strategy officer and as chair of the Department of Radiology at Mayo Clinic in Rochester.

Farrugia will remain CEO through December 31 and will work closely with Callstrom as he moves into the new leadership role. Farrugia has led Mayo Clinic for the past seven years, a period that included embracing cloud-enabled artificial intelligence and the launch of Mayo Clinic Platform. Callstrom's own work has led to hundreds of publications and patents, and he has served as president of the Society of Interventional Oncology. He earned degrees in chemical engineering and chemistry from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Harvard, and earned his medical degree from Mayo Clinic Alix School of Medicine, with residency and fellowship at Mayo Clinic in Rochester.

Richard K. Davis, chair of the Board of Trustees, said Callstrom's leadership across patient care, research, strategy and innovation prepares him exceptionally well to lead Mayo Clinic into its next chapter. Davis said Callstrom understands Mayo Clinic as a physician caring for patients, a scientist translating discovery into clinical care and a leader shaping strategy for the future. Farrugia called it the privilege of his career to serve as president and CEO and said Callstrom knows Mayo Clinic deeply and has the vision and experience to build on the progress made. Callstrom said he was deeply honored to lead Mayo Clinic in this moment and that the organization has always been at its best when it brings the full power of its clinical expertise, science and innovation to the needs of patients.

Callstrom has been vocal about AI's potential to enable advances in research and care when properly deployed. He said Mayo's aspiration for AI is to meaningfully improve patient outcomes by detecting disease early enough to intervene, and that what was once a hypothetical is now becoming reality thanks to AI and advanced computing. He previously explained why Mayo chose Cerebras as its first generative AI collaborator, citing its large-scale, domain-specific AI expertise to accelerate breakthrough insights for patients. He told Reuters that weighing all the factors for each patient requires a lot of experience, and that is where AI comes in to augment that.

stories.Headline: Gary Marcus says the AI bubble has popped as Oracle falls about 61 percent
stories.Summary:
Gary Marcus wrote on November 16, 2026 that the AI bubble appears to have finally popped, pointing to Oracle's roughly 61 percent decline since he called the OpenAI deal "peak bubble" the previous September. Tech stocks kept falling sharply that day after a rout the week before, and even Axios acknowledged before the market opened that the jig was up. Ben Thompson of Stratechery published what Marcus described as an obituary for Jensen Huang, saying his demise ended many things including Nvidia's long-term prospects and the AI bubble. Marcus also cited a Wall Street Journal article reporting that Nvidia's days as an open checkbook for the AI economy were numbered.

The Journal article said interim CEO Colette Kress is expected to rein in deals after a stretch in which Nvidia aggressively financed computing deals and startup investments. Marcus argued that the LLM companies still lack a technical moat and still struggle to be profitable, which was true in 2023 and remains true. He said Nvidia could not sustain its growth indefinitely because you cannot sell chips endlessly if the buyers are not making profits from them. He also noted hints that some funny business in Asia may have made things look better than they were, and that circular financing made it hard to tell what was really happening.

Marcus wrote that it pretty much looks like game over for the current AI bubble, adding that the midterms no doubt contributed and that the free pass AI companies had in the first half of the Trump era is over. He said the critical question is whether any of this affects Thursday's planned IPO for Anthropic, or whether people simply leap from one fad to another as they did from crypto to NFTs to generative AI. He said the financial fundamentals do not justify the hoped-for valuation once liabilities are factored in, and that selling a deeply speculative IPO amid an AI stock crash will not be easy. He added that he cannot say whether there are enough hopeful suckers who are bad at reading profit-and-loss and liability statements.

stories.Headline: Audible launches an AI audio feature that summarizes books for listeners
stories.Summary:
Audible, which is owned by Amazon, launched an audio discovery feature on Monday that gives listeners a short spoken overview of a book before they decide to listen to it. The overview combines a summary of the book's themes, a roundup of what readers liked about it, and commentary from an Audible editor or the author, and it plays alongside the narrated sample. The summary audio is generated with AI, while the commentary is taken from recordings of past Audible interviews, according to the company. Audible says the expanded introduction is meant to help people choose their next listen, especially when they are on the go and do not have time to scroll through comments or reviews. The feature will first be available for select English-language titles in the United States, and it will arrive with new personalized collections based on each user's listening taste.

Audible says the overviews will also draw on other public materials, such as synopses and metadata, and the reader reactions come from publicly available reviews. The launch follows last month's release of AI tools that let users interact with characters, catch up through recaps, or ask questions about a story. Those Recaps and Ask a Question features are now expanding to more U.S. titles and will become more broadly available in December, but only for customers who bought a title or have it through their Audible membership. Andy Tsao, Audible's chief product and analytics officer, said picking your next listen should feel like getting a tip from a friend. He said the feature gives listeners a quick audio take on why a title might suit them, from editors, fellow listeners, or the author.

He added that some of the best listening experiences are rare finds and hidden gems, and the company wants those discoveries to happen more often and more easily. The article notes that pulling only positive remarks could limit users' exposure to negative reviews, though it says further testing would be needed to see if that is the case. The launch comes as Audible faces new competition in the audiobooks market, particularly from Spotify, which added audiobook listening hours to its paid subscriptions and expanded that service to more than 180 markets last month. Audible's approach echoes how Amazon already uses AI on its storefront, where the technology summarizes buyer reviews so shoppers can quickly grasp the pros and cons of an item. The article does not say what Audible plans beyond the December expansion of its other AI features.

Articles.Title: Audible turns to AI to help users discover audiobooks

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public on Thursday in an offering estimated to raise about $64.35 billion
stories.Summary:
Capital Economics wrote on Monday that the AI stock boom is “in its final stages,” and Anthropic is going public on Thursday in a deal estimated to raise about $64.35 billion at the top of its range. That is nearly twice what every U.S. IPO raised together last quarter, according to Renaissance Capital. The economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter while employers added an average of 48,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September, before a 165,000 gain in October. AI spending drove more than half of business-investment growth in the first three quarters of the year, Goldman Sachs estimates. Bloomberg reported on Nov. 12 that the Anthropic deal was about six times oversubscribed, days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO.

J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s David Kelly sees real GDP growth slowing to 1.6% over the next four quarters, with hiring stuck near 50,000 a month. Morgan Stanley’s research digest on Monday, summarizing chief U.S. economist Michael Gapen’s 2027 outlook, put the breakeven at about 50,000 jobs a month. Federal Reserve economists Seth Murray and Ivan Vidangos think labor force growth “could be near-zero starting this year,” which would put the breakeven near zero too. Goldman estimates AI investment will add 0.6 percentage points to “true” GDP growth in 2027 and only 0.2 points to the GDP that actually gets counted. Gapen sees hyperscalers spending $1.6 trillion on capex in 2027, adding 0.9 points to growth.

Capital Economics markets economist Joe Maher pointed to falling share issuance and “investors’ waning appetite for new shares of AI-firms at lofty valuations,” and wrote that Anthropic is “a key test.” Kelly said two years of 2.3% growth “should have led to a monthly gain of roughly 155,000 net new jobs,” and mainly blames “a lack of available workers due to a sharp reversal of immigration policy.” Gapen’s outlook says the AI money is mostly propping up upper-income households, while low- and middle-income consumers lead the slowdown, and he expects AI disruption and tighter Fed policy to keep hiring subdued. Goldman calls today’s job market “low-hire, low-fire,” a phrase made famous by former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. Goldman economists expect that job market to hold for about another year “before AI displacement begins to have a larger impact in subsequent years.”

Morgan Stanley sees 2.5% growth in 2027 and Goldman 2.4%, against JPMAM’s 1.6% over the next four quarters. Nvidia is still buying about $10 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the offering, and Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the first two of 22 underwriters named on the cover of Anthropic’s prospectus. Employers hired at a 3.4% rate in September, according to the Labor Department’s JOLTS report, and the unemployment rate for 20- to 24-year-olds was 7.5% in October, against 4.1% overall. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found in August that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs was about 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed work. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the 12 months through October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said, and JPMAM points out that “despite a tight labor market, real year-over-year wage growth has been negative for seven consecutive months.”

Productivity in the nonfarm business sector rose at a 3.6% annual rate in the third quarter, the BLS said Nov. 5, while labor’s share of output fell to 53.0%, the lowest since the series began in 1947. Indeed Hiring Lab’s Aubrey Woessner wrote that AI investment “appear[s] to be contributing” to the productivity gains, but that “increased labor productivity has not yet translated into higher real pay.” Apollo Global Management economists Sania Edlich and Torsten Slok sorted occupations by how heavily their tasks show up in Claude conversations, using Anthropic’s own Economic Index, and found that after 2023 real wage growth in the most-exposed occupations has run about 6.7 percentage points behind less-exposed jobs, with no statistically significant effect on employment. Workers in the lowest wage quartile of those jobs took the biggest hit, about 10.7 points, and the authors wrote that “the first measurable labor market effect of AI adoption has been wage compression rather than employment displacement.” Apollo estimates about 5.8 million workers are in the most-exposed occupations, and the authors caution that the period “may be partially confounded by post-pandemic labor market dynamics.”

Advertised salaries in the most AI-exposed occupations have risen 46% since 2021, against 25% for the least exposed, according to Indeed data reported in September. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index stood at 51.0 in its preliminary November reading, and survey director Joanne Hsu wrote that “about 57% spontaneously mentioned that their living standards have been eroded by high prices.” Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s co-founder and CEO, and Google CEO Sundar Pichai spoke to the press after a September 29 meeting with US President Donald Trump and technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House. Generative AI was used for research assistance and/or transcription of the article, and the reporter independently reported and verified the factual claims, with a human editor reviewing it before publication. The article gives no date for when Anthropic’s shares begin trading beyond Thursday, and no figure for what the offering would raise below the top of its range.
